title: Lecture 1: Foundations of Convex Sets and Functions
description: This lecture introduces the geometric and analytic pillars of convex optimization, focusing on set definitions, function properties, and tests for convexity.
content:
Learning objectives: Understand how to prove set and function convexity, recognize Hessian positive semidefiniteness, and apply calculus rules to preserve convexity. 

Convex optimization revolves around sets and functions that lack local traps. A set is convex if the line segment connecting any two points in the set remains entirely inside it. A function is convex if its epigraph forms a convex set, leading to the Jensen inequality. To verify convexity in practical applications, we rely on first-order and second-order conditions. If a function is twice differentiable, it is convex if and only if its Hessian matrix is positive semidefinite everywhere in its domain. 

Consider the function f(x) = exp(x) plus x cubed, restricted to the positive domain x greater than zero. Let us compute its derivatives to test convexity. The first derivative is f_prime(x) = exp(x) plus three times x squared. The second derivative is f_double_prime(x) = exp(x) plus six times x. For all x greater than zero, exp(x) is strictly positive and six times x is strictly positive, meaning the second derivative is strictly greater than zero. Thus, the Hessian is positive definite, proving the function is strictly convex on the positive domain. 

In class exercise: Determine whether the function f(x, y) = x squared plus two times y squared minus two times x times y is convex by computing its eigenvalues.

title: Lecture 2: Canonical Problem Classes and Standard Forms
description: This lecture categorizes optimization problems into standard families, identifying linear, quadratic, conic, and semidefinite programs.
content:
Learning objectives: Classify optimization problems into standard forms, identify conic structures, and map real-world tasks to tractable problem classes. 

Recognizing the exact problem class dictates which algorithm can solve it efficiently. Standard convex optimization minimizes a convex objective subject to convex inequality and affine equality constraints. Within this framework, several notable subclasses exist. Least squares and linear programs feature completely explicit analytical or simplex-based solutions. Moving beyond linear boundaries, quadratic programs handle quadratic objectives with linear constraints, while second-order cone programs manage hyperboloid constraints useful in robust filtering. Semidefinite programs optimize over positive semidefinite matrix cones, representing the apex of tractable convex paradigms. 

Let us analyze a concrete quadratic program: minimize the objective function 0.5 times x_1 squared plus x_2 squared minus x_1 minus x_2, subject to the linear constraint x_1 plus x_2 less than or equal to one, with x_1 and x_2 greater than or equal to zero. Writing the Lagrangian reveals the optimality conditions. By checking the constraints, if the inequality constraint is inactive, the unconstrained minimizer is x_1 = 1 and x_2 = 0.5. Substituting these values into the constraint gives 1 plus 0.5 = 1.5, which violates the constraint x_1 plus x_2 less than or equal to one. Hence, the constraint is active, and the true optimal point lies on the boundary where x_1 plus x_2 equals one. 

In class exercise: Formulate a portfolio optimization problem with a variance objective and a budget constraint as a quadratic program.

title: Lecture 3: Lagrangian Duality and Slater Constraint Qualification
description: This lecture explores Lagrangian duality, weak and strong duality theorems, and the conditions guaranteeing zero duality gap.
content:
Learning objectives: Formulate the dual function, interpret weak and strong duality geometrically, and apply Slater condition to convex problems. 

Every constrained optimization problem possesses a dual counterpart that provides a lower bound on the optimal primal value. We construct the Lagrangian by augmenting the objective with weighted constraint violations using Lagrange multipliers. Maximizing this Lagrangian with respect to the primal variables yields the dual function, which is always concave regardless of the primal problem convexity. Weak duality states that the dual optimal value is always less than or equal to the primal optimal value. Strong duality, where the duality gap is zero, occurs under constraint qualifications such as Slater condition, which requires the existence of a strictly feasible interior point. 

Consider the primal problem: minimize x squared subject to x squared minus four less than or equal to zero. The Lagrangian is L(x, lambda) = x squared plus lambda times (x squared minus four). To find the dual function, we minimize L with respect to x by setting the derivative to zero, yielding two times x times (one plus lambda) = 0. Assuming lambda is greater than minus one, the minimizer is x = 0. Substituting x = 0 back into the Lagrangian gives the dual function g(lambda) = minus four times lambda for lambda greater than or equal to zero. Maximizing g(lambda) subject to lambda greater than or equal to zero gives lambda star = 0, leading to a dual optimal value of zero, matching the primal optimal value. 

In class exercise: Write down the dual function for a linear program in inequality form.

title: Lecture 4: Optimality Conditions and Iterative Algorithms
description: This lecture covers Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions and core numerical algorithms including gradient descent and interior-point methods.
content:
Learning objectives: Derive KKT conditions for constrained problems, interpret complementary slackness, and implement descent steps. 

Optimality in smooth constrained optimization is characterized by the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions: stationarity of the Lagrangian, primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementary slackness. Complementary slackness dictates that either a constraint is active or its corresponding multiplier is zero. When analytical solutions are impossible, we rely on iterative numerical algorithms. Gradient descent takes steps proportional to the negative gradient, suitable for unconstrained smooth objectives. Newton method incorporates second-order curvature information via the inverse Hessian for quadratic convergence near the optimum. Interior-point methods handle inequalities by adding barrier functions, traversing the central path to exact solutions. 

Let us review the KKT system for minimizing f(x) = x squared subject to x greater than or equal to one. We rewrite the constraint as 1 minus x less than or equal to zero. The Lagrangian is L(x, lambda) = x squared plus lambda times (1 minus x). The stationarity condition requires the derivative with respect to x to be zero, giving two times x minus lambda = 0, so lambda = two times x. The complementary slackness condition is lambda times (1 minus x) = 0. Substituting lambda gives two times x times (1 minus x) = 0. Since x = 0 violates the primal feasibility constraint x greater than or equal to zero from the problem statement, we must have x star = 1, which implies lambda star = 2. 

In class exercise: Compute the first gradient descent update step for f(x_1, x_2) = 3 times x_1 squared plus 5 times x_2 squared starting from the point (2, 3) with step size 0.1.

title: Lecture 1: Foundations of Linear Programming
description: This lecture introduces mathematical modeling, formulation of linear programs, and graphical solution techniques for two-variable optimization problems.
content:
Learning objectives: Understand how to translate a resource allocation scenario into decision variables, objective functions, and constraints. Master the graphical method to locate optimal extreme points.

Linear programming involves optimizing a linear objective function subject to linear equality and inequality constraints. Every linear program defines a geometric feasible region bounded by constraint lines. Because the objective function is linear, the optimal solution always resides at one of the corner points, or vertices, of this region.

Consider a manufacturer making two products, A and B. Product A yields a profit of 4 dollars, and Product B yields 6 dollars. Product A requires 1 hour of labor, while Product B requires 2 hours of labor. Total available labor is 10 hours per day. Furthermore, market demand limits Product B to at most 4 units per day. We formulate this as maximize 4A + 6B subject to A + 2B <= 10, B <= 4, and A >= 0, B >= 0. The boundary lines intersect at several corners. Testing the corner points: origin (0,0) gives profit 0; (0,4) gives 4(0) + 6(4) = 24; (2,4) gives 4(2) + 6(4) = 32; and (10,0) gives 4(10) + 6(0) = 40. Wait, check constraint A + 2B <= 10 at point (2,4): 2 + 2(4) = 10, which is valid. Check point (10,0): 10 + 2(0) = 10, valid. Check point (2,4) versus (10,0): profit at (10,0) is 40, while at (2,4) it is 32. Thus, producing 10 units of A and 0 units of B yields the maximum profit of 40 dollars.

In class exercise: Sketch the feasible region for maximizing 5x + 3y subject to 2x + y <= 12, x + y <= 8, and x >= 0, y >= 0. Identify all corner points and find the optimal profit.

title: Lecture 2: The Simplex Algorithm and Duality
description: This lecture explores algebraic pivoting using the simplex method, handles artificial variables via Big-M, and interprets shadow prices through duality.
content:
Learning objectives: Apply simplex tableaus with slack and artificial variables to solve higher-variable linear programs. Interpret dual variables and shadow prices for economic decision-making.

When problems exceed two variables, graphical methods fail. The simplex method algebraically navigates from one basic feasible solution to an adjacent better corner point by evaluating reduced costs. For non-standard forms with greater-than or equality constraints, we introduce slack, surplus, and artificial variables, utilizing the Big-M method to penalize artificial violations in the objective function.

Every primal maximization linear program has a dual minimization counterpart. The dual variables, also called shadow prices, measure the marginal value of relaxing resource constraints. Suppose a primal resource constraint is 3x + y <= 18 with an optimal shadow price of 2.50 dollars. This means that if the resource limit increases by 1 unit from 18 to 19, the optimal objective value will increase by 2.50 dollars, assuming the current optimal basis remains unchanged.

Consider a simple maximization of 10x + 15y subject to 2x + y <= 100 and x + 2y <= 80. Adding slack variables s1 and s2, the initial tableau sets basic variables s1 = 100 and s2 = 80 with objective value 0. Pivoting on the most negative coefficient in the objective row brings y into the basis, replacing s2 after 40 units. Continuing to optimality yields x = 36 and y = 22 with an objective value of 360 + 330 = 690.

In class exercise: Set up the initial simplex tableau for maximizing 3x + 2y subject to x + y <= 5 and 2x + y <= 8, with non-negativity.

title: Lecture 3: Transportation, Assignment, and Network Models
description: This lecture covers specialized network structures including transportation models, assignment algorithms, shortest paths, and project scheduling networks.
content:
Learning objectives: Solve transportation problems using the least cost method and assignment problems using the Hungarian method. Calculate critical paths using CPM and PERT.

Network flow structures optimize the movement of goods or timelines through interconnected nodes. The transportation problem allocates goods from supply sources to demand sinks at minimum cost, starting with feasible allocations like the northwest corner or least cost method. The assignment problem matches agents to tasks on a one-to-one basis using the Hungarian method. For project management, Critical Path Method (CPM) and Program Evaluation and Review Technique (PERT) use precedence relationships to determine the minimum completion time and identify bottleneck tasks.

Consider an assignment problem matching 3 workers to 3 tasks with the following cost matrix: Worker 1 costs [9, 2, 7], Worker 2 costs [6, 4, 3], Worker 3 costs [5, 8, 1]. To solve using the Hungarian method, we first subtract row minimums, then column minimums, and cover zeros with minimum lines. Subtracting row minimums (2, 3, 1) gives modified costs: Worker 1 [7, 0, 5], Worker 2 [3, 1, 0], Worker 3 [4, 7, 0]. Next, subtract column minimums if necessary. Finding the independent zero assignment yields: Worker 1 takes Task 2 (cost 2), Worker 2 takes Task 3 (cost 3), and Worker 3 takes Task 1 (cost 5). Total minimum cost is 2 + 3 + 5 = 10.

In class exercise: Apply the least cost method to a transportation problem with supply 30, 40; demand 20, 25, 25; and cost matrix [[2, 3, 1], [5, 4, 2]].

title: Lecture 4: Integer Programming and Advanced Topics
description: This lecture introduces integer programming via branch and bound, and provides an overview of queuing theory and decision analysis under uncertainty.
content:
Learning objectives: Formulate integer constraints and solve small mixed-integer programs using branch and bound trees. Understand basic queuing metrics and decision criteria.

Many real-world decisions require discrete choices, such as whether to build a facility or hire personnel, modeled using integer or binary variables. Linear programming relaxations allow fractional solutions, which are then branched into sub-problems enforcing integer bounds. Beyond optimization, operations research addresses probabilistic systems like waiting lines (queuing) and decisions under uncertainty using expected monetary value.

Consider maximizing 5x + 8y subject to x + y <= 6, 9x + 5y <= 45, where x and y must be integers. First, solve the continuous linear relaxation. The relaxed optimum occurs where x + y = 6 and 9x + 5y = 45. Solving this linear system: from x = 6 - y, substitute into 9(6 - y) + 5y = 45, yielding 54 - 4y = 45, so 4y = 9, giving y = 2.25 and x = 3.75. The relaxed objective value is 5(3.75) + 8(2.25) = 18.75 + 18.00 = 36.75. Since variables must be integers, we branch on x. Sub-problem 1 adds constraint x <= 3; Sub-problem 2 adds constraint x >= 4. Solving Sub-problem 1 with x <= 3 gives integer solution x = 3 and y = 3, yielding objective 5(3) + 8(3) = 39. Solving Sub-problem 2 with x >= 4 gives y = 1.8, yielding non-integer results inferior to 39. Thus, the optimal integer solution is x = 3, y = 3 with value 39.

In class exercise: Draw a branch and bound tree for maximizing 4x + 3y subject to 2x + y <= 7 with x, y being non-negative integers.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Operations Research Problem Set
description: This assignment tests student proficiency across linear programming formulation, simplex calculations, network optimization, and integer programming.
content:
Task 1: Formulate a blending problem. A refinery blends two crude oils into regular and premium gasoline. Crude A costs 40 dollars per barrel, Crude B costs 60 dollars. Regular fuel requires at least 40 percent Crude A and sells for 70 dollars. Premium fuel requires at least 60 percent Crude B and sells for 90 dollars. Total available Crude A is 500 barrels; Crude B is 400 barrels. Define variables, objective function, and all constraints. (Marks: 4)

Task 2: Solve a maximization linear program graphically and algebraically. Maximize Z = 6x + 8y subject to 5x + 2y <= 20, 3x + 5y <= 30, and x, y >= 0. Find all corner points, identify the optimal vertex, and state the shadow price of the first resource constraint assuming standard slack behavior. (Marks: 4)

Task 3: Transportation allocation. Three plants with supplies 15, 25, and 10 serve three warehouses with demands 10, 20, and 20. Unit shipping costs are [[8, 6, 10], [9, 4, 12], [5, 7, 8]]. Find an initial feasible solution using the least cost method and calculate the total shipping cost. (Marks: 4)

Task 4: Project management network. A project has five tasks with the following immediate predecessors and durations in weeks: Task A (none, 3), Task B (none, 4), Task C (A, 2), Task D (B, 5), Task E (C, D, 3). Construct the network, perform a forward and backward pass, determine the critical path, and state the total project completion time. (Marks: 4)

Task 5: Integer programming branch and bound. Maximize Z = 7x + 10y subject to -x + 3y <= 6, 7x + y <= 35, where x and y are non-negative integers. Solve the continuous relaxation, perform the first level of branching on the fractional variable, and evaluate the resulting bounds to find the optimal integer solution. (Marks: 4)

title: Lecture 1: Electrostatics and Gauss's Law
description: This session covers electric forces, the electric field concept, and the powerful application of Gauss's law for symmetric charge distributions.
content: Learning objectives: Master Coulomb's force calculations between point charges, evaluate electric fields using superposition, and apply Gauss's law to solve symmetrical geometries. Electrostatics governs the interactions of stationary electric charges. Coulomb's law establishes that the electrostatic force between two point charges is proportional to the product of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance separating them. Extending this, the electric field represents the force per unit test charge exerted at any point in space. While Coulomb's law suffices for discrete charges, calculating fields for continuous distributions often becomes analytically intractable. Gauss's law provides an elegant alternative by relating the net electric flux passing through a closed Gaussian surface directly to the charge enclosed within that surface. For example, consider a spherical shell of radius 0.05 meters carrying a total charge of 4 microcoulombs. To find the electric field at a radial distance of 0.10 meters from the center, we construct a concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius 0.10 meters. The enclosed charge is 4 microcoulombs. Using Gauss's law, the electric flux is the electric field multiplied by the surface area of our Gaussian sphere, which is 4 times pi times radius squared. Solving for the electric field yields eight point nine nine times ten to the ninth power multiplied by four microcoulombs divided by zero point one zero squared, resulting in three million five hundred ninety-six thousand newtons per coulomb radially outward. In class exercise: Calculate the electric field at a distance of 0.02 meters from a very long thin wire carrying a uniform linear charge density of 5 nanocoulombs per meter using cylindrical symmetry.

title: Lecture 2: Electric Potential and Capacitance
description: Students will explore potential energy, electric potential differences, and how charge storage devices operate with and without dielectrics.
content: Learning objectives: Compute electric potential from fields and vice versa, analyze multi-plate capacitor networks, and evaluate stored electrical energy. The electric potential is defined as the potential energy per unit charge, providing a scalar perspective that simplifies many electrostatic problems compared to vector fields. The electric field is fundamentally the negative gradient of the electric potential, meaning fields point naturally from regions of high potential to regions of low potential. Capacitors store electrical energy in this potential difference by holding equal and opposite charges on conducting plates. The capacitance depends purely on the physical geometry of the system and the surrounding material properties. Inserting an insulating dielectric material between the plates polarizes the material, effectively reducing the internal electric field and increasing the capacitance by a factor known as the dielectric constant. For example, consider a parallel plate capacitor constructed with a plate area of 0.002 square meters and a separation distance of 0.001 meters, with air between the plates. The permittivity of free space is approximately 8.854 times ten to the negative twelfth farads per meter. The capacitance is calculated as permittivity multiplied by area divided by distance, yielding 1.77 nanofarads. If this capacitor is connected to a 9 volt battery, the stored charge is capacitance multiplied by voltage, giving 15.93 nanocoulombs. The total electrostatic energy stored in the device is one-half multiplied by capacitance multiplied by voltage squared, which evaluates to approximately 71.69 microjoules. In class exercise: Determine the equivalent capacitance of a 6 microfarad capacitor connected in series with a 3 microfarad capacitor.

title: Lecture 3: Current, Circuits, and Magnetism
description: This lecture transitions into electrodynamics, examining steady currents, resistance, Kirchhoff's circuit rules, and magnetic force phenomena.
content: Learning objectives: Apply Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's laws to complex resistive networks, analyze transient charging in RC circuits, and compute magnetic forces on moving charges. Electric current represents the macroscopic flow of charge carriers through a medium. Resistance quantifies the opposition to this flow, leading to power dissipation in the form of heat. For transient systems, charging an uncharged capacitor through a resistor via a DC voltage source follows an exponential curve, where the time constant is the product of resistance and capacitance. At exactly one time constant, the capacitor reaches approximately 63 percent of its ultimate maximum charge. When these charges move, they interact with magnetic fields. A moving point charge experiences a magnetic force equal to the cross product of its velocity vector and the magnetic field vector multiplied by its charge. Similarly, a current-carrying wire experiences a macroscopic magnetic force. For example, consider a straight wire of length 0.5 meters oriented perpendicularly to a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 teslas, carrying a steady current of 3 amperes. The magnitude of the magnetic force is calculated as current multiplied by length multiplied by magnetic field multiplied by the sine of the angle between them. Since the wire is perpendicular, the sine of 90 degrees is 1. Multiplying 3 amperes by 0.5 meters by 0.4 teslas yields a magnetic force magnitude of 0.6 newtons directed out of the plane via the right-hand rule. In class exercise: Find the current flowing through a 10 ohm resistor connected across a 12 volt ideal voltage source.

title: Lecture 4: Induction, Maxwell's Equations, and Waves
description: The final lecture unifies electricity and magnetism through electromagnetic induction, displacement current, and the foundation of wave propagation.
content: Learning objectives: Apply Faraday's law of induction and Lenz's law to solve for induced electromotive forces, analyze RL circuit transients, and understand Maxwell's synthesis. Electromagnetic induction proves that changing magnetic environments can generate electric currents. Faraday's law states that the induced electromotive force in a closed loop equals the negative time rate of change of the magnetic flux enclosed by that loop. Lenz's law dictates the physical sign in Faraday's law by ensuring that any induced current will flow in such a direction that its own magnetic field opposes the original change in magnetic flux that produced it. Inductors store energy in magnetic fields, leading to exponential transient behaviors in RL circuits characterized by a time constant equal to inductance divided by resistance. James Clerk Maxwell completed classical electrodynamics by adding the displacement current term to Ampere's law, demonstrating that changing electric fields create magnetic fields. This symmetry allows electromagnetic fields to propagate self-sustainingly through empty space as transverse waves traveling at the speed of light. For example, consider a circular coil with 50 turns and a cross-sectional area of 0.01 square meters placed inside a uniform magnetic field. If the magnetic field magnitude increases uniformly from zero to 0.8 teslas over a time interval of 0.04 seconds, the magnitude of the induced electromotive force is the number of turns multiplied by the area multiplied by the change in field divided by the time interval. This calculates as 50 multiplied by 0.01 multiplied by 0.8 divided by 0.04, resulting in an induced electromotive force of 10 volts. In class exercise: Determine the time constant of an RL circuit featuring a 2 henry inductor and a 4 ohm resistor.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Problem Set on Field Theory and Circuit Dynamics
description: This assignment tests student competency across electrostatic fields, Gauss's law applications, circuit analysis, and electromagnetic induction.
content:
1. Use Gauss's law to derive the electric field expression at a radius r greater than the outer radius R for a solid insulating sphere carrying a total uniform positive charge Q. (4 marks)
2. A parallel plate capacitor has square plates of side length 0.1 meters separated by a vacuum gap of 0.002 meters. Calculate its capacitance and determine the energy stored when charged to 50 volts. (4 marks)
3. For a single-loop RC circuit with a resistance of 1000 ohms and a capacitance of 47 microfarads connected to a 12 volt DC source, compute the time constant and find the exact charge on the capacitor at time t equals infinity. (4 marks)
4. A long straight wire carries a current of 5 amperes. Using the Biot-Savart law or Ampere's law, calculate the magnitude of the magnetic field at a radial distance of 0.05 meters from the center of the wire. (4 marks)
5. A circular loop of wire with a radius of 0.1 meters is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 teslas. The field drops to zero linearly over 0.2 seconds. Calculate the magnitude of the induced electromotive force in the loop. (4 marks)

title: Lecture 1: Foundations of Special Relativity
description: This lecture introduces the postulates of special relativity and explores consequences such as time dilation and mass-energy equivalence.
content: Learning objectives: understand the constancy of the speed of light, apply the Lorentz factor to calculate dilated time intervals, and compute relativistic energy values. Welcome to modern physics, where classical Newtonian mechanics breaks down near the speed of light. Einstein built his theory on two postulates: the principle of relativity and the universal constancy of the speed of light in a vacuum. A direct consequence of these rules is that moving clocks run slow. We measure time intervals using the relation delta t equals gamma times delta t0, where gamma is the Lorentz factor equal to one divided by the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. Let us work through an example: calculate the dilated lifetime of a muon traveling at nine-tenths of the speed of light, given its proper lifetime at rest is two point two microseconds. First, compute gamma: one divided by the square root of one minus zero point nine squared, which gives approximately two point two nine four. Multiplying this factor by the proper time yields two point two microseconds times two point two nine four, resulting in five point zero four microseconds. Furthermore, mass and energy merge into a single conserved quantity governed by the famous relation E equals m c squared. In class exercise: calculate the total energy of an electron with a rest mass energy of five hundred eleven kiloelectronvolts when it moves at half the speed of light.

title: Lecture 2: The Quantum Nature of Light and Matter
description: This lecture examines blackbody radiation, the photoelectric effect, and the wave-particle duality of light and matter.
content: Learning objectives: explain how Planck's hypothesis resolves the ultraviolet catastrophe, analyze threshold frequencies in the photoelectric effect, and compute de Broglie wavelengths. Classical physics failed to explain the spectrum of thermal radiation until Max Planck proposed that energy is emitted in discrete packets called quanta, described by the relation E equals hf. Albert Einstein extended this concept to explain the photoelectric effect, showing that light consists of particles called photons. The maximum kinetic energy of an ejected electron is given by K max equals hf minus phi, where phi is the work function. Let us review a concrete example: if ultraviolet light with a wavelength of two hundred nanometers strikes a metal surface with a work function of two point three electronvolts, what is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons? First, calculate the photon energy using the convenient constant product hc equal to twelve hundred forty electronvolt nanometers. Dividing twelve hundred forty by two hundred yields six point two electronvolts. Subtracting the work function of two point three electronvolts gives three point nine electronvolts. Louis de Broglie later postulated that all matter possesses wave properties, with a wavelength lambda equal to h divided by momentum p. In class exercise: determine the de Broglie wavelength of a proton with a momentum of three times ten to the minus twenty kilogram meters per second.

title: Lecture 3: Quantum Mechanics of Bound Systems
description: This lecture covers the Bohr model of hydrogen, the Schrödinger wave equation, and the probabilistic interpretation of wavefunctions.
content: Learning objectives: calculate energy levels in the Bohr model, interpret the physical meaning of the squared wavefunction, and solve energy eigenvalues for a particle in a box. The early twentieth century saw attempts to describe atomic structure, culminating in Bohr's semiclassical model of hydrogen. The allowed energy levels are quantized according to E n equals minus thirteen point six divided by n squared in electronvolts. To move beyond this semi-classical approach, we rely on Erwin Schrödinger's wave equation. The square of the wavefunction magnitude represents the probability density of finding a particle at a specific spatial location. Let us examine a classic quantum problem: a free electron confined inside a one-dimensional box of length one nanometer. What is the ground state energy of this electron? Using the particle in a box energy formula E n equals n squared h squared divided by eight m L squared, we substitute the values for mass of an electron, Planck's constant, and the box length. For n equal to one, the ground state energy evaluates to approximately zero point three seven six electronvolts. Any measurement on this system must also obey Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, stating that the product of position and momentum uncertainties is greater than or equal to h bar over two. In class exercise: calculate the minimum position uncertainty for a neutron if its momentum uncertainty is specified as one times ten to the minus twenty-four kilogram meters per second.

title: Lecture 4: Applications in Solid State and Nuclear Physics
description: This lecture applies quantum principles to multi-electron atoms, energy band formation in solids, semiconductor devices, and nuclear physics.
content: Learning objectives: describe how energy bands form in crystalline solids, explain the operational mechanism of quantum tunneling in electronic devices, and outline basic nuclear binding energy concepts. When individual atoms are brought together to form a solid lattice, their discrete atomic energy levels split into continuous energy bands separated by band gaps. This band structure forms the foundation of modern electronics, distinguishing conductors, insulators, and semiconductors. Another striking quantum mechanical prediction is tunneling, where a particle penetrates a potential energy barrier higher than its kinetic energy. A practical application of this phenomenon is the resonant tunneling diode or the scanning tunneling microscope. Let us work through a concrete calculation related to nuclear binding energy. Consider a helium-4 nucleus, which contains two protons and two neutrons. The mass of an isolated proton is one point zero zero seven two seven atomic mass units, and a neutron is one point zero zero eight six six atomic mass units, giving a total constituent mass of four point zero three three zero units. The actual mass of a helium-4 nucleus is four point zero, one five zero atomic mass units. The mass defect is zero point zero one eight zero units. Multiplying this mass defect by the conversion factor of nine hundred thirty-one point five megaelectronvolts per atomic mass unit yields a total binding energy of approximately sixteen point seven seven megaelectronvolts. In class exercise: determine the binding energy per nucleon for this helium-4 nucleus.

content:
Task 1: A spaceship travels at eighty percent of the speed of light relative to Earth. If an onboard clock measures a trip duration of ten hours, calculate the time interval measured by an observer on Earth using the Lorentz transformation. (4 marks)

title: Lecture 1: Wave Optics Foundations and Interference
description: This lecture establishes the wave model of light, analyzing superposition, coherence, and division of wavefront interference.
content: Learning objectives: understand optical coherence conditions, derive double-slit fringe spacing, and calculate thin-film phase shifts. Today we examine light as an electromagnetic wave. When two coherent waves overlap, they interfere. For Young's double slit, path length differences create alternating maxima and minima. Bright fringes occur when d sin theta equals m lambda. Consider a setup with slit separation d = 0.2 millimeters, wavelength lambda = 500 nanometers, and screen distance L = 2 meters. The fringe spacing delta y is given by lambda L over d. Substituting these numbers yields (500 times 10 to the power of minus 9 meters) times 2 meters divided by (0.2 times 10 to the power of minus 3 meters), resulting in 0.005 meters, or 5 millimeters. We also discuss thin-film interference, where reflections at higher refractive index media introduce a phase shift of pi radians, influencing constructive and destructive reflection conditions. In class exercise: Calculate the third bright fringe angle for a double slit with separation 0.15 millimeters and light wavelength 600 nanometers, assuming small angle approximations.

title: Lecture 2: Advanced Interferometry and Diffraction Phenomena
description: This lecture investigates precision optical measurement via interferometers and explores single-slit and circular aperture diffraction limits.
content: Learning objectives: analyze Michelson interferometer fringe shifts, compute single-slit diffraction minima, and apply the Rayleigh resolution criterion. Interferometers split a single wavefront to measure microscopic displacements with high accuracy. The Michelson interferometer achieves this by recombining beams reflected from two perpendicular mirrors. Turning the mirror by a distance delta d shifts the interference pattern by N fringes according to delta d equals N lambda over 2. Moving to diffraction, when waves encounter obstacles comparable to their wavelength, bending occurs. For a single slit of width a, destructive interference minima satisfy a sin theta equals m lambda, where m is a non-zero integer. Furthermore, optical instruments face diffraction limits. The Rayleigh criterion states that two point sources are barely resolved when the center of one Airy disk falls on the first minimum of the other, defining the angular resolution limit as theta equals 1.22 lambda over D. Consider a telescope with aperture D = 0.1 meters observing light of lambda = 550 nanometers. The minimum resolvable angle is 1.22 times (550 times 10 to the power of minus 9) divided by 0.1, yielding 6.71 times 10 to the power of minus 6 radians. In class exercise: Determine the mirror displacement in a Michelson interferometer using 632 nanometers light if 500 fringe shifts are counted.

title: Lecture 3: Polarization Principles and Applications
description: This lecture explores light polarization states, analytical laws governing polarizers, and anisotropic media behavior.
content: Learning objectives: apply Malus law for transmitted intensity, compute Brewster angle for dielectric interfaces, and describe birefringence. Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave, meaning its electric field vector oscillates perpendicular to the direction of propagation. Unpolarized light has random field orientations, while linear polarization restricts oscillations to a single plane. When linearly polarized light with initial intensity I0 passes through a polarizing filter whose transmission axis makes an angle theta with the electric field, the transmitted intensity obeys Malus law: I equals I0 times the cosine squared of theta. For example, if unpolarized light of intensity 100 watts per square meter passes through a first ideal polarizer, intensity drops to 50 watts per square meter. Passing this through a second polarizer at an angle of 30 degrees to the first gives intensity I equals 50 times (cosine of 30 degrees squared). Since cosine of 30 degrees is the square root of 3 decimal 75 over 2 or roughly 0.866, its square is 0.75. Thus, transmitted intensity is 50 times 0.75, equaling 37.5 watts per square meter. We also examine reflection polarization, where light reflected from a dielectric surface becomes completely polarized parallel to the surface at Brewster angle theta B, defined by tangent of theta B equals n2 over n1. In class exercise: Calculate Brewster angle for light traveling from air (n = 1.0) into glass (n = 1.5).

title: Lecture 4: Optical Fibers and Laser Fundamentals
description: This lecture connects physical optics principles to modern photonics, covering total internal reflection, fiber transmission, and laser action.
content: Learning objectives: calculate critical angles for optical fibers, evaluate acceptance cones, and explain stimulated emission basics. Modern optical communication relies heavily on dielectric waveguides known as optical fibers. These fibers trap light through total internal reflection, which occurs when light travels from a higher refractive index core n1 to a lower cladding refractive index n2 at an angle exceeding the critical angle theta c. The critical angle satisfies the sine of theta c equals n2 over n1. Consider a core with refractive index 1.48 and cladding with refractive index 1.46. The critical angle is the arcsine of 1.46 divided by 1.48, which evaluates to approximately 80.6 degrees from the normal, meaning the internal incidence angle relative to the interface must exceed 9.4 degrees. We define the numerical aperture to quantify light gathering capacity, given by the square root of (n1 squared minus n2 squared). For our values, numerical aperture equals the square root of (1.48 squared minus 1.46 squared), yielding approximately 0.24. Finally, we introduce lasers, contrasting spontaneous emission with stimulated emission, population inversion, and optical cavity resonance. In class exercise: Find the numerical aperture of a fiber with core index 1.52 and cladding index 1.50.

title: Lecture 1: Elasticity and Solid Deformation
courses: Mechanical properties of Matter and Thermodynamics
description: This lecture explores how solid materials deform under applied mechanical forces, focusing on stress, strain, and moduli.
content: Learning objectives: Understand the definitions of engineering stress and strain, apply Hooke's law using Young's modulus, and analyze distinct regions of the stress-strain curve. When an external force acts on a solid, internal restoring forces develop. Stress sigma is defined as force per unit area, sigma = F/A, measured in Pascals. Strain epsilon is the fractional change in dimension, epsilon = Delta L / L, which is dimensionless. For linear elastic behavior, Young's modulus E relates stress to strain via sigma = E * epsilon. Beyond the elastic limit, materials undergo permanent plastic deformation leading to yield and ultimate tensile strengths. Worked example: Consider a brass rod of initial length 1.5 meters and cross-sectional area 2 square centimeters subjected to a tensile force of 15 kilonewtons. Given that brass has a Young's modulus of 100 gigapascals, we calculate the elongation. First, convert area to square meters: 2e-4 square meters. The stress is 15000 divided by 2e-4, yielding 7.5e7 Pascals. Using epsilon = sigma / E, we find 7.5e7 / 1e11 = 0.00075. Multiplying by the initial length of 1.5 meters yields a stretch Delta L of 0.001125 meters, or 1.125 millimeters. In class exercise: Calculate the strain energy density stored in this brass rod prior to reaching its elastic limit.

title: Lecture 2: Fluid Statics and Dynamics
courses: Mechanical properties of Matter and Thermodynamics
description: This lecture examines fluid behavior at rest and in motion, covering pressure gradients, conservation laws, and fluid friction.
content: Learning objectives: Apply hydrostatic principles to pressure variations, use the continuity equation for incompressible flow, and analyze energy conservation in fluids using Bernoulli's equation. Fluids exert forces perpendicular to any surface they contact. Hydrostatic pressure increases linearly with depth due to gravity, expressed as P = rho * g * h. For moving fluids, mass conservation dictates that the volumetric flow rate remains constant, formulated as A1 * v1 = A2 * v2, where A is cross-sectional area and v is flow speed. Bernoulli's equation links pressure, kinetic energy per unit volume, and potential energy per unit volume along a streamline. Viscosity introduces internal friction, opposing relative motion between adjacent fluid layers. Worked example: Water flows through a horizontal pipe that narrows from an inner radius of 4 centimeters to 2 centimeters. If the flow speed in the wider section is 2 meters per second, determine the speed in the narrow section and the pressure drop. Using continuity, A1 * v1 = A2 * v2, the areas scale with the square of the radius. Thus, pi * (0.04)^2 * 2 = pi * (0.02)^2 * v2. Solving gives v2 = 8 meters per second. Applying Bernoulli for a horizontal pipe, P1 + 0.5 * rho * v1^2 = P2 + 0.5 * rho * v2^2. With water density at 1000 kilograms per cubic meter, the pressure difference P1 - P2 is 0.5 * 1000 * (8^2 - 2^2), resulting in 30000 Pascals or 30 kilopascals. In class exercise: Determine the buoyant force on a submerged aluminum sphere of volume 0.005 cubic meters.

title: Lecture 3: Thermal Properties and Heat Transfer
courses: Mechanical properties of Matter and Thermodynamics
description: This lecture covers thermal expansion, calorimetry, and the fundamental mechanisms of thermal energy transport.
content: Learning objectives: Calculate dimensional changes resulting from temperature variations, solve phase change and specific heat problems, and apply Fourier's law of thermal conduction. Temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy. When thermal energy is added without changing phase, the temperature rises according to Q = m * c * Delta T, where c is specific heat capacity. During phase transitions, latent heat governs energy absorption at constant temperature. Solids expand linearly such that Delta L = alpha * L * Delta T, where alpha is the coefficient of thermal expansion. Heat transfers via three modes: conduction, convection, and radiation. Conduction rate is governed by Fourier's law, stating that heat flux is proportional to the temperature gradient and thermal conductivity. Radiation follows the Stefan-Boltzmann law, emitting energy proportional to absolute temperature raised to the fourth power. Worked example: A copper plate with thermal conductivity 400 watts per meter kelvin has a thickness of 0.02 meters and a surface area of 0.5 square meters. If the inner and outer surface temperatures are held at 100 degrees Celsius and 20 degrees Celsius respectively, find the steady-state rate of heat conduction. Using Fourier's law, Q/t = k * A * (T1 - T2) / d. Substituting the values yields 400 * 0.5 * (100 - 20) / 0.02, which equals 800000 watts, or 800 kilowatts. In class exercise: Compute the final equilibrium temperature when 200 grams of water at 20 degrees Celsius is mixed with 50 grams of ice at 0 degrees Celsius.

title: Lecture 4: Thermodynamics and Energy Conversion
courses: Mechanical properties of Matter and Thermodynamics
description: This lecture investigates the laws of thermodynamics, ideal gas behavior, thermodynamic cycles, and engine efficiency limits.
content: Learning objectives: Apply the first law of thermodynamics to standard gas processes, calculate work done during expansion, and evaluate heat engine efficiencies using the second law. The ideal gas law PV = nRT links macroscopic state variables. The first law of thermodynamics states that change in internal energy equals heat added minus work done, written as Delta U = Q - W. Common idealized processes include isothermal, isobaric, isochoric, and adiabatic paths, each modifying pressure, volume, and temperature differently. Heat engines absorb heat from a hot reservoir, perform useful work, and exhaust waste heat to a cold reservoir. The second law establishes that no cyclic engine can convert all absorbed heat into work. The maximum theoretical efficiency for any engine operating between hot temperature Th and cold temperature Tc is the Carnot efficiency, given by eta = 1 - (Tc / Th), using absolute Kelvin temperatures. Entropy measures microscopic disorder and remains constant in reversible cycles while increasing in irreversible ones. Worked example: A Carnot engine operates between a high temperature of 600 Kelvin and a low temperature of 300 Kelvin. If the engine absorbs 2000 Joules of heat from the hot reservoir per cycle, calculate its maximum efficiency, the work performed, and the exhaust heat rejected. The efficiency is eta = 1 - (300 / 600) = 0.50, or 50 percent. Work done W = eta * Qh = 0.50 * 2000 = 1000 Joules. The exhaust heat Qc = Qh - W = 2000 - 1000 = 1000 Joules. In class exercise: Determine the final pressure of an ideal monoatomic gas compressed adiabatically to half its volume.

content:
Task 1: An iron wire of length 3 meters and diameter 2 millimeters is subjected to a tensile load of 500 Newtons. Given that the Young's modulus of iron is 210 gigapascals, calculate the resulting elongation in millimeters and the stored elastic potential energy. (4 marks) 

Task 2: Water flows through a variable cross-section pipe system. If a pipe section with a 10 centimeter diameter has a fluid velocity of 1.5 meters per second, determine the required diameter of a downstream section where the velocity reaches 6 meters per second, assuming steady incompressible flow. The interior and exterior surface temperatures are 22 degrees Celsius and minus 5 degrees Celsius. Calculate the heat flux through the composite wall in watts per square meter. (4 marks)

Determine the work done by the gas, the change in internal energy, and the total heat added to the system. (4 marks) 

Task 5: A power plant operates using a Carnot cycle between a geothermal source at 450 Kelvin and surface cooling water at 300 Kelvin. If the plant generates 5 megawatts of net power output, calculate the thermal efficiency, the rate of heat input required from the source, and the rate of heat exhausted to the environment. (4 marks)

title: Lecture 1: Particle Kinematics and Coordinate Systems
description: This lecture covers the mathematical description of particle motion using rectangular, normal-tangential, and polar coordinates.
content: Learning objectives: Master the derivation of velocity and acceleration vectors across different coordinate systems and apply them to trajectory analysis. In this lecture, we examine how particles move through space without considering the forces causing the motion. Rectilinear and curvilinear paths are analyzed by differentiating position vectors with respect to time. For normal and tangential coordinates, acceleration splits into a tangential component reflecting speed changes along the path and a normal component pointing toward the center of curvature. For instance, consider a particle traveling along a circular path of radius 25 meters with a constant speed of 10 meters per second. The tangential acceleration is zero, while the normal acceleration is calculated as velocity squared divided by the radius, yielding 100 divided by 25, which equals 4 meters per second squared. In polar coordinates, radial and transverse components govern motion, proving vital for central force problems and orbital mechanics. Understanding these geometric relationships forms the foundation for solving kinetic equations in subsequent modules. In class exercise: A motorist drives along a curve with a radius of curvature of 80 meters at a speed of 16 meters per second. Calculate the magnitude of the normal acceleration.

title: Lecture 2: Particle Kinetics, Work, Energy, and Power
description: This lecture explores Newton's second law and the work-energy principles governing particle motion under various force fields.
content: Learning objectives: Apply equations of motion in various coordinate systems and utilize work-energy theorems to solve for dynamic states. Having established kinematics, we now introduce kinetics by applying Newton's second law, stating that the sum of forces equals mass times acceleration. When forces vary with position, integrating the equation of motion along a path leads directly to the work-energy principle, expressed as initial kinetic energy plus work done equals final kinetic energy. Conservative forces such as gravity and spring elasticity allow us to define potential energy, simplifying conservation equations where mechanical energy remains constant throughout the trajectory. Power, defined as the rate of doing work, and mechanical efficiency are also evaluated for engines and mechanical linkages. For example, consider a 50 kilogram crate pushed up a smooth horizontal floor by a constant force of 200 Newtons over a distance of 10 meters. The work done is 2000 Joules, which directly increases the kinetic energy of the crate from rest to a final speed calculated by taking the square root of 4000 divided by 50, resulting in an end speed of 8.94 meters per second. In class exercise: A 2 kilogram particle drops from rest through a vertical height of 5 meters. Determine its final velocity using conservation of energy, ignoring air resistance.

title: Lecture 3: Impulse, Momentum, and Rigid-Body Kinematics
description: This lecture investigates linear and angular momentum principles, impact phenomena, and the fundamental kinematics of rigid bodies.
content: Learning objectives: Solve impact problems using the coefficient of restitution and analyze planar rigid-body motion using instantaneous centers. Systems involving transient forces are best analyzed using the principle of linear and angular impulse-momentum, which relates integrated forces over time directly to changes in momentum. During direct and oblique impacts, the coefficient of restitution quantifies energy loss and relative velocity transformations before and after collision. Transitioning from point particles to extended bodies, rigid-body kinematics analyzes translation, rotation about a fixed axis, and general plane motion. Every general plane motion can be viewed as pure rotation about an instantaneous centre of zero velocity at any given instant. For example, consider two identical spheres colliding head-on, where ball one moves at 6 meters per second and ball two is stationary, with a coefficient of restitution of 0.5. Applying conservation of linear momentum and the restitution equation yields post-impact velocities of 1.5 meters per second for the first ball and 4.5 meters per second for the second ball. In class exercise: A uniform slender bar of length 2 meters rotates freely about one end with an angular velocity of 3 radians per second. Find the linear speed of its midpoint.

title: Lecture 4: Rigid-Body Kinetics and Introduction to Vibrations
description: This lecture addresses the equations of motion for rigid bodies in plane motion and provides an introduction to mechanical vibrations.
content: Learning objectives: Formulate equations of motion for rotating rigid bodies and analyze the natural frequency of single-degree-of-freedom vibratory systems. The final core topic unites kinetics and kinematics for rigid bodies undergoing planar motion, applying the governing equation where the sum of moments about the center of mass equals the moment of inertia multiplied by angular acceleration. Special attention is given to rolling without slipping, where the kinematic constraint links linear acceleration of the center to angular acceleration multiplied by the wheel radius, dictating the required friction force. Finally, we introduce mechanical vibrations, focusing on undamped single-degree-of-freedom mass-spring systems governed by second-order differential equations. For instance, consider a solid disk with a mass of 10 kilograms and a radius of 0.5 meters rolling without slipping down an incline. Using the mass moment of inertia for a disk, which is one-half times mass times radius squared, the resulting angular acceleration is derived from the balance of gravitational and frictional torque. In class exercise: A spring with stiffness 400 Newtons per meter supports a mass of 4 kilograms. Calculate the natural frequency of the system in radians per second.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Dynamics Problem Set
description: This assignment tests student comprehension across particle kinematics, work-energy principles, impulse-momentum collisions, and rigid-body dynamics.
content:
1. Particle Kinematics: A particle moves along a spiral path such that its radial distance is r = 2t meters and its theta angle is 0.5t radians, where t is in seconds. Determine the magnitude of its velocity vector at t = 2 seconds. (Marks: 4)
2. Particle Kinetics: A 10 kilogram block is pulled up a 30 degree inclined plane by a constant force of 80 Newtons parallel to the incline. If the kinetic coefficient of friction is 0.15, find the speed of the block after traveling 4 meters from rest. (Marks: 4)
3. Impulse and Momentum: A 3 kilogram sphere traveling at 5 meters per second strikes an identical stationary sphere obliquely. The impact line is along the x-axis and the coefficient of restitution is 0.8. Calculate the velocity vector of both spheres after impact. (Marks: 4)
4. Rigid-Body Kinematics: A uniform disk of radius 0.3 meters rolls without slipping on a flat horizontal surface with a constant angular velocity of 10 radians per second counterclockwise. Determine the velocity of the highest point on the disk. (Marks: 4)
5. Rigid-Body Kinetics and Vibrations: A slender rod of length 1.5 meters and mass 6 kilograms is pinned at one end and allowed to swing freely from the horizontal position. Using energy methods, calculate the angular velocity of the rod as it passes through the lowest vertical position. (Marks: 4)

Submission instructions: Submit your complete working out, free-body diagrams, and final numerical answers compiled into a single PDF document via the university portal.

title: Lecture 1: Foundations of Engineering Graphics
description: This session covers essential drawing instruments, line conventions, lettering, scale selection, and sheet layout standardisation.
content:
Learning Objectives: Master the standard line types used in technical documentation, and understand how to properly layout a drawing sheet with a title block.

Explanation: Technical drawing relies on strict conventions so that designs can be interpreted without ambiguity worldwide. Different line types convey specific geometric intent. For instance, visible outlines use a thick continuous line of 0.5 millimetres, hidden details use a thin dashed line, and centre lines use a thin alternating long and short dash pattern. Consider drawing a rectangular mounting plate measuring 100 millimetres wide by 50 millimetres high. The outer perimeter is drawn with a thick continuous line. If there is an internal circular bore of diameter 20 millimetres located at coordinates X equal to 30, Y equal to 25 from the bottom left corner, its hidden boundaries inside a solid block are represented by dashed lines, while its central axis is marked by intersecting centre lines. The title block must clearly display the projection symbol, scale ratio such as 1 to 1, and drawing units.

In class: Sketch a border frame for an A4 sheet, construct a standard title block in the bottom right corner, and practice drawing the four primary line types across a 50 millimetre span.

title: Lecture 2: Multi-View and Pictorial Projections
description: Students will learn how to translate three-dimensional objects into precise orthographic multi-views and intuitive pictorial representations.
content:
Learning Objectives: Differentiate between first-angle and third-angle projection standards, and construct accurate multi-view and isometric drawings.

Explanation: Orthographic projection uses parallel projectors to create two-dimensional views of a three-dimensional object. In third-angle projection, commonly used in North America, the top view is placed directly above the front view, and the right-side view is placed to the right of the front view. Conversely, first-angle projection places the top view below the front view. To construct these views, imagine a rectangular block of length 80, height 40, and depth 30 millimetres with a top step. The front view shows the full 80 by 40 profile with the step cut out. Projecting vertically upwards from this view yields the top view, displaying the width and depth dimensions of 80 by 30. Isometric pictorial drawings present a 3D view where all vertical lines remain vertical, and horizontal axes are drawn at 30 degrees to the horizontal baseline, allowing engineers to visualise the complete assembly instantly.

In class: Given a physical L-bracket model, sketch its front, top, and right-side orthographic views using third-angle projection conventions on grid paper.

title: Lecture 3: Advanced Visualisation and Sectioning
description: This lecture explores internal feature standardisation through sectional views and precise handling of inclined surfaces using auxiliary projections.
content:
Learning Objectives: Apply appropriate sectioning techniques to reveal internal features and construct auxiliary views for true-shape representation of inclined surfaces.

Explanation: When an object contains complex internal cavities, hidden lines can clutter the drawing and lead to manufacturing errors. Sectional views solve this by cutting through the object along a specified cutting plane line. For example, if a cylindrical housing has an inner bore stepping from diameter 30 to diameter 50 millimetres, a full sectional view removes the front half of the object. The exposed solid material is indicated using hatching lines drawn at a 45-degree angle spaced 2 millimetres apart. Furthermore, if a component features an inclined face at an angle of 30 degrees to the horizontal, standard orthographic views will show this surface foreshortened. An auxiliary view projects lines perpendicular to the inclined surface to display its true geometric shape and dimensions accurately.

In class: Convert a provided multi-view drawing of a hollow flanged sleeve into a full sectional view, applying correct 45-degree hatching to the cut regions.

title: Lecture 4: Dimensioning Rules and Computer-Aided Design
description: The final lecture covers rigorous dimensioning standards and transitions manual drafting principles into modern parametric CAD software workflows.
content:
Learning Objectives: Apply professional dimensioning rules without duplication and execute basic 2D sketches and 3D extrusions within a CAD environment.

Explanation: Dimensioning must provide all necessary size and location data for manufacturing without redundant or conflicting figures. Rules dictate that dimensions should be placed outside the part geometry where possible, never duplicate a dimension between views, and reference from established datum features. For a stepped block of total length 100 millimetres with a central slot of width 20 millimetres, dimension the overall length and locate the slot from one fixed datum edge, rather than dimensioning every individual sub-segment. In modern engineering, these principles translate directly into CAD systems like AutoCAD or SolidWorks. The workflow begins by opening a sketch plane, applying geometric constraints such as horizontal, vertical, and concentric relations, and defining size parameters. Finally, executing an extrude command transforms the 2D closed profile into a solid 3D model with a specified depth, from which 2D production drawings are automatically generated.

In class: Create a constrained 2D sketch of a rectangular plate with a central hole in SolidWorks, extrude it to a depth of 15 millimetres, and generate a 2D drawing sheet with proper dimensioning.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Technical Drawing and CAD Workflow
description: This assignment assesses the student's ability to apply geometric construction, orthographic projection, sectioning, dimensioning rules, and CAD modeling to a complete mechanical component.
content:
1. Construct the orthographic front, top, and right-side views of a mechanical bearing block in third-angle projection, ensuring all visible and hidden lines are correctly styled. (Marks: 4)
2. Redraw the top view as a half-sectional view to expose an internal keyway slot, applying precise 45-degree section hatching. (Marks: 4)
3. Draw a secondary auxiliary view for an inclined mounting flange situated at a 45-degree angle to reveal its true shape and fastener hole locations. (Marks: 4)
4. Dimension the complete multi-view drawing adhering strictly to non-duplication rules, datum referencing, and standard tolerance formats. (Marks: 4)
5. Model the bearing block in SolidWorks or AutoCAD, applying geometric constraints and parametric dimensions, and export the resulting 3D part and 2D drawing sheet. (Marks: 4)

Total Marks: 20

Submission Instructions: Submit a single compressed ZIP archive containing all hand-drawn PDF sheets and the native CAD part files named according to your student ID number.

title: Lecture 1: Materials, Casting, and Metal Forming Fundamentals
description: This session explores how raw engineering materials are selected and shaped through primary manufacturing processes like casting and bulk deformation.
content: Learning objectives include understanding mechanical property requirements for production, identifying sand and die casting mechanisms along with common defects, and calculating forces in bulk deformation. Material selection dictates processing routes, balancing ductility, yield strength, and thermal behavior. Casting transforms liquid metal into complex geometries inside molds, whereas forming processes like forging and rolling improve structural grain flow and mechanical integrity. Consider a flat rolling operation where a steel plate with an initial thickness of 50 millimeters is reduced to 40 millimeters in a single pass. If the roll radius is 200 millimeters and the roll rotates at 60 revolutions per minute, the absolute draft is 10 millimeters, and the maximum possible draft based on a coefficient of friction of 0.12 is calculated as 0.12 squared multiplied by 200, which equals 2.88 millimeters. Because the actual draft exceeds this limit, the mill would slip unless the draft is reduced or friction is increased. In class exercise: calculate the final length of a 200-millimeter aluminum billet drawn to a cross-sectional area reduction of 25 percent, assuming uniform plastic deformation and constant volume.

title: Lecture 2: Machining Operations, Cutting Mechanics, and Joining Technologies
description: Students will learn chip formation mechanics, cutting parameter optimization, and permanent joining methods used in assembly.
content: Learning objectives focus on computing appropriate spindle speeds for various turning and milling operations, analyzing tool wear progression, and evaluating weld joint integrity. Machining removes material through shear deformation, generating heat and friction that dictate tool life through Taylor equation parameters. Turning utilizes single-point tools on rotating workpieces, while milling employs multi-tooth rotary cutters. Joining encompasses fusion welding processes like MIG and TIG, solid-state variants, and adhesive bonding. Let us calculate the required spindle speed for turning a titanium alloy bar with a diameter of 80 millimeters, given a recommended cutting speed of 50 meters per minute. Using the standard formula N = 1000 multiplied by V divided by pi multiplied by D, we compute 1000 multiplied by 50 divided by 3.14159 multiplied by 80, which results in approximately 199 revolutions per minute. If the feed rate is set to 0.2 millimeters per revolution, the material removal rate can be estimated by factoring in the depth of cut. In class exercise: determine the machining time required for a 300-millimeter long steel shaft turned in a single pass at a feed of 0.25 millimeters per revolution and a spindle speed of 400 revolutions per minute.

title: Lecture 3: Metrology, Tolerances, and Conventional Automation
description: This lecture covers dimensional metrology, fit classifications, and the integration of numerical control in manufacturing systems.
content: Learning objectives involve interpreting geometric dimensioning and tolerancing callouts, calculating clearance and interference fits, and translating basic part geometries into G-code sequences. Quality control relies on precision measurement instruments such as micrometers and coordinate measuring machines to verify that manufactured parts conform to engineering blueprints. Fits are standardized into clearance, transition, and interference categories to ensure proper assembly functionality. Numerical control automates machine tool axes using discrete coordinate commands. Consider a linear interpolation G-code block reading G01 X50.0 Y25.0 F150. Moving from the origin at a feed rate of 150 millimeters per minute, the tool travels along a straight path to the specified coordinates. If the distance from the start point is 55.90 millimeters, the total cutting time for this single linear move is calculated as 55.90 divided by 150, yielding approximately 0.373 minutes or 22.38 seconds. In class exercise: write a G-code snippet to machine a square pocket with a side length of 40 millimeters starting from the bottom left corner at X0 Y0.

title: Lecture 4: Modern Additive Manufacturing and Smart Factory Automation
description: The final lecture examines advanced additive manufacturing techniques, industrial robotics, and Industry 4.0 paradigms in modern production environments.
content: Learning objectives include differentiating between FDM, SLA, and SLS 3D printing technologies, analyzing industrial robot workspace configurations, and conceptualizing smart factory data flows. Additive manufacturing builds parts layer by layer from digital computer-aided design models, offering unmatched geometric freedom for lightweight components and rapid prototyping. Conversely, smart manufacturing integrates internet of things sensors, cloud analytics, and cyber-physical systems to monitor equipment health and dynamically schedule production orders in real time. For instance, evaluating build time for a fused deposition modeling part with a volume of 120,000 cubic millimeters, printed with a deposition rate of 500 cubic millimeters per hour and an overhead factor of 1.3 for perimeters and infill patterns, yields a total estimated build time of 120,000 multiplied by 1.3 divided by 500, which equals 312 hours. Safety protocols must be strictly maintained around high-powered lasers in selective laser sintering and automated robotic welding cells to prevent operator injury. In class exercise: list three distinct advantages and two limitations of powder bed fusion compared to traditional subtractive milling for aerospace brackets.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Manufacturing Process Analysis and Calculations
description: This assignment evaluates student comprehension across casting, forming, machining parameters, and numerical control programming.
content:
Task 1: Calculate the solidification time for a brass component in the shape of a sphere with a diameter of 60 millimeters, using Chvorinov rule with a mold constant of 3.5 seconds per square millimeter. (Marks: 4)
Task 2: Determine the true strain and final length of a copper wire drawn from an initial diameter of 10 millimeters down to 6 millimeters, assuming ideal deformation without friction. (Marks: 4)
Task 3: Compute the exact spindle speed in revolutions per minute and the material removal rate in cubic millimeters per minute for face milling a steel block 150 millimeters wide using a 100-millimeter diameter cutter with 6 teeth, a cutting speed of 120 meters per minute, a feed per tooth of 0.15 millimeters, and a depth of cut of 3 millimeters. (Marks: 5)
Task 4: Write a complete sequence of standard G-code and M-code commands to safely start the spindle at 1200 revolutions per minute clockwise, execute a linear cut along a rectangular contour of 60 by 40 millimeters, turn off the coolant, stop the spindle, and return the machine to the home position. (Marks: 5)
Task 5: Discuss the primary failure modes associated with cemented carbide cutting inserts during high-speed continuous turning operations and propose two mitigation strategies. (Marks: 2)
Submission instructions: Submit your complete solution as a single PDF document containing all handwritten or typed calculations, derivations, and G-code listings clearly labeled by task number.

title: Lecture 1: AC Fundamentals and Three-Phase Systems
courses: Introduction to Power and Machines Engineering
description: This lecture introduces alternating current power metrics and explores the mechanics of balanced three-phase electrical circuits.
content: Learning objectives: Understand complex power relationships and calculate line-to-line parameters in star and delta configurations. In alternating current systems, energy transfer involves real power, reactive power, and apparent power. Real power performs useful work, while reactive power sustains magnetic and electric fields. The apparent power triangle links these quantities through the power factor angle phi. Low power factor increases current drawn from the source, magnifying transmission losses. Power factor correction employs capacitor banks to supply reactive power locally, reducing line current and freeing system capacity. Three-phase systems deliver electrical energy more efficiently than single-phase networks using balanced sinusoidal voltages separated by 120 degrees. In a star connected load, the line voltage equals root three times the phase voltage, and the line current equals the phase current. For a delta connected load, the line voltage equals the phase voltage, and the line current equals root three times the phase current. Consider a balanced star connected load operating with a line voltage of 400 volts and a line current of 20 amperes at a lagging power factor of 0.80. The magnitude of the phase voltage is 400 divided by root three, yielding 230.94 volts. The total three phase real power is calculated as root three multiplied by 400 volts multiplied by 20 amperes multiplied by 0.80, resulting in 11085.12 watts. In class exercise: Determine the total apparent power and reactive power for this load, given the apparent power is 13856.41 volt-amperes.

title: Lecture 2: Magnetic Circuits and Transformers
courses: Introduction to Power and Machines Engineering
description: This lecture examines magnetic core behavior and the operational principles of single-phase transformers.
content: Learning objectives: Analyze magnetic flux paths and evaluate transformer voltage transformation, losses, and efficiency. Transformers change alternating voltage and current levels through electromagnetic induction without changing frequency. The core guides magnetic flux created by the primary winding, inducing a voltage in the secondary winding proportional to the turns ratio. The voltage ratio equals the turns ratio, expressed as V1 over V2 equals N1 over N2. Real transformers depart from ideal behavior due to winding resistance, leakage flux, core hysteresis, and eddy currents. These imperfections are modeled using an equivalent circuit containing series impedances and shunt branches representing core losses. Efficiency is defined as the ratio of output real power to input real power, maximized when variable copper losses equal constant iron losses. Consider a step-down transformer with a primary winding of 500 turns connected to a 2300 volt supply, featuring a secondary winding with 50 turns. The voltage transformation ratio is 500 divided by 50, which simplifies to 10 to 1. The secondary terminal voltage is 2300 divided by 10, yielding 230 volts. If the transformer delivers 10 amperes to a load at this secondary voltage, the secondary apparent power is 2300 volt-amperes. Assuming total internal losses of 50 watts under these conditions, the input power is the output real power plus losses. In class exercise: Calculate the percentage efficiency of this transformer assuming a unity load power factor.

title: Lecture 3: Principles of DC Machines
courses: Introduction to Power and Machines Engineering
description: This lecture covers the construction, operating characteristics, and speed regulation of direct current generators and motors.
content: Learning objectives: Apply electromechanical energy conversion principles and compute operating speeds for direct current motors. Direct current machines utilize commutators and brushes to convert mechanical energy into electrical energy or vice versa. When an armature rotates within a stationary magnetic field, conductors cut flux lines, inducing a voltage known as back electromotive force in a motor. This back electromotive force opposes the applied terminal voltage, self-regulating armature current based on mechanical load demands. The generated voltage and developed electromagnetic torque depend directly on flux per pole, rotational speed, and machine design constants. Speed control in direct current motors is achieved by adjusting armature terminal voltage, field circuit resistance, or series connected impedances. Consider a separately excited direct current motor connected to a 240 volt direct current supply with an armature circuit resistance of 0.5 ohms. When operating under a steady mechanical load, the armature draws a current of 20 amperes. The voltage drop across the armature resistance is 20 amperes multiplied by 0.5 ohms, yielding 10 volts. The resulting back electromotive force is the applied voltage minus this resistance drop, calculated as 240 minus 10, equaling 230 volts. If the machine constant and field flux are such that the motor rotates at a speed corresponding to 2.3 volts per revolutions per minute, the operational speed is 230 divided by 2.3, resulting in 100 revolutions per minute. In class exercise: Determine the new armature current if the mechanical load increases, causing the speed to drop to 90 revolutions per minute.

title: Lecture 4: AC Rotating Machines and Power Systems
courses: Introduction to Power and Machines Engineering
description: This lecture explores induction motor slip dynamics, synchronous machine operation, and large scale electrical transmission infrastructure.
content: Learning objectives: Calculate induction motor slip parameters and explain high voltage transmission loss reduction methods. Induction motors rely on a rotating magnetic field produced by stator windings supplied with polyphase alternating current. This rotating field induces currents in the rotor conductors, creating a mechanical torque that drives the rotor in the direction of the field. The synchronous speed depends on supply frequency and the number of poles, calculated as 120 times frequency divided by number of poles. The rotor never reaches synchronous speed under load; the speed difference relative to synchronous speed defines slip. Synchronous machines operate at a fixed speed locked to the system frequency, functioning as generators in power plants or motors in industrial drives. Power systems link generation sources including thermal, hydroelectric, and renewable facilities to load centers through high voltage transmission lines. High voltage transmission minimizes thermal energy losses because line losses are proportional to the square of the current multiplied by resistance. By stepping up voltage for transmission, current decreases for the same power transfer, drastically reducing resistive losses. Consider a 6-pole synchronous generator driven at a frequency of 60 hertz. The synchronous speed is 120 multiplied by 60 divided by 6, yielding 1200 revolutions per minute. For an induction motor with 4 poles operating on 50 hertz, synchronous speed is 1500 revolutions per minute. If this induction motor runs at a measured speed of 1425 revolutions per minute, the slip is 1500 minus 1425 divided by 1500, which equals 0.05 or 5 percent. In class exercise: Compute the rotor frequency of this induction motor under the given operating condition.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Power and Machines Analysis
courses: Introduction to Power and Machines Engineering
description: This assignment evaluates student comprehension of ac circuit metrics, transformer equivalent parameters, dc machine dynamics, and induction motor slip calculations through quantitative problem solving.
content:
1. A single-phase load draws 15 kilowatts at a lagging power factor of 0.707 from a 230 volt, 50 hertz supply. Calculate the initial apparent power, reactive power, and total line current. (4 marks)

2. Design a power factor correction scheme for the load in task 1 by determining the required capacitance in microfarads to improve the overall power factor to 0.95 lagging at 50 hertz. (4 marks)

3. A single-phase transformer has 1000 primary turns and 250 secondary turns. When connected to a 400 volt primary source, the measured secondary open-circuit voltage is 98 volts, and under full load it supplies 15 amperes at 95 volts with a power factor of 0.85 lagging. Calculate the voltage regulation percentage. (4 marks)

4. A 220 volt direct current shunt motor has an armature resistance of 0.4 ohms and a field circuit resistance of 220 ohms. When running light, the motor draws a total current of 5 amperes while rotating at 1200 revolutions per minute. Compute the rotational losses and the back electromotive force under no-load conditions. (4 marks)

5. An 8-pole, 50 hertz three-phase induction motor operates with a slip of 3.5 percent. Determine the synchronous speed in revolutions per minute, the actual rotor mechanical speed, and the frequency of the rotor induced currents. (4 marks)
