title: Lecture 1: Fundamentals of Acoustic Waves and Human Perception
description: This lecture introduces the fundamental wave equation for sound, propagation speeds in various media, and the logarithmic scale of human hearing.
content: Learning objectives: Understand the derivation and parameters of the wave equation, calculate sound speeds using bulk modulus and density, and manipulate decibel intensity levels. The mathematical foundation of acoustics starts from the linearized hydrodynamic equations, yielding the wave equation for acoustic pressure. The propagation speed c is determined by the material properties, specifically the square root of the ratio of the bulk modulus B to the mass density rho. For air, this yields roughly 343 meters per second, while in water it is about 1500 meters per second due to a much higher incompressibility. Human hearing spans frequencies from 20 Hz to 20 kHz and intensities from the threshold of hearing at 10 to the power of negative 12 Watts per meter squared up to the threshold of pain. Because the ear responds logarithmically, sound intensity level L is quantified in decibels using ten times the base ten logarithm of intensity divided by the reference intensity. Example: If a sound intensity is measured at 0.01 Watts per meter squared, the sound level is calculated as L equals 10 times the logarithm of 0.01 divided by 10 to the power of negative 12, which simplifies to 10 times the logarithm of 10 to the power of 10, resulting in exactly 100 decibels. In class exercise: Calculate the acoustic speed in a hypothetical fluid with a bulk modulus of 2.2 gigapascals and a density of 1000 kilograms per cubic meter, and determine the new decibel level if the starting intensity of 10 to the power of negative 9 Watts per meter squared is multiplied by five.

title: Lecture 2: Boundary Interactions and Architectural Acoustics
description: This lecture examines acoustic impedance, wave reflection at material boundaries, and foundational principles of room acoustics and noise control.
content: Learning objectives: Compute acoustic impedance and reflection coefficients at interfaces, and apply Sabine's equation to evaluate reverberation times for rooms. When an acoustic wave strikes a boundary between two different media, part of the wave reflects and part transmits. The extent of reflection is governed by the specific acoustic impedance Z, defined as the product of density rho and wave speed c. The acoustic impedance mismatch determines the pressure and intensity reflection coefficients. In architectural acoustics, managing these reflections is critical for speech intelligibility and music quality. Sound absorption by interior surfaces reduces reflections, which is quantified through Sabine's empirical reverberation formula. Sabine's reverberation time T is given by 0.161 multiplied by the room volume V in cubic meters, divided by the total absorption area A in metric sabins. Example: Consider a lecture hall with a volume of 500 cubic meters and a total surface absorption area of 25 metric sabins. The reverberation time T is calculated as 0.161 times 500 divided by 25, which equals 80.5 divided by 25, yielding a reverberation time of 3.22 seconds. This long reverberation time would cause severe echo and speech blurring, requiring additional acoustic treatment. In class exercise: If the total absorption area in the same 500 cubic meter room is increased to 100 metric sabins by adding wall panels, compute the new reverberation time using Sabine's formula.

title: Lecture 3: Transducer Technologies and Electroacoustic Systems
description: This lecture explores the operating principles of microphones, loudspeakers, and piezoelectric elements used in acoustic sensing and generation.
content: Learning objectives: Differentiate between acoustic transduction mechanisms, analyze piezoelectric behavior, and evaluate electroacoustic conversion efficiency. Transducers act as the bridge between electrical signals and mechanical acoustic waves. Common microphones and loudspeakers rely on electromagnetic, electrostatic, or dynamic principles, converting diaphragm motion into electrical voltage or vice versa. For high frequency applications and ultrasound generation, piezoelectric elements are standard. These materials, such as lead zirconate titanate, exhibit direct and inverse piezoelectric effects, straining when an electric field is applied or generating charge under mechanical stress. The efficiency of these devices depends on matching electrical driving impedances to the mechanical load of the medium. Example: A piezoelectric crystal driven by a sinusoidal voltage produces a displacement wave in a medium where the longitudinal wave speed is 4000 meters per second. If the driving frequency is set to 2 megahertz, the wavelength lambda of the ultrasound inside the crystal medium is computed as speed divided by frequency, yielding 4000 meters per second divided by 2 million Hertz, which equals 0.002 meters or 2 millimeters. In class exercise: Determine the operational frequency required for a piezoelectric transducer to emit an ultrasound wave with a wavelength of 0.5 millimeters in a solid material where sound travels at 6000 meters per second.

title: Lecture 4: Ultrasonic Waves, Attenuation, and Industrial Applications
description: This lecture covers the generation, propagation characteristics, attenuation, and practical engineering applications of high frequency ultrasound.
content: Learning objectives: Explain ultrasonic wave propagation phenomena, calculate pulse-echo depths, and analyze non-destructive testing and medical imaging techniques. Ultrasonics involves acoustic waves with frequencies exceeding the upper limit of human hearing, typically above 20 kHz. Because high frequency waves have short wavelengths, they can be formed into directional beams and used for high resolution imaging and flaw detection. As ultrasound travels through matter, it experiences attenuation due to absorption and scattering, meaning intensity decreases exponentially with distance. In pulse-echo systems, a transducer emits a short pulse and measures the time delay of the returning echo. Using the known propagation speed in the medium, engineers can accurately locate internal structures or defects. Example: In a medical ultrasound scan, a pulse is sent into soft tissue where the average sound speed is 1540 meters per second. If the reflection echo returns after a total round-trip time delay of 30 microseconds, the depth of the reflecting boundary is calculated as speed multiplied by time divided by 2, which is 1540 meters per second multiplied by 30 times 10 to the power of negative 6 seconds, divided by 2, yielding 0.0231 meters or 2.31 centimeters. In class exercise: Calculate the round-trip time delay for an ultrasonic flaw detector inspecting a steel block with a longitudinal wave speed of 5900 meters per second when a defect is located exactly 5 centimeters deep.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Acoustic and Ultrasonic Engineering Problems
description: This assignment assesses student mastery of wave equations, decibel manipulations, acoustic impedance boundaries, room reverberation, and pulse-echo calculations.
content:
1. Calculate the acoustic impedance of sea water given a density of 1025 kilograms per cubic meter and an acoustic propagation speed of 1500 meters per second. Marks: 3.
2. Determine the exact decibel increase in sound intensity level when a factory machine increases its sound output intensity from 0.002 Watts per meter squared to 0.016 Watts per meter squared. Marks: 4.
3. A sound wave transitions from air (impedance 400 Pascal seconds per meter) into a dense acoustic tile (impedance 40000 Pascal seconds per meter). Calculate the intensity reflection coefficient at this normal incidence boundary using the standard impedance formula. Marks: 5.
4. A conference room has a volume of 300 cubic meters. Using Sabine's formula, calculate the total absorption area required in metric sabins to achieve an optimal speech reverberation time of exactly 0.6 seconds. Marks: 4.
5. In a non-destructive testing scenario, an ultrasonic transducer operating in an aluminum block (sound speed 6320 meters per second) detects an internal crack reflection after a round-trip time of 25 microseconds. Compute the exact depth of the crack in millimeters. Marks: 4.

title: Lecture 1: Fundamentals of Heat Transfer and Reliability
description: This lecture introduces the core principles of heat transfer modes, thermal degradation, and basic resistance networks in electronic systems.
content: Learning objectives: Understand the empirical relationship between temperature and failure rates, apply fundamental heat transfer modes, and compute junction temperatures using thermal resistance networks. Reliability physics dictates that the semiconductor failure rate approximately doubles for every ten degree Celsius increase in junction temperature, making thermal management mandatory. Heat transfers from the silicon die to the ambient environment through three primary mechanisms: conduction governed by Fourier's law, convection described by Newton's law of cooling, and radiation. For internal package and external heatsink analysis, we use thermal resistance networks analogous to Ohm's law, where temperature acts as voltage, heat dissipation as current, and thermal resistance as electrical resistance. Consider an integrated circuit dissipating 15 watts of power. The junction-to-case resistance is 0.8 degrees Celsius per watt, the case-to-sink interface resistance is 0.4 degrees Celsius per watt, and the sink-to-ambient resistance is 2.5 degrees Celsius per watt. If the ambient temperature is fixed at 35 degrees Celsius, we first sum the resistances to find total thermal resistance: 0.8 plus 0.4 plus 2.5 equals 3.7 degrees Celsius per watt. Multiplying this total resistance by the 15 watt power dissipation yields a temperature rise of 55.5 degrees Celsius. Adding the 35 degree ambient temperature results in a final junction temperature of 90.5 degrees Celsius. In class exercise: Calculate the junction temperature for a device dissipating 8 watts with a total thermal resistance of 5.0 degrees Celsius per watt in a 25 degree ambient environment.

title: Lecture 2: Convective Cooling and Heat Sink Optimization
description: This lecture explores the design, material selection, and optimization of heat sinks and forced air convection mechanisms.
content: Learning objectives: Evaluate fin efficiency for extended surfaces, compare aluminum versus copper heat sink materials, and analyze forced air cooling performance. When natural convection is insufficient to maintain safe operating temperatures, engineers employ extended surfaces known as heat sinks, combined with forced airflow generated by fans. The overall thermal performance depends heavily on the convective heat transfer coefficient, surface area, and fin efficiency. While copper offers superior thermal conductivity compared to aluminum, aluminum remains the dominant choice due to its lower cost and lighter weight. Fans drive air through the fin channels, but designers must carefully account for system pressure drop against fan curves to ensure the required volumetric flow rate is achieved. Consider a rectangular aluminum fin array subjected to forced convection with a convective heat transfer coefficient of 40 watts per square meter Kelvin. The total effective surface area of the fins is 0.15 square meters, and the temperature difference between the base and the ambient air is 40 degrees Celsius. Using the convective heat transfer equation, the heat dissipated by the fins is calculated by multiplying the heat transfer coefficient by the area and the temperature difference: 40 times 0.15 times 40, which equals 240 watts. In class exercise: Determine the heat dissipation for a finned surface with an area of 0.08 square meters, a heat transfer coefficient of 50 watts per square meter Kelvin, and a temperature difference of 30 degrees Celsius.

title: Lecture 3: Advanced Thermal Solutions and Two-Phase Devices
description: This lecture covers advanced cooling technologies including heat pipes, vapor chambers, liquid cooling loops, and thermoelectric modules.
content: Learning objectives: Explain the operating principles of two-phase heat transfer devices, identify applications requiring liquid cooling, and analyze thermoelectric cooler limits. As power densities in modern electronics soar beyond the limits of air cooling, advanced thermal solutions become necessary. Heat pipes and vapor chambers exploit latent heat by utilizing a sealed phase-change cycle where a working fluid vaporizes at the evaporator, travels to the condenser, and returns via capillary action through a porous wick structure. For extreme heat fluxes found in high-performance computing, direct liquid cooling loops pump fluids with high specific heat capacity through cold plates attached directly to processor packages. Thermoelectric coolers, operating on the Peltier effect, allow active sub-ambient cooling but introduce inefficiency due to Joule heating and parasitic power consumption. Consider a vapor chamber transporting 200 watts of thermal energy over a short distance with an effective thermal resistance of 0.05 degrees Celsius per watt. The temperature drop across the vapor chamber is calculated by multiplying the heat load by the thermal resistance: 200 watts times 0.05 degrees Celsius per watt, resulting in a minor temperature drop of 10.0 degrees Celsius. In class exercise: Calculate the temperature drop across a heat pipe operating at a 50 watt heat load with an effective thermal resistance of 0.2 degrees Celsius per watt.

title: Lecture 4: Printed Circuit Board Thermal Design and Testing
description: This lecture addresses board-level thermal management techniques, thermal simulation methodologies, and empirical measurement validation.
content: Learning objectives: Design effective thermal paths on printed circuit boards using copper planes and vias, and apply measurement tools like thermocouples and infrared cameras. Thermal management begins at the printed circuit board level, where internal copper planes act as spreading spreaders to conduct heat away from surface-mounted components. Because FR4 is a poor thermal conductor, designers insert arrays of plated through-hole thermal vias directly beneath high-power components to channel heat down to internal or bottom-side ground planes. To validate these designs, thermal engineers rely on computer-aided engineering simulation tools coupled with physical testing using calibrated thermocouples and infrared thermography cameras. Consider a printed circuit board thermal via array consisting of 25 individual copper-plated vias. Each via has a thermal resistance of 400 degrees Celsius per watt. Assuming the vias act thermally in parallel, the equivalent thermal resistance of the array is calculated by dividing the individual resistance by the total number of vias: 400 divided by 25, which equals 16.0 degrees Celsius per watt. In class exercise: Compute the equivalent thermal resistance of an array of 50 thermal vias, each having a resistance of 600 degrees Celsius per watt connected in parallel.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Thermal Management Analysis
description: Students will solve four practical engineering problems covering thermal resistance networks, fin design, advanced cooling limits, and PCB thermal via optimization.
content:
Task 1: Calculate the junction temperature of a power transistor dissipating 12 watts, given a junction-to-case resistance of 0.5 degrees Celsius per watt, a thermal interface material resistance of 0.3 degrees Celsius per watt, a heatsink resistance of 2.0 degrees Celsius per watt, and an ambient temperature of 45 degrees Celsius. (5 marks)

Task 2: A forced-air cooled aluminum heat sink has a base temperature of 80 degrees Celsius in an ambient air temperature of 30 degrees Celsius. If the total convective heat dissipation is 100 watts, determine the required convective heat transfer coefficient given a total effective fin surface area of 0.12 square meters. (5 marks)

Task 3: Compare a standard solid copper spreading plate with a vapor chamber for a high-power graphics processing unit dissipating 300 watts. If the solid plate introduces a temperature drop of 25 degrees Celsius and the vapor chamber introduces 6 degrees Celsius, calculate the percentage improvement in thermal resistance provided by the vapor chamber. (5 marks)

Task 4: Design a thermal via array for a surface-mount voltage regulator dissipating 5 watts. If the maximum allowable temperature rise from the board surface to the internal copper plane is 15 degrees Celsius, determine the minimum number of parallel thermal vias required if each via has a thermal resistance of 500 degrees Celsius per watt. (5 marks)

title: Lecture 1: Hardware and Data Foundations
description: This lecture explores physical computer components and how machines represent numbers and text internally using binary and hexadecimal systems.
content:
Learning objectives: Understand how the CPU interacts with memory and buses, and master conversions between binary, hexadecimal, and decimal formats.

At the core of any computing system lies the von Neumann architecture, which connects the central processing unit, memory modules, input and output peripherals, and system buses. The central processing unit executes instructions, while primary memory or random access memory provides volatile, fast workspace. Secondary storage retains data permanently. Because digital circuits operate using electrical voltage states, data is represented fundamentally in binary using zeros and ones. Grouping binary digits yields hexadecimal notation for human readability. For example, to convert the hexadecimal value 0x3A into decimal, you multiply the first digit by sixteen and add the second digit. Here, three times sixteen is forty-eight, and ten from the letter A gives fifty-eight in decimal.

In class exercise: Convert the hexadecimal value 0x4B into a decimal number, showing each step of your multiplication and addition clearly.

title: Lecture 2: Software Systems and Problem Solving
description: This lecture bridges physical hardware with logical execution by examining operating systems, translators, and algorithmic problem solving techniques.
content:
Learning objectives: Distinguish between compilers and interpreters, and design structured algorithms using flowcharts and pseudocode.

Software orchestrates hardware resources to perform useful tasks. Operating systems manage memory allocation and hardware drivers, whereas application software serves end users directly. To execute human-written source code, translators are required. Compilers translate the entire source code into machine code prior to execution, optimizing performance. Interpreters translate and execute code line by line at runtime, offering flexibility during debugging. Before writing any code, programmers must design robust algorithms. An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure for solving a problem, which can be visualized through flowcharts or written in plain language as pseudocode.

In class exercise: Write pseudocode for an algorithm that takes a list of integer scores, iterates through them, and calculates their mathematical average.

title: Lecture 3: Programming Essentials and Networks
description: This lecture introduces fundamental programming constructs alongside the architectural principles of computer networks and the Internet.
content:
Learning objectives: Implement basic control structures in code and explain how data travels across interconnected networks using standard protocols.

Programming basics allow us to instruct computers dynamically. Variables store data values in memory, associated with specific data types like integers, floats, or strings. Conditional statements direct execution paths based on evaluated boolean expressions, while loops automate repetitive tasks. Functions encapsulate reusable logic blocks. Moving beyond single machines, computer networks link systems together. Devices on the internet rely on internet protocol addresses for identification and routing. The web, email systems, and cloud services all operate on top of these foundational networking layers to deliver distributed computing power.

In class exercise: Trace a loop that starts with a variable count set to zero and increments by two until count reaches six, listing the value of count at each iteration.

title: Lecture 4: Information Systems, Security, and Ethics
description: This lecture surveys database fundamentals, emerging information systems, and critical practices in cybersecurity and digital ethics.
content:
Learning objectives: Understand the role of databases in information systems and identify key strategies for mitigating malware and protecting personal privacy.

Modern organizations rely heavily on databases and information systems to store, retrieve, and process vast quantities of structured data efficiently. Relational databases organize information into tables with rows and columns, establishing relationships between different entities. However, managing digital assets introduces significant security and ethical challenges. Cyber threats such as malware, ransomware, and phishing attacks continuously target vulnerabilities in software and human behavior. Effective defense mechanisms include robust password policies, encryption, and regular system patching. Furthermore, professionals must respect intellectual property rights and user privacy regulations.

In class exercise: Discuss in pairs one real-world consequence of a weak password policy and propose two methods to strengthen user authentication.

title: Lecture 1: Introduction to Program Structure and Data Types
description: This lecture introduces the foundational architecture of programs, basic input and output operations, and how memory stores different variable types.
content: Learning Objectives: Understand how source code transforms into an executable program, and master the declaration and manipulation of primitive data types and arithmetic operators. To build any software, you must first understand how computers process instructions sequentially. A program begins execution at a designated entry point and runs line by line. We use variables as named memory containers to store data. In strongly typed languages like C++, you must declare a type before using a variable. Common types include integers for whole numbers, doubles for decimals, characters for single symbols, booleans for true or false values, and strings for text. Operators allow us to perform calculations, but we must remain mindful of operator precedence and integer division. For example, dividing the integer 5 by the integer 2 yields 2, not 2.5, because fractional parts are truncated during integer division. Consider this worked example for calculating the average of three scores: int score1 = 85; int score2 = 90; int score3 = 95; double average = (score1 + score2 + score3) / 3.0; here, dividing by 3.0 instead of 3 ensures floating-point division occurs, resulting in 90.0. Common pitfalls include using the assignment operator equals instead of the equality operator double equals, and leaving variables uninitialized. In class exercise: write a short code snippet that declares an integer for temperature in Fahrenheit, converts it to Celsius using the formula Celsius equals Fahrenheit minus 32 times 5 divided by 9, and prints the result.

title: Lecture 2: Control Flow via Selection and Repetition
description: This lecture explores decision-making structures and looping constructs used to control the execution path of a program.
content: Learning Objectives: Implement conditional branching using if-else statements and switches, and construct efficient loops with proper initialization and termination conditions. Programs rarely run in a straight line; they must make decisions and repeat tasks. Selection statements like if, else if, else, and switch allow your program to execute specific blocks of code based on dynamic conditions. When tasks need to be repeated, we rely on iteration loops: for loops when the iteration count is known, and while or do-while loops when repetition depends on a dynamic condition. Counters track iterations, accumulators maintain running totals, and sentinel values signal the end of user input. Using break and continue statements grants finer control over loop execution. A classic error in looping is the off-by-one boundary mistake, such as running a loop one time too many or too few. Consider this worked example summing numbers from 1 to 3: int total = 0; for(int count = 1; count <= 3; count++) { total += count; } tracing this execution gives count 1, total 1; count 2, total 3; count 3, total 6. The final output stored in total is 6. Always ensure your loop variables are correctly initialized and updated so you avoid infinite loops. In class exercise: write a while loop that reads positive integers from the user until a negative sentinel value is entered, and then prints the total sum of all positive numbers entered.

title: Lecture 3: Modular Programming with Functions and Scope
description: This lecture covers the creation of modular code using functions, parameter passing mechanisms, variable scope, and recursion.
content: Learning Objectives: Design reusable functions with appropriate parameters and return values, distinguish between pass by value and pass by reference, and grasp basic recursion. As programs grow larger, placing all code in a single main routine becomes unmaintainable. Functions allow us to break complex problems into smaller, manageable sub-problems. When defining a function, you specify its return type, name, and parameter list. Arguments can be passed by value, meaning the function receives a copy of the data, or by reference, allowing the function to modify the original variable directly using the address-of or reference operator. Variable scope dictates where a variable can be accessed; local variables exist only within their defining block, whereas global variables persist throughout the program. Recursion occurs when a function calls itself to solve a smaller instance of the same problem, requiring a clear base case to prevent infinite recursion. Consider this worked example of a function calculating a factorial recursively: int factorial(int n) { if(n <= 1) return 1; return n * factorial(n - 1); } calling factorial(3) computes 3 times factorial(2), which computes 2 times factorial(1), returning a final product of 6. In class exercise: write a function that takes an integer reference and doubles its value in place without returning anything.

title: Lecture 4: Managing Data Structures and Effective Debugging
description: This lecture examines arrays, string manipulation, sorting techniques, and systematic debugging methodologies.
content: Learning Objectives: Store and traverse collections of data using arrays, implement basic searching and sorting algorithms, and systematically isolate syntax and logic errors. When programs need to handle collections of related data, single variables are no longer sufficient. Arrays provide a contiguous block of memory to store multiple elements of the same type, indexed starting at zero. Traversing an array typically involves a for loop that visits each index sequentially. Beyond traversal, you can write algorithms to search for specific elements or perform simple sorting, such as bubble sort, to order data. Programming inevitably involves errors. Syntax errors prevent the program from compiling, whereas logic errors allow compilation but produce incorrect results. Tracing tables help developers manually track variable values step by step across execution time. Additionally, testing edge cases—such as empty inputs, maximum boundaries, or negative numbers—ensures your code is robust. Consider this worked example finding the maximum value in an array: int nums[] = {4, 9, 2}; int maxVal = nums[0]; for(int i = 1; i < 3; i++) { if(nums[i] > maxVal) maxVal = nums[i]; } the loop evaluates 9 and 2 against the initial maximum of 4, correctly concluding that maxVal is 9. In class exercise: write a snippet that initializes an array of five integers and prints them in reverse order.

content:

2. Implement a function named isEven that accepts an integer parameter and returns true if the number is even and false otherwise. In your main function, use a loop to test this function with numbers 1 through 5 and print the corresponding boolean outputs. (Marks: 4)

5. Write a complete program that populates an array of 5 integers with user input, calls a sorting function to arrange them in ascending order, and prints the sorted array to the console. (Marks: 5)

title: Lecture 1: Foundations of Classes and Encapsulation
description: This lecture introduces the core mechanics of defining user-defined types, managing object lifecycles, and protecting internal state through information hiding.
content: Learning objectives: Understand how to structure state and behavior inside a class blueprint, and learn to restrict direct data access using access specifiers. In object-oriented programming, a class acts as a template defining fields for state and methods for behavior. Constructors initialize memory upon instantiation, while destructors handle teardown. Encapsulation bundles this data together while keeping variables private to prevent unauthorized external mutation. For example, consider a BankAccount class with a private balance field. Direct access from outside is blocked. Instead, we provide public methods: deposit(double amount) which checks if amount > 0 before adding it to the balance, and getBalance() which returns the current total. If an account starts with 100.0 and we call deposit(50.0), the balance safely becomes 150.0. This prevents invalid states, such as a negative balance set arbitrarily by external code. In class exercise: Write a Person class with private string name and int age fields, a constructor that validates age is non-negative, and a public getter method for the name.

title: Lecture 2: Inheritance and Polymorphism
description: This lecture explores hierarchical code reuse through derived classes and dynamic dispatch via virtual functions.
content: Learning objectives: Master the syntax and semantics of class inheritance, and implement runtime polymorphism using virtual functions. Inheritance allows a derived class to inherit fields and methods from a base class, establishing an is-a relationship. When base methods are marked virtual, derived classes can override them to provide specialized behavior. Dynamic binding ensures that the correct overridden method executes at runtime even when accessed via base class pointers. Consider a base class Employee with a virtual method double calculatePay(). A derived class SalariedEmployee overrides this to return a fixed monthly rate of 4000.0, whereas another derived class HourlyEmployee overrides it to calculate hours multiplied by rate, yielding 1600.0 for 40 hours at 40.0 per hour. If we store both in a container of Employee pointers and loop through them calling calculatePay(), the program correctly computes the specific salary or hourly wage for each object dynamically. In class exercise: Create a base class Animal with a virtual makeSound method, and a derived class Cat that overrides it to print meow.

title: Lecture 3: Advanced C++ Features and Relationships
description: This lecture covers structural design choices like composition versus inheritance, along with C++ specific features like static members, friend functions, and operator overloading.
content: Learning objectives: Differentiate between has-a composition and is-a inheritance, and apply operator overloading and friend mechanisms safely. Composition models has-a relationships where an object contains other objects as member variables, which is often favored over deep inheritance hierarchies to reduce coupling. Static members belong to the class rather than any single instance, sharing state globally across all objects. Friend functions grant non-member functions access to private class internals. Operator overloading lets developers redefine standard operators for custom types. For example, consider a Vector2D class representing a 2D coordinate with x and y. We can overload the plus operator such that Vector2D v3 = v1 + v2 adds their respective x and y coordinates. If v1 is (1.0, 2.0) and v2 is (3.0, 4.0), the resulting vector v3 holds coordinates (4.0, 6.0). This makes mathematical and geometric code much more readable than calling explicit add methods. In class exercise: Overload the equality operator for a Point class comparing two coordinates.

title: Lecture 4: Exception Handling and Design Principles
description: This lecture addresses robust error management techniques and architectural guidelines using SOLID principles and UML modeling.
content: Learning objectives: Implement try-catch-throw blocks for runtime error handling, and design maintainable software using SOLID principles and UML diagrams. Exceptions separate normal execution logic from error handling. When an unrecoverable state occurs, code throws an exception object, which propagates up the call stack until a matching catch block handles it. Architectural design relies on SOLID principles, where each class should have a single responsibility, and UML class diagrams visually map out these relationships. For example, consider a division function that takes two numbers, numerator and denominator. If the denominator equals 0.0, the function throws a runtime_error with the message division by zero. The calling code wraps this inside a try block. If the error occurs, execution jumps immediately to the catch block, printing the error message instead of crashing the program. In class exercise: Write a try-catch block that attempts to parse a string to an integer and catches invalid argument exceptions.

2. Create a derived class Book that inherits from LibraryItem, adds a private int pageCount field, overrides displayInfo(), and correctly invokes the base constructor via constructor chaining. (4 marks)

5. Add exception handling to the item addition method so that attempting to add an item with a duplicate ID throws a custom DuplicateItemException caught gracefully in the main function. (4 marks)

title: Lecture 1: Asymptotic Analysis, Arrays, and Linked Lists
description: This lecture introduces asymptotic notation to measure algorithm efficiency alongside foundational linear data structures like dynamic arrays and linked lists.
content: Learning objectives: Master Big-O notation for worst-case analysis and differentiate memory allocation trade-offs between contiguous arrays and pointer-based linked lists. When analyzing algorithms, we evaluate how execution time scales with input size n. For instance, an algorithm checking all pairs in a list uses nested loops, resulting in O(n^2) growth, whereas a binary search halves the search space each step, yielding O(log n). Contiguous arrays permit random access in O(1) time via index arithmetic, but resizing a dynamic array requires allocating a larger block, copying elements, and achieving an amortized O(1) append cost. Conversely, linked lists consist of nodes containing data and reference pointers. Consider a singly linked list with nodes containing values 10, 20, and 30 in sequence. Inserting a new node with value 15 immediately after the head node requires updating only two pointers: the new node points to the node holding 20, and the head points to the new node. This pointer redirection takes strictly O(1) time once the position is located. However, finding an arbitrary value like 30 requires traversing the list sequentially from the head, resulting in O(n) search time due to the lack of direct indexing. In class exercise: Draw the memory layout of a doubly linked list after inserting node X between nodes A and B, writing out the four pointer updates required.

title: Lecture 2: Stacks, Queues, and Trees
description: This lecture examines hierarchical data structures and restricted access linear structures used for parsing expressions and hierarchical traversal.
content: Learning objectives: Implement LIFO and FIFO structures, and perform depth-first and breadth-first traversals on binary trees. Stacks process elements via Last-In-First-Out rules where push and pop operations occur at one end in O(1) time, making them ideal for tracking active function scopes. Queues follow First-In-First-Out semantics. Expanding beyond linear models, trees represent hierarchical relationships. A binary search tree maintains the invariant where every node in the left subtree holds a value less than the parent, and the right subtree holds greater values. Consider inserting numbers in this exact sequence: 50, 30, 70, 20, and 40 into an initially empty binary search tree. First, 50 becomes the root. Next, 30 is placed as the left child of 50. Then, 70 is placed as the right child of 50. Afterwards, 20 goes to the left of 30. Finally, 40 goes to the right of 30. To read these values in sorted order, we apply an inorder traversal which visits the left subtree, processes the root, and visits the right subtree. Following this recursive path for our constructed tree, the printed sequence evaluates strictly to: 20, 30, 40, 50, and 70. Self-balancing trees like AVL trees prevent performance degradation by maintaining height constraints. In class exercise: Trace the push and pop operations on an empty stack given the sequence of inputs: push 5, push 2, pop, push 8, pop, pop.

title: Lecture 3: Heaps, Priority Queues, and Hash Tables
description: This lecture explores priority management through binary heaps and rapid key-value association using hash tables with collision resolution strategies.
content: Learning objectives: Build and manipulate binary heaps for priority queues and analyze collision resolution techniques in hash tables. A binary heap is a complete binary tree satisfying the heap property, where every parent node contains a key less than or equal to its children in a min-heap. Inserting a new element appends it to the next available bottom-level position, followed by an upward bubbling phase taking O(log n) time. Priority queues leverage heaps to extract the minimum element efficiently in O(log n) time. Hash tables achieve near-instantaneous average O(1) lookups by applying a hash function to map keys to array indices. However, two distinct keys may map to the same index, causing a collision. To handle collisions, chaining stores a linked list of entries at each array index, while open addressing probes for the next available slot using linear or quadratic probing. A hash table degrades from its optimal average O(1) performance down to O(n) lookup time when a poor hash function or an excessive number of insertions without resizing maps every single key into the exact same bucket, transforming the table into a single linear linked list of entries. In class exercise: Compute the index for key 45 in a hash table of size 7 using the modulo hash function h(k) = k mod 7.

title: Lecture 4: Graphs and Sorting Algorithms
description: This lecture covers graph traversal algorithms and comparison-based sorting techniques with their respective time and space complexities.
content: Learning objectives: Represent graphs using adjacency matrices and lists, execute graph traversals, and contrast sorting algorithm efficiencies. Graphs model networks using vertices and edges, which can be directed or undirected and weighted or unweighted. In memory, sparse graphs are typically stored as adjacency lists, consuming O(V plus E) space, whereas dense graphs favor adjacency matrices requiring O(V squared) space. Breadth-first search uses a queue to explore neighbors level by level, whereas depth-first search uses a stack or recursion to explore as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking. Sorting organizes elements into a defined order. Elementary sorting algorithms like bubble sort and insertion sort compare adjacent elements iteratively, yielding an inefficient worst-case time complexity of O(n squared). In contrast, advanced algorithms employ divide-and-conquer strategies. Merge sort divides the array into halves, sorts them recursively, and merges the results, while quick sort partitions elements around a chosen pivot. Both merge sort and quick sort guarantee an optimal average time complexity of O(n log n) for comparison-based sorting. In class exercise: Trace the first complete partition step of quick sort on the array with elements 7, 2, 1, 6, 8 using 6 as the pivot.

1. Implement a standard queue data structure using two separate stacks without utilizing any built-in queue libraries. Your implementation must support enqueue and dequeue operations, explaining how the amortized cost remains efficient. (Marks: 5)
2. Write a recursive function in Python or Java that computes and returns the height of any given binary tree node, stating the base case clearly. (Marks: 4)
3. Given a binary search tree initially empty, simulate the exact insertion of keys in the following order: 60, 20, 80, 10, 40, 70, 90. Output the resulting sequence for a postorder traversal. (Marks: 4)
4. Analyze the worst-case time complexity of a poorly implemented hash table that suffers from continuous clustering during linear probing, and explain how resizing the underlying array mitigates this issue. (Marks: 3)
5. Design an algorithm that takes a directed acyclic graph and determines if a valid topological sort exists, detailing the step-by-step logic and time complexity. (Marks: 4)

title: Lecture 1: Asymptotic Analysis and Divide-and-Conquer Paradigms
description: This lecture establishes the mathematical foundations of algorithm efficiency through asymptotic growth bounds and recursive problem-decomposition techniques.
content: Learning Objectives: Master formal definitions of Big-O, Omega, and Theta notations, apply the Master Theorem to solve standard recurrences, and analyze divide-and-conquer strategies. Asymptotic analysis allows us to evaluate scalability by observing how execution time grows with input size n. To formalize growth rates, we use the Master Theorem for recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n). Consider merge sort, which splits an array of size n into two halves, recursively sorts them, and merges the results in linear time, yielding the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. Comparing this to the Master Theorem cases, a equals 2, b equals 2, and f(n) equals n. Because n equals n to the power of log base 2 of 2, we fall into case 2, resulting in a tight bound of Theta(n log n). For a concrete numerical example, sorting an array of 8 elements requires log base 2 of 8, which is 3 levels of recursion, multiplied by 8 operations per level, totaling 24 fundamental steps. In contrast, an inefficient naive search or naive sorting method would scale quadratically to 64 steps. In class exercise: Apply the Master Theorem to solve the recurrence T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n squared and determine its tight asymptotic bound.

title: Lecture 2: Greedy Choice and Dynamic Programming Strategies
description: This lecture contrasts locally optimal greedy heuristics with exhaustive dynamic programming approaches for optimization problems.
content: Learning Objectives: Identify the greedy-choice property in graph and scheduling problems, recognize overlapping subproblems, and formulate multi-stage dynamic programming solutions. Optimization problems often require making a sequence of choices to achieve the best outcome. Greedy algorithms make the locally optimal choice at each step, hoping to yield a globally optimal solution, as seen in Kruskal algorithm for minimum spanning trees or Huffman coding for data compression. However, when local choices fail due to hidden dependencies, dynamic programming guarantees optimality by storing solutions to overlapping subproblems. For instance, computing the standard Fibonacci sequence recursively results in redundant exponential work of O(2 to the power of n). By introducing memoization or bottom-up tabulation, we store previously computed values in an array. Let us compute F(4) bottom-up: F(0) equals 0, F(1) equals 1, F(2) equals F(1) plus F(0) which is 1, F(3) equals F(2) plus F(1) which is 2, and F(4) equals F(3) plus F(2) which is 3. This reduces the time complexity from exponential to linear O(n) and the space complexity to O(n). In class exercise: Write the bottom-up dynamic programming table values to solve the edit distance between strings cat and cut.

title: Lecture 3: Advanced Graph Exploration and Shortest Path Algorithms
description: This lecture explores sophisticated graph traversal techniques, connectivity algorithms, and shortest path computations under various edge weight constraints.
content: Learning Objectives: Implement breadth-first and depth-first traversals for topological sorting, apply Dijkstra algorithm for non-negative weights, and utilize Bellman-Ford for negative edge detection. Graphs model complex relational data using vertices and edges. When finding the shortest path from a single source, Dijkstra algorithm greedily selects the unvisited vertex with the smallest tentative distance, relaxing all outgoing edges. For example, consider a graph with vertices A, B, and C. Edge AB has weight 2, edge AC has weight 5, and edge BC has weight 1. Starting at A, tentative distances are initialized to A equals 0, B equals infinity, and C equals infinity. We visit B, updating C through B to a distance of 2 plus 1, which equals 3, successfully improving upon the direct path of 5. Dijkstra fails when negative edge weights are present because a greedy choice locks in an incorrect path before accounting for subsequent negative cost reductions. For graphs containing negative weights without negative cycles, the Bellman-Ford algorithm must be used instead, relaxing all edges V minus 1 times. In class exercise: Trace Dijkstra algorithm on a directed graph with 4 nodes where edge weights include negative values to demonstrate the exact point of failure.

title: Lecture 4: Backtracking, Branch-and-Bound, and Computational Intractability
description: This lecture investigates exhaustive search optimization techniques and establishes the theoretical boundaries of polynomial-time computability through NP-completeness.
content: Learning Objectives: Design backtracking algorithms for combinatorial search, optimize search spaces using branch-and-bound pruning, and understand polynomial-time reductions in complexity theory. When problems cannot be solved efficiently by greedy or dynamic programming methods, we often rely on systematic exploration of the solution space. Backtracking builds candidates incrementally, abandoning a path as soon as it violates problem constraints. Consider the N-queens problem: placing 4 queens on a 4 by 4 chessboard such that no two threaten each other. Backtracking places a queen in row 0, column 0, then row 1, column 2, but finds row 2 blocked, prompting an immediate backtrack to try column 3. Branch-and-bound enhances this by maintaining a global best cost to prune subtrees that cannot possibly improve upon the current optimal solution. Beyond exact exponential algorithms, computational theory classifies problems into complexity classes. A problem is in NP if its proposed solution can be verified in polynomial time. We prove hardness by polynomial-time reduction, transforming a known NP-complete problem, such as 3-SAT, into a new problem instance. In class exercise: Draw the search tree for solving the subset sum problem with set elements 2, 3, 5 and target sum 5 using backtracking.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Algorithm Design and Complexity Analysis
description: This assignment evaluates students' mastery of asymptotic analysis, divide-and-conquer recurrences, dynamic programming formulations, graph shortest paths, and complexity reductions.
content:
1. Asymptotic Growth Analysis: Order the following four functions by asymptotic growth rate from slowest to fastest, providing a formal mathematical proof for your ordering: f1(n) = n squared log n, f2(n) = 2 to the power of n, f3(n) = n to the power of 1.5, f4(n) = n log cubed n. (4 marks)
2. Divide and Conquer Recurrence: Use the Master Theorem to find the exact asymptotic Theta bound for the recurrence T(n) = 3T(n/4) + n squared. Show all steps and verify that regularity conditions hold. (4 marks)
3. Dynamic Programming Implementation: Write a Python function that computes the 0/1 knapsack problem using a bottom-up table. Given weights [2, 3, 4, 5] and values [3, 4, 5, 8] with a maximum capacity of 5, state the maximum achievable value and show the final row of the DP table. (4 marks)
4. Graph Shortest Path Trace: Given a directed graph with vertices P, Q, R and edge weights PQ = 4, PR = 2, QR = minus 3, apply the Bellman-Ford algorithm from source P. Show the distance vector after each of the two passes. (4 marks)
5. NP-Completeness Concept: Explain why verifying a solution for the Travelling Salesperson Problem takes polynomial time while finding the optimal tour is believed to require exponential time, defining the classes P and NP in your explanation. (4 marks)

title: Lecture 1: Foundations, Modes, and Processes
description: This lecture introduces the role of the operating system, dual-mode execution, system calls, and the fundamental abstractions of processes and threads.
content: Learning objectives: understand how the kernel protects hardware resources using dual-mode execution, and trace process state transitions alongside the process control block. The operating system acts as both an extended machine that hides hardware complexity and a resource manager that allocates CPU, memory, and devices fairly. User applications execute in user mode with restricted capabilities. When an application requires hardware services, it triggers a trap or software interrupt, shifting the processor into kernel mode to safely execute a system call. Inside the kernel, the process scheduler manages execution units called processes. Each process owns a dedicated address space and a Process Control Block containing its register set, state, and priority. Processes transition through new, ready, running, waiting, and terminated states. For instance, when process A requests disk read operations, the kernel moves process A from the running state to the waiting state and invokes a context switch. A context switch saves the current CPU register values into the PCB of process A, loads the register values from the PCB of the incoming process B into the CPU hardware, and resumes execution at process B. In class exercise: draw the five-state process transition diagram and trace the exact modifications made to the CPU program counter and stack pointer during a context switch from process X to process Y.

title: Lecture 2: CPU Scheduling and Synchronization
description: Students will explore core scheduling algorithms and mechanisms for managing concurrent access to shared resources.
content: Learning objectives: calculate scheduling metrics such as turnaround and waiting time, and implement synchronization constructs to eliminate race conditions. CPU scheduling determines which ready process gets the processor. Non-preemptive and preemptive algorithms optimize metrics including turnaround time and waiting time. Consider three jobs arriving at time zero with CPU burst requirements: Job A takes 8 milliseconds, Job B takes 4 milliseconds, and Job C takes 2 milliseconds. Under First-Come-First-Served scheduling in order A, B, then C, Job A finishes at 8, Job B at 12, and Job C at 14. The waiting times are 0 for Job A, 8 for Job B, and 12 for Job C, yielding an average waiting time of 6.66 milliseconds. Under Shortest Job First, the execution order becomes C, B, then A. Job C finishes at 2, Job B at 6, and Job A at 14. Their waiting times are 0 for Job C, 2 for Job B, and 6 for Job A, reducing the average waiting time to 2.66 milliseconds. Concurrently running processes often share data structures, causing race conditions in critical sections. To prevent race conditions, synchronization primitives like mutexes and counting semaphores enforce mutual exclusion. A semaphore uses an internal integer counter protected by atomic operations. In class exercise: write the pseudo-code for a producer-consumer bounded buffer using two semaphores named empty and full, ensuring no buffer overflows occur.

title: Lecture 3: Deadlock and Memory Management
description: This lecture covers deadlock characterization, prevention, the banker algorithm, virtual memory paging, and page replacement.
content: Learning objectives: evaluate system safety using the banker algorithm and compute page fault rates for different replacement policies. Deadlock occurs when a set of blocked processes each hold a resource and wait for another resource acquired by another process. Four necessary conditions must hold simultaneously: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. To avoid deadlocks, the banker algorithm examines resource allocation requests dynamically. Consider a system with available resources of vector (3, 3, 2) and three processes P0, P1, and P2. Given current allocation matrices and maximum demand matrices, the algorithm simulates requests to verify if a safe sequence exists that allows all processes to finish without entering an unsafe state. Beyond CPU and deadlock, memory management maps virtual addresses to physical memory. Paging divides physical memory into fixed-size frames and logical memory into pages of the same size. A page table translates virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers, accelerated by a Translation Lookaside Buffer. When a referenced page is not resident in physical memory, a page fault triggers. Using the Least Recently Used replacement policy with 3 memory frames and the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, the first four references cause compulsory misses. As execution continues, LRU evicts the page that has not been used for the longest time, resulting in a total of 10 page faults. In class exercise: compute the final page fault count if the reference string uses an optimal replacement policy instead.

title: Lecture 4: File Systems and Input Output Fundamentals
description: This final lecture investigates storage organization, file allocation strategies, directory structures, and input output subsystem architecture.
content: Learning objectives: analyze file block allocation methods and explain the layered structure of operating system input output software. File systems provide long-term data storage by organizing raw disk blocks into logical files and hierarchical directories. The operating system must map logical file structures to physical disk blocks using various allocation methods. Contiguous allocation assigns each file to a set of contiguous blocks on the disk, which enables rapid sequential and direct access but suffers from external fragmentation and difficulty in growing files dynamically. Linked allocation maintains a pointer in each disk block pointing to the next block of the file, eliminating external fragmentation and allowing files to grow easily, though random access becomes inefficient because the system must traverse pointers sequentially. Indexed allocation brings all pointers together into an index block, combining the benefits of direct access and flexible file sizing without external fragmentation. Underlying these file operations is the input output subsystem. The kernel standardizes device access through device drivers, manages buffering and caching to smooth out performance discrepancies between fast CPUs and slow peripheral devices, and handles interrupts generated by hardware controllers upon I/O completion. In class exercise: calculate the maximum file size supported by an inode containing 12 direct pointers, one single indirect pointer, one double indirect pointer, and one triple indirect pointer, assuming a block size of 4 kilobytes and 4-byte block pointers.

content:

title: Lecture 1: File Systems and Mass Storage Architecture
description: This lecture explores advanced file system structures, allocation techniques, journaling mechanics, and disk scheduling algorithms for mass storage optimization.
content: Learning objectives: understand inode-based block allocation, analyze disk scheduling performance metrics, and explain how journaling ensures data integrity. Modern operating systems manage persistent data using sophisticated structures. Inode allocation separates file metadata from actual data blocks, pointing directly to direct, indirect, doubly indirect, and triply indirect blocks to support very large files efficiently. To prevent data corruption during unexpected power losses, journaling file systems write transaction intentions to a log before committing modifications to the primary disk structure. For instance, updating a file size of 2 megabytes with a block size of 4 kilobytes requires allocating 512 data blocks plus metadata updates; journaling records these operations sequentially so that recovery requires simply replaying or rolling back incomplete transactions. Mass storage performance relies heavily on disk arm scheduling. Consider a disk request queue with cylinders 82, 170, 43, 140, 24, 16, 190, and head currently at cylinder 50. Using the Shortest Seek Time First algorithm, the head services requests closest to its current position, moving from 50 to 43 (distance 7), then 24 (distance 19), 16 (distance 8), 82 (distance 66), 140 (distance 58), 170 (distance 30), and finally 190 (distance 20), yielding a total seek movement of 208 cylinders. In class exercise: calculate the total head movement for the same request queue using the SCAN algorithm starting direction toward higher numbered cylinders.

title: Lecture 2: I/O Subsystems and Protection Mechanisms
description: This lecture covers hardware-software interfaces, interrupt handling, direct memory access, and granular system protection and security architectures.
content: Learning objectives: trace the lifecycle of an I/O request using interrupts and DMA, and design robust access control schemes using lists and capabilities. Input and output management forms the backbone of operating system responsiveness. When a peripheral device requires attention, it triggers a hardware interrupt, saving the current central processing unit state and jumping to a specific kernel interrupt service routine. To prevent central processing unit saturation during high-throughput block transfers, Direct Memory Access controllers take over data movement between devices and main memory, raising an interrupt only after an entire buffer transfer is complete. For example, transferring a 64 kilobyte network packet byte-by-byte via programmed I/O would consume thousands of central processing unit cycles; instead, a Direct Memory Access controller initiates a single burst transfer, freeing the processor to execute other user processes. Security and protection dictate how subjects access objects within the system. Access Control Lists attach a list of authorized users and permissions directly to each resource object, whereas capabilities act as unforgeable tokens given to domains, specifying exact operational rights. Suppose a file object requires an Access Control List containing user Alice with read-write permissions and user Bob with read-only permissions; checking permission involves traversing the list upon every system open call, while capability systems verify the token directly. In class exercise: outline the exact steps taken by the kernel when a disk Direct Memory Access transfer finishes.

title: Lecture 3: Virtualization and Containerization
description: This lecture examines hardware virtualization layers, hypervisor types, and operating system-level container isolation technologies.
content: Learning objectives: contrast type 1 and type 2 hypervisors, and explain how namespaces and control groups enable lightweight containerization. Virtualization abstracts physical hardware, allowing multiple isolated operating system instances to run concurrently. Type 1 hypervisors run directly on bare metal for optimal performance and efficiency, while type 2 hypervisors run as applications on top of a conventional host operating system. Containers represent a paradigm shift, utilizing host kernel virtualization features rather than virtualizing full hardware stacks. Linux containers achieve isolation primarily through namespaces, which restrict what a process can see, and control groups, which limit resource consumption such as central processing unit shares and memory limits. For example, configuring a control group limit of 512 megabytes on a container process ensures that if the process attempts to allocate 600 megabytes, the kernel memory subsystem invokes the out-of-memory killer within that specific control group context without crashing the host system. Similarly, mounting a isolated mount namespace ensures the container views a private root filesystem directory tree. In class exercise: write a conceptual command line description of how a process is restricted to a separate process identification namespace.

title: Lecture 4: Distributed Operating Systems and Multiprocessor Scheduling
description: This lecture investigates symmetric multiprocessing load balancing strategies and distributed file system coordination in networked environments.
content: Learning objectives: analyze symmetric multiprocessing scheduling policies, evaluate load balancing algorithms, and understand distributed file system consistency. Multiprocessor and distributed systems extend operating system principles across multiple computing nodes and processing cores. In symmetric multiprocessing architectures, every core has equal access to system resources, requiring sophisticated scheduling algorithms like the Completely Fair Scheduler to balance threads and minimize cache misses. Load balancing dynamically redistributes workloads from heavily loaded processor queues to idle or lightly loaded queues. Consider a dual-core system where core 1 has a run queue load metric of 80 and core 2 has a load metric of 10; push migration will automatically transfer runnable threads from core 1 to core 2 until equilibrium is reached within acceptable threshold limits. Distributed file systems enable transparent access to files stored on remote network servers, requiring robust protocols to handle network latency and concurrent modifications. For instance, caching file blocks locally on client machines improves read performance, but introduces cache consistency challenges when another client updates the master file on the server storage node. In class exercise: describe how a distributed lock manager prevents race conditions when two remote nodes attempt to modify the same file block simultaneously.

title: Lecture 1: Von Neumann Architecture and Instruction Set Architecture
description: This lecture introduces the foundational hardware components of a computer and how different instruction set architectures dictate software execution.
content:
Learning objectives: Understand the core components of the Von Neumann model and analyze the differences between RISC and CISC design philosophies.

The Von Neumann architecture organizes a computer system into a central processing unit containing the arithmetic logic unit, control unit, and registers, alongside main memory, input-output devices, and system buses that transfer data. The instruction set architecture acts as the abstract interface between hardware and software, defining instruction formats and addressing modes such as immediate, direct, register, indirect, and indexed. Addressing modes dictate how the operand of an instruction is located. For instance, consider an immediate addressing mode instruction like addi $t0, $s0, 5, where the value 5 is encoded directly within the instruction bits, avoiding any extra memory access. In contrast, indirect addressing uses a register to hold the memory address of the actual data. RISC architectures prioritize a small, highly optimized set of fixed-length instructions executed in a single clock cycle, whereas CISC architectures feature variable-length instructions capable of performing complex memory-to-memory operations.

In class exercise: Determine the exact memory address accessed by an indexed instruction where the base register holds 2000 and the index offset is 32, assuming byte-addressable memory.

title: Lecture 2: Assembly Programming and Computer Arithmetic
description: Students will learn how to write low-level assembly routines and perform fundamental binary arithmetic operations including floating point representation.
content:
Learning objectives: Translate high-level control structures into MIPS assembly and execute signed integer and IEEE 754 floating point arithmetic.

Assembly programming exposes the raw mechanics of arithmetic, conditional branching, loops, and procedure calls utilizing a runtime stack. High-level structures like a for-loop require a loop counter, a conditional branch instruction to terminate execution, and a jump to repeat the body. Computer arithmetic operates primarily on two's complement numbers to handle negative values seamlessly, where overflow occurs if the sign of the result does not match the operands in an addition. Multiplication and division rely on shifted partial products or restoring division hardware algorithms. Furthermore, the IEEE 754 standard governs single-precision floating point numbers using 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits with a bias of 127, and 23 fraction bits. For example, to represent the decimal number 5.0, we convert it to binary 101.0, normalize it to 1.01 times 2 to the power of 2, resulting in a sign bit of 0, an exponent of 129 encoded as 10000001, and a mantissa of 01000000000000000000000, yielding the hex value 0x40A00000.

In class exercise: Convert the decimal value -6 into an 8-bit two's complement binary integer and verify its negation.

title: Lecture 3: Datapath, Control, and Pipelining
description: This lecture examines how hardware datapaths execute instructions and how pipelining accelerates throughput while introducing synchronization hazards.
content:
Learning objectives: Design single-cycle and multi-cycle execution datapaths and resolve pipeline hazards using forwarding and stalls.

Instruction execution relies on a datapath orchestrated by either hardwired control logic using boolean gates or microprogrammed control utilizing a small internal ROM. To improve instruction throughput, modern processors employ pipelining broken down into five distinct stages: instruction fetch, instruction decode, execution, memory access, and write back. Pipelining introduces hazards that disrupt smooth execution. Structural hazards occur when hardware cannot support concurrent resource usage, control hazards arise from conditional branches, and data hazards happen when an instruction depends on the result of a previous uncompleted instruction. Data hazards can often be bypassed using forwarding paths, where the ALU result from the execution stage is routed directly back to the input of the execution stage for the next instruction. If forwarding is impossible, such as a load-use hazard, pipeline stalls must be inserted. For example, if a load instruction fetches data into register $t1 at cycle 2, and the subsequent instruction immediately tries to add $t1 at cycle 3, a one-cycle stall is required before forwarding can supply the correct value.

In class exercise: Identify the type of hazard present when a branch instruction depends on the ALU result of the instruction immediately preceding it.

title: Lecture 4: Memory Hierarchy and Input-Output Systems
description: We explore memory organization through cache mapping techniques and analyze how processors communicate with external peripherals.
content:
Learning objectives: Calculate cache mapping parameters, evaluate average memory access time, and compare I/O transfer mechanisms.

To bridge the speed gap between the CPU and main memory, systems utilize a memory hierarchy consisting of fast, small caches and slower, larger main memory. Cache mapping determines where memory blocks reside in the cache using direct mapping, fully associative mapping, or set-associative mapping. Given a 32-bit memory address, a direct-mapped cache determines the block index and tag bits based on cache size and block size. Performance is measured by the hit ratio and average access time. For instance, given a hit time of 2 nanoseconds, a miss rate of 10 percent, and a miss penalty of 80 nanoseconds, the average memory access time is calculated as hit time plus miss rate multiplied by miss penalty, resulting in 2 plus 0.10 multiplied by 80, which equals 10 nanoseconds. Finally, input-output systems handle data transfer through programmed polling, interrupt-driven I/O, or direct memory access, where a specialized controller moves data blocks directly to memory without continuous CPU intervention.

In class exercise: Calculate the average memory access time if the hit time is 1 nanosecond, miss rate is 5 percent, and miss penalty is 40 nanoseconds.

title: Lecture 1: Quantitative Principles and Instruction Set Architecture
description: This lecture covers foundational performance metrics, Amdahl's Law, and fundamental RISC instruction set design principles.
content:
Learning objectives: Master the CPU performance equation and quantify parallel speedup limits using Amdahl's Law. Understand tradeoffs in RISC instruction set architectures.

Performance evaluation relies on the CPU execution time formula: CPU time equals instruction count multiplied by cycles per instruction and the clock period. To optimize execution, we must balance all three factors without letting an improvement in one degrade the others. When considering hardware enhancements, Amdahl's Law bounds the maximum expected speedup. For instance, suppose an application spends 60 percent of its total execution time in a routine that can be parallelized, while the remaining 40 percent must run serially. If we upgrade our system to execute the parallelizable portion 3 times faster, the new execution time fraction is 0.40 plus 0.60 divided by 3, which equals 0.40 plus 0.20, totaling 0.60. The overall system speedup is one divided by 0.60, yielding approximately 1.67 times faster. Even if we accelerate that same routine by infinity, the maximum possible speedup is one divided by 0.40, which equals 2.5 times. This illustrates that optimizing non-dominant fractions yields diminishing returns.

In class exercise: Calculate the overall speedup if 70 percent of a workload is accelerated by a factor of 5, and discuss which metric dominates if instruction count increases by 10 percent during the optimization.

title: Lecture 2: Pipelining and Advanced Branch Prediction
description: This lecture examines pipelined datapath hazards, structural constraints, and dynamic branch prediction mechanisms.
content:
Learning objectives: Analyze data, structural, and control hazards in deep pipelines. Evaluate static and dynamic branch prediction strategies.

Pipelining increases instruction throughput by overlapping execution stages, but hazards limit ideal performance. Control hazards occur when instructions depend on branch outcomes, creating pipeline bubbles. Deeper pipelines increase the penalty of a branch misprediction because more speculative instructions must be flushed from the datapath. To mitigate this, dynamic branch predictors use history bits to forecast outcomes. Consider a 2-bit saturating counter starting in the weakly taken state, which has a binary encoding of 10. If the actual branch outcome is not taken, the counter transitions to weakly not taken state 01, and then to strongly not taken state 00 upon another untaken branch. If a taken branch occurs next, the state shifts back to weakly not taken 01. This hysteresis prevents a single anomalous branch outcome from immediately flipping the prediction state. Delayed branching is an alternative software approach where the instruction immediately following the branch is always executed regardless of outcome.

In class exercise: Trace the state transitions of a 2-bit predictor given the execution sequence taken, taken, not taken, taken, and determine how many mispredictions occur assuming initialization at state 11.

title: Lecture 3: Instruction-Level Parallelism and Tomasulo's Algorithm
description: This lecture explores dynamic instruction scheduling, out-of-order execution, register renaming, and speculation.
content:
Learning objectives: Understand how out-of-order execution overcomes data dependencies. Explain register renaming and Tomasulo's algorithm.

Instruction-level parallelism allows multiple instructions to execute concurrently in every clock cycle using superscalar issue logic. While true RAW data dependencies represent real flow dependencies, name dependencies such as write-after-read and write-after-write hazards arise purely from a limited set of architectural register names. Tomasulo's algorithm solves this by implementing hardware register renaming through reservation stations, which buffer operands and dispatch instructions as soon as their inputs become ready, bypassing sequential program order. When an instruction writes to a register, the register file points to the reservation station producing the value rather than the physical register itself, effectively eliminating false dependencies. Speculative execution further boosts performance by allowing instructions beyond conditional branches to execute early, using a reorder buffer to commit results in strict program order only when branches resolve correctly.

In class exercise: Identify the data dependencies (RAW, WAR, WAW) in the sequence: R1 equals R2 plus R3, R2 equals R4 minus R5, and R3 equals R1 multiplied by R6.

title: Lecture 4: Memory Hierarchy, Coherence, and Consistency
description: This lecture details multi-level cache organizations, virtual memory translation, and multicore cache coherence protocols.
content:
Learning objectives: Calculate cache performance metrics and miss penalties. Explain the MESI cache coherence protocol and memory consistency.

Memory hierarchy design bridges the speed gap between fast processors and slow main memory using caching principles. Multi-level caches balance capacity and latency, while write-back policies defer main memory updates until cache blocks are evicted, using dirty bits to track modifications. Virtual memory provides isolated address spaces and translates virtual addresses to physical addresses using translation lookaside buffers. In multi-core processors, independent local caches can create stale data copies, requiring hardware coherence protocols. The MESI protocol uses four states: Modified, Exclusive, Shared, and Invalid. When a core wants to write to a cache block currently in the Shared state, it issues a bus invalidation request to transition its local block to Modified and force all other cached copies into the Invalid state. This ensures that subsequent reads from other cores observe the most up-to-date memory value.

In class exercise: Trace the state transitions of a cache block in core zero under the MESI protocol when core one attempts a read operation on that same shared memory address.

Then, determine the maximum theoretical overall speedup if a cryptographic module that consumes 40 percent of this execution time is accelerated by a factor of 8. (4 marks)
2. Pipeline Hazard Analysis: Consider a 5-stage RISC pipeline without bypassing. Given the code sequence: load R1, 0(R2); add R3, R1, R4; store R3, 4(R2), identify all data hazards and calculate the exact number of stall cycles required to complete execution. (4 marks)
3. Branch Prediction Evaluation: A loop containing a branch instruction executes 100 times. The branch is taken 90 times and not taken 10 times in a repeating pattern of 9 taken followed by 1 not taken. Calculate the prediction accuracy percentage for a static predictor that always predicts taken versus a dynamic 2-bit saturating counter initialized to strongly taken. (4 marks)
4. Tomasulo's Algorithm: Given a stream of instructions with name dependencies, explain step-by-step how reservation stations and register renaming eliminate WAW and WAR hazards, providing a small trace table of status changes. (4 marks)
