title: Lecture 1: Front-End Branch Prediction and Speculative Control Flow
description: This lecture explores advanced branch prediction mechanisms and the mitigation of control hazards in deep pipelines.
content: Learning objectives: Understand how global and local history are combined in tournament predictors, and analyze the mechanics of return address stacks. Control flow bottlenecks severely limit instruction fetch bandwidth in deep pipelines. Modern processors resolve this using advanced structures like the TAGE predictor, which employs multiple tables indexed by geometrically increasing history lengths to resolve complex branching patterns. Consider a branch instruction inside a loop executing with a history bit pattern of 101101. A tournament predictor dynamically selects between a local history table and a global history table based on past accuracy. For a branch with a taken probability of 0.85, suppose the misprediction penalty is 15 cycles. If a fetch block contains 16 instructions and the branch frequency is 20 percent, a prediction accuracy drop from 98 percent to 90 percent introduces an average performance degradation of 1.92 wasted cycles per instruction packet. Furthermore, return address stacks maintain call and return targets independently of conditional branch predictors to prevent stack underflow or corruption during deep function recursion. In class exercise: Calculate the effective instructions per cycle drop for a pipeline operating at 95 percent branch prediction accuracy versus 99 percent accuracy, assuming a baseline IPC of 3.5 and a fixed 18-cycle penalty for every mispredicted branch.

title: Lecture 2: Out-of-Order Execution, Speculation, and Memory Disambiguation
description: This lecture covers wide-issue superscalar scheduling, load and store queues, and hardware memory disambiguation techniques.
content: Learning objectives: Master the implementation of load and store queues for memory disambiguation, and evaluate the trade-offs of wide-issue dynamic scheduling. To sustain instructions per cycle greater than four, modern cores utilize complex out-of-order execution engines driven by reservation stations and reorder buffers. Speculative execution allows instructions dependent on unresolved branches or loads to execute early. However, data dependencies through memory create severe hazards because effective addresses may not be known until execution time. Memory disambiguation handles potential aliasing between loads and stores using dedicated load queues and store queues. For example, if Store instruction S1 writes to address 0x1000 with value 0x55 and subsequent Load instruction L1 reads from address 0x1000 before S1 retires, L1 must bypass the data directly from the store queue rather than waiting for the cache write. If L1 executes prematurely before an older store S2 with an unknown address computes 0x1000, a memory dependence violation triggers a pipeline flush. Let the load queue hold 64 entries and the store queue hold 32 entries; if 4 stores and 8 loads are processed per cycle, explain how address comparison logic scales quadratically. In class exercise: Trace the state transitions in a load queue when a store queue forwards a data word to a younger load that hit a false address aliasing condition.

title: Lecture 3: Multithreading, Multicore Topologies, and Directory-Based Coherence
description: This lecture examines simultaneous multithreading, scalable on-chip interconnect topologies, and directory-based cache coherence protocols.
content: Learning objectives: Contrast fine-grained and coarse-grained multithreading with simultaneous multithreading, and calculate latency impacts in mesh versus ring interconnects. As single-core frequency scaling plateaued due to power walls, architectural focus shifted to thread-level parallelism and multicore configurations. Simultaneous multithreading shares execution datapath resources dynamically among multiple hardware threads, hiding memory latency and functional unit stalls. For instance, if Thread A stalls on an L3 cache miss, Thread B utilizes the remaining execution slots, maintaining high utilization of the issue width. Scaling beyond eight cores requires robust on-chip networks. In a 4x4 mesh network with deterministic dimension-ordered routing, the worst-case hop count between opposite corners is 6 hops. If each router traversal takes 1 cycle and link traversal takes 1 cycle, a packet traveling 6 hops incurs a base latency of 12 cycles, ignoring network congestion. To maintain memory consistency across these distributed tiles, directory-based cache coherence protocols replace snooping buses. The directory tracks the sharing status of every cache block in system memory. If Core 1 requests a write permission for a shared line, the directory sends invalidation messages to all other sharers, tracking acknowledgments before granting exclusive ownership. In class exercise: Compute the maximum zero-load latency for a packet crossing an 8x8 mesh network, assuming a 2-cycle router delay per hop and a 1-cycle link delay.

title: Lecture 4: Accelerator Architectures, Power Bounds, and Microarchitectural Security
description: This lecture analyzes GPU SIMT execution models, power and thermal management constraints, and hardware security vulnerabilities.
content: Learning objectives: Analyze SIMT execution efficiency and memory coalescing in GPUs, and evaluate the root causes of microarchitectural side-channel attacks like Spectre. Graphics processing units achieve massive throughput via Single Instruction Multiple Threads execution, grouping threads into warps of 32 execution lanes. When warp threads access global memory, memory coalescing combines individual requests into fewer wide memory transactions. If 32 threads in a warp access 32 consecutive 4-byte integers, the hardware coalesces this into a single 128-byte cache line request. Conversely, if access strides are random, up to 32 separate cache line requests may be generated, reducing effective memory bandwidth to 3.125 percent of peak. On the power front, dynamic power consumption follows the equation P = C * V^2 * f, where C is switched capacitance, V is supply voltage, and f is clock frequency. Because voltage and frequency scaling are bounded by leakage currents and thermal design power, dark silicon describes the fraction of a chip that must remain unpowered at any given time to avoid thermal runaway. Finally, microarchitectural optimization techniques introduce security vulnerabilities. Speculative execution leaves transient state traces in caches, enabling side-channel attacks such as Spectre, where unauthorized data values are leaked via cache hit or miss timing measurements. In class exercise: Calculate the dynamic power reduction percentage if operating voltage is reduced by 20 percent and frequency is reduced by 25 percent.

title: Assignment 1: Advanced Processor Design and Evaluation
description: A comprehensive practical assignment covering branch prediction analysis, memory queue sizing, interconnect latency, and power scaling.
content:
1. Analyze a TAGE branch predictor trace with 4 history tables. Calculate the net prediction accuracy given a sequence of 1000 conditional branches where table 1 correctly predicts 600, table 2 predicts 250, table 3 predicts 100, and the base predictor handles the remainder with a 50 percent success rate. (Marks: 4)
2. Implement a simplified Python simulator function for a load/store queue that detects memory dependence violations. Given an array of 5 load instructions and 3 store instructions with overlapping address ranges, output the exact instruction index that triggers a flush. (Marks: 4)
3. Compute the average routing latency for uniform random traffic on a 6x6 2D mesh network with wormhole routing, assuming a flit size of 64 bytes, link bandwidth of 16 bytes per cycle, and a router pipeline delay of 2 cycles per hop. (Marks: 4)
4. Given a core running at 3.0 GHz with a supply voltage of 1.2V consuming 85 Watts, of which 15 Watts is static leakage power, calculate the new total power consumption if frequency is scaled down to 2.0 GHz and voltage is scaled down to 1.0V, assuming dynamic power scales proportionally and static power scales linearly with voltage. (Marks: 4)
5. Explain the exact mechanism by which a Spectre variant 1 bounds-check bypass attack leaks a secret byte across a speculative execution window, and propose a specific hardware countermeasure at the reorder buffer level. (Marks: 4)

Submission instructions: Submit your solutions as a single PDF document containing your mathematical derivations, code snippets, and clear explanatory text. Graphs must be clearly labeled if included.

title: Lecture 1: Modern Processors and Memory Hierarchies
description: This lecture examines how multicore CPUs, GPUs, and hierarchical memory systems process instructions and manage data bandwidth.
content: Learning objectives: Understand hardware parallelism limits, differentiate between CPU and GPU compute models, and analyze memory access latencies across the hierarchy. Modern computing systems rely heavily on parallelism to overcome the physical limits of clock frequency scaling. CPUs are designed for low-latency serial processing using complex control logic and large caches, whereas GPUs utilize thousands of smaller arithmetic logic units executing massive SIMD threads. For example, multiplying two square matrices of size 1024 by 1024 requires roughly two billion floating-point operations. On a standard CPU core executing four operations per cycle at 3 gigahertz, this takes about 0.17 seconds without vectorization. By utilizing AVX-512 vector registers processing sixteen floats simultaneously, throughput increases significantly, dropping execution time to approximately 0.011 seconds. GPUs scale this further by distributing blocks of the output matrix across sixty-eight streaming multiprocessors, reducing the compute phase to milliseconds. However, overall performance is frequently bounded by memory latency. Accessing main DRAM requires roughly 100 nanoseconds, whereas L1 cache access takes less than 1 nanosecond. In class exercise: Calculate the execution time for a vector addition of one million 32-bit floating-point numbers on a single CPU core that processes one element per 5-nanosecond clock cycle, assuming zero cache misses.

title: Lecture 2: Virtualization, Containers, and Cloud Infrastructure
description: This lecture explores the software abstraction layers that enable multi-tenancy, elastic resource allocation, and containerized deployment in data centres.
content: Learning objectives: Compare hypervisor-based virtualization with OS-level containerization, and analyze resource isolation mechanisms in cloud data centres. Cloud computing abstracts physical infrastructure into flexible software-defined pools of compute, storage, and networking. Traditional hypervisors operate by running guest operating systems on top of a virtual machine monitor, which introduces overhead due to CPU and memory emulation. Containers bypass this overhead by sharing the host operating system kernel while using namespaces for process isolation and cgroups for resource limiting. Consider a cloud provider hosting virtual machines versus containers on a physical server with 64 gigabytes of RAM. A hypervisor might allocate 2 gigabytes of static overhead solely for running four guest OS instances, leaving 60 gigabytes for user applications. In contrast, running twenty lightweight containers on the same host might consume only 200 megabytes of total OS overhead, leaving 63.8 gigabytes available. This higher packing density improves resource utilization and lowers operational costs. Furthermore, data centre orchestration tools dynamically migrate these workloads across physical nodes based on real-time telemetry data. In class exercise: Estimate the maximum number of independent web server instances you can deploy on a server with 16 CPU cores and 32 gigabytes of RAM if each instance requires a minimum of 2 cores and 3 gigabytes of memory.

title: Lecture 3: Distributed Systems, Parallel Models, and Reliability
description: This lecture covers distributed computing paradigms, message passing protocols, and fault-tolerance strategies for large-scale clusters.
content: Learning objectives: Design parallel data processing pipelines using MapReduce principles, and apply redundancy techniques to handle hardware failures. As data volumes scale beyond single-machine limits, computations must be distributed across networked clusters. The MapReduce model simplifies this by dividing tasks into a map phase that processes records independently and a reduce phase that aggregates intermediate results. For instance, counting the frequency of five billion log entries across a cluster of 50 machines involves partitioning the input into 50 equal blocks of 100 million entries each. Each machine processes its local block independently in parallel, generating intermediate key-value pairs. A network shuffle phase then groups keys by hash value before sending them to 10 reducer nodes. If a single worker node crashes during the map phase due to a hardware fault, the master node detects the heartbeat failure and reschedules that exact task on an available backup node. System reliability in these environments depends on replication and checkpointing rather than ultra-reliable individual components. Assuming an individual server has a Mean Time Between Failures of 10,000 hours, a cluster of 1,000 servers will experience a failure roughly every 10 hours, necessitating robust fault-tolerance mechanisms. In class exercise: Determine the expected number of cluster failures in a 30-day continuous operation period for a system containing 500 nodes, given an individual node failure rate of 0.0002 per hour.

title: Lecture 4: Emerging Paradigms, Edge Computing, and AI Hardware
description: This lecture investigates edge computing architectures, energy-efficient IoT devices, and specialized hardware accelerators designed for artificial intelligence.
content: Learning objectives: Evaluate the trade-offs between edge and cloud processing for latency-sensitive applications, and understand specialized AI chip architectures. Modern computing extends far beyond centralized data centres into resource-constrained edge and IoT devices. Smart cameras, autonomous vehicles, and industrial sensors generate massive amounts of real-time data that cannot always be transmitted to the cloud due to bandwidth constraints and strict latency requirements. For example, a smart traffic camera streaming uncompressed 4K video at 30 frames per second generates roughly 12 gigabits per second of network traffic. Transmitting this raw stream to a remote cloud data centre introduces a round-trip latency of 50 milliseconds, which is unacceptable for collision avoidance systems. By deploying a low-power specialized neural network accelerator directly on the edge device, inference runs locally in 4 millisecond per frame, reducing outbound network traffic to tiny metadata JSON payloads of less than 1 kilobyte per event. Energy efficiency becomes the primary design constraint for these edge systems, often measured in tera operations per watt. To maximize battery life, hardware designers use mixed-precision arithmetic, such as 8-bit integer quantization instead of 32-bit floating-point numbers. In class exercise: Calculate the bandwidth savings in megabits per second when an edge device processes a video stream locally and sends only 10 text events per second, compared to streaming a constant 5 megabits per second video feed to the cloud.

title: Assignment 1: System Performance, Virtualization, and Distributed Scaling
description: A comprehensive practical assignment covering hardware performance metrics, memory hierarchies, containerization resource limits, and distributed data processing estimations.
content:
Task 1: Compute the theoretical maximum memory bandwidth in gigabytes per second for a dual-channel DDR4 memory system operating at a clock frequency of 1600 megahertz, where each channel is 64 bits wide and transfers data twice per clock cycle. (4 marks)
Task 2: Write a Python function that takes a list of execution times in milliseconds for a distributed job across 10 worker nodes and returns the median time, the average time, and the slowest node identifier. (4 marks)
Task 3: Analyze a virtualization scenario where a hypervisor hosts four virtual machines, each configured with 4 virtual CPUs sharing 8 physical CPU cores. Explain how CPU scheduling affects performance during peak load and calculate the overcommit ratio. (4 marks)
Task 4: Design a fault-tolerance strategy for a distributed database cluster of 12 nodes using primary-backup replication. Calculate the minimum number of nodes required to tolerate up to 3 simultaneous node failures using quorum-based writes. (4 marks)
Task 5: Evaluate the operational trade-offs between running an inference workload on a centralized cloud GPU instance versus an edge TPU. List two specific architectural advantages and two specific deployment challenges for the edge option. (4 marks)
Submission instructions: Submit your solutions in a single PDF document containing your mathematical derivations, code snippets, and written analyses.

title: Lecture 1: Number Systems, Codes and Boolean Algebra
description: This lecture introduces binary arithmetic, error detection codes, and fundamental algebraic laws for manipulating logic expressions.
content:
Learning objectives: Master base conversions and parity calculations, apply De Morgan laws to simplify boolean equations, and convert between standard sum of products and product of sums forms.

Digital systems process information using binary abstractions. Converting numbers between bases requires successive division by the target base for integers or multiplication for fractions. For error detection in transmission, even or odd parity bits are appended to data words. Boolean algebra provides the mathematical framework for analyzing switching circuits. Postulates and theorems allow us to reduce complex expressions into minimal gates. A foundational theorem is De Morgan law, stating that the complement of a product is equal to the sum of the complements.

Worked example: Simplify the boolean function F = A B + A (B + C) + B (B + C). First, distribute the terms: F = A B + A B + A C + B B + B C. Using idempotent laws (X + X = X and X B = B), this reduces to F = A B + A C + B + B C. Since B + B C absorbs to B, we obtain F = A B + A C + B. Finally, A B + B simplifies to A + B, giving the final minimal expression F = A + B + A C, which further reduces to F = A + B + C.

In class exercise: Convert decimal 45 to binary, compute its odd parity bit, and apply De Morgan law to expand the expression (X + Y Z)'.

title: Lecture 2: Logic Gates, Minimization and Combinational Building Blocks
description: This session explores gate-level implementation, Karnaugh map minimization, and standard combinational components like adders and multiplexers.
content:
Learning objectives: Construct universal gate implementations, utilize Karnaugh maps to reduce multi-variable functions, and design arithmetic or routing components.

Logic gates form the physical building blocks of digital hardware. Universal gates like NAND and NOR can emulate any boolean operation, reducing chip count. When expressions grow beyond three variables, algebraic minimization becomes tedious. Karnaugh maps offer a visual technique using adjacent cell grouping in Gray code order. Essential prime implicants must be identified to ensure minimal cost. Beyond simple gates, combinational networks process current inputs without memory. Examples include multiplexers that route data and adders that compute arithmetic sums with carry propagation.

Worked example: Minimize the function F(A,B,C,D) = sum of minterms (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15) using a four-variable Karnaugh map. Plotting these minterms reveals they occupy the entire right half of the grid where D equals 1. Grouping these adjacent ones into a single octet eliminates variables A, B, and C. Thus, the minimized expression evaluates simply to F = D.

In class exercise: Implement an XOR gate using only four NAND gates, and verify its truth table for all four input combinations.

title: Lecture 3: Sequential Circuits, Latches, and Flip-Flops
description: Here we transition to time-dependent circuits by examining latches, clock-edge triggered flip-flops, and timing parameters.
content:
Learning objectives: Differentiate between level-sensitive latches and edge-triggered flip-flops, analyze characteristic tables for SR, D, JK, and T devices, and account for propagation delay.

Unlike combinational circuits, sequential systems possess internal memory, allowing outputs to depend on historical inputs. Latches are level-sensitive storage elements susceptible to transparency hazards during active clock phases. To eliminate race conditions, master-slave arrangements and edge-triggered flip-flops sample inputs strictly on rising or falling clock edges. The D flip-flop transfers input directly to output, the T flip-flop toggles state, and the JK flip-flop generalizes SR behavior by preventing invalid states. Setup and hold times dictate maximum operational frequency.

Worked example: Given a positive edge-triggered JK flip-flop where J = 1 and K = 0, with the current state Q = 0 prior to the clock edge. Applying the characteristic equation Q_next = J Q' + K' Q, we substitute the values: Q_next = 1 * (0)' + (0)' * 0 = 1 * 1 + 1 * 0 = 1. The output transitions to 1 on the active clock edge.

In class exercise: Draw the timing waveform for a D flip-flop output Q given an asynchronous clear pulse and a continuous data stream alternating every half clock cycle.

title: Lecture 4: Registers, Counters and Finite State Machines
description: This final lecture covers clocked storage chains, synchronous/asynchronous counters, and systematic finite state machine design.
content:
Learning objectives: Design shift registers for serial-parallel conversion, construct synchronous binary counters with specific moduli, and translate word problems into Moore or Mealy state machines.

Registers aggregate multiple flip-flops to store multi-bit data words, while shift registers enable serial data transmission. Counters are specialized sequential circuits that cycle through a predefined sequence of states. Asynchronous ripple counters cascade clock inputs, introducing cumulative propagation delays, whereas synchronous counters update all flip-flops simultaneously via a shared clock signal. For complex control logic, finite state machines provide a structured design methodology. State diagrams map inputs, current states, next states, and outputs, categorizing behavior into Moore machines (outputs depend only on state) or Mealy machines (outputs depend on state and inputs).

Worked example: Design the next-state logic for a 2-bit binary up-counter using T flip-flops. Let the current state be Q1 Q0. For Q0, the bit toggles on every clock pulse, so T0 = 1. For Q1, the bit toggles only when Q0 is 1, so T1 = Q0. The resulting equations yield synchronous binary counting behavior.

In class exercise: Construct the state transition table for a sequence detector that outputs 1 whenever the serial input stream contains the pattern 101.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Digital Logic Design Project
description: This assignment evaluates student proficiency across number systems, Boolean minimization, combinational building blocks, sequential counters, and finite state machines.
content:
Task 1: Perform base conversion of hex value 3AE1 to decimal and binary, and compute its even parity bit. (3 marks)
Task 2: Minimize the completely specified Boolean function F(A,B,C,D) = sum of minterms (0, 2, 8, 10, 12, 14) using a Karnaugh map, and draw the resulting circuit using only NAND gates. (4 marks)
Task 3: Design a combinational magnitude comparator that outputs 1 if a 2-bit binary number A is strictly greater than a 2-bit binary number B, using logic gates. (4 marks)
Task 4: Design a synchronous mod-5 counter using D flip-flops, showing the state transition table, excitation equations, and optimized logic diagram. (5 marks)
Task 5: Create a Mealy finite state machine state diagram and state table that detects overlapping occurrences of the input sequence 011. (4 marks)

Submission instructions: Compile all answers, truth tables, K-map drawings, and logic schematics into a single PDF document or a zipped folder containing digital simulation files, and submit via the university learning portal.

title: Lecture 1: Internal Architecture and Memory Segmentation
description: This lecture covers the internal structural units of the 8086 microprocessor, internal registers, and how the segmentation scheme computes physical memory addresses.
content: Learning objectives: Understand the division between the Bus Interface Unit and Execution Unit, identify register functions, and calculate physical addresses from segment and offset pairs. The Intel 8086 internal organization is split into two independent functional sections. The Bus Interface Unit handles all external bus operations, instruction fetching, and memory reading or writing. It contains the segment registers, instruction queue, and the instruction pointer. The Execution Unit fetches instructions from the queue, decodes them, executes them, and manages the general-purpose registers along with the arithmetic logic unit. Because the 8086 uses a twenty-bit address bus to access one megabyte of memory but relies on sixteen-bit internal registers, it employs memory segmentation. A logical address consists of a segment base and an offset value. To find the exact physical address sent to the memory chips, the processor multiplies the segment register value by sixteen in hexadecimal terms by shifting it left by four bits, and then adds the offset register value. For instance, if the Code Segment register contains the hexadecimal value 1234 and the Instruction Pointer holds the offset 00F6, the calculation proceeds as follows: 12340 hexadecimal plus 00F6 hexadecimal equals the physical address 12436 hexadecimal. In class exercise: Calculate the physical memory address if the Data Segment register holds 4500 hexadecimal and the effective offset address is 1A2B hexadecimal.

title: Lecture 2: Addressing Modes and Instruction Set Architecture
description: This lecture explores the different ways the 8086 accesses operands and introduces fundamental data transfer and arithmetic instructions.
content: Learning objectives: Master instruction operand accessing techniques and write basic assembly instructions for arithmetic and data manipulation. The 8086 instruction set provides rich ways to locate data, known as addressing modes. These include immediate addressing where the operand is part of the instruction, register addressing where data is inside a CPU register, direct addressing using a memory offset, and various indirect modes like base-plus-index which are essential for accessing arrays and data structures. Data movement is handled by the move instruction, while arithmetic operations are performed using add, subtract, multiplication, and division commands. When executing arithmetic operations, the flags register is automatically updated to reflect the status of the result, such as zero, sign, or carry flags. Consider a sequence that adds two numbers stored in memory. If register BX points to the base address of an array, the instruction add ax, [bx] loads the word from the memory location pointed to by BX and adds it to the accumulator register AX. Suppose BX contains 2000 hexadecimal and the memory word at data segment offset 2000 hexadecimal is 000A hexadecimal. Executing this instruction adds 000A hexadecimal to the current value of AX and stores the outcome in AX. In class exercise: Write an instruction sequence using register indirect addressing to subtract the contents of the memory word at BX from the accumulator AX.

title: Lecture 3: Assembly Programming, Stack Operations, and Procedures
description: This lecture focuses on modular programming constructs, stack mechanisms, and string manipulation instructions in 8086 assembly.
content: Learning objectives: Implement subroutines using call and return, manage the stack with push and pop, and utilize string operations effectively. Modular programming in assembly relies heavily on procedures and the system stack. The stack operates on a last-in, first-out principle managed by the stack pointer register and the stack segment register. When a subroutine is invoked using the call instruction, the processor automatically saves the current instruction pointer onto the stack so that execution can return properly when the subroutine finishes via the ret instruction. Manual preservation of general-purpose registers is achieved using push and pop instructions to prevent unintended data corruption during nested routine calls. Furthermore, string instructions such as load string and store string permit efficient block data transfers when paired with repeat prefixes and the count register CX. For example, executing a call instruction to a subroutine named compute_sum causes the 8086 to push the current address of the next instruction onto the stack, decrement the stack pointer by two, and load the starting address of compute_sum into the instruction pointer. When the subroutine executes its final return instruction, the saved address is popped off the stack back into the instruction pointer, resuming the main program flow seamlessly. In class exercise: Trace the exact value of the stack pointer after executing three consecutive push instructions starting from an initial stack pointer value of 1000 hexadecimal.

title: Lecture 4: Interrupts, Input Output Interfacing, and Microcontrollers
description: This lecture investigates interrupt handling mechanisms, memory decoding fundamentals, and contrasts microprocessors with microcontrollers.
content: Learning objectives: Understand the interrupt vector table, analyze basic address decoding for memory chips, and differentiate microprocessors from microcontrollers. Microprocessor systems respond to asynchronous external events and internal exceptional conditions through interrupts. The interrupt mechanism uses an interrupt vector table located in the lowest one kilobyte of physical memory, containing segment and offset addresses for interrupt service routines. When an interrupt occurs, the processor saves its flag register and return address, then jumps directly to the corresponding service routine. Input and output interfacing requires address decoding logic, typically constructed using logic gates or decoders, to map peripheral chips into the memory or port address space. Finally, system designers must choose between general-purpose microprocessors and microcontrollers. While a microprocessor like the 8086 requires external random access memory, read-only memory, and input-output chips to form a complete computer, a microcontroller integrates processor cores, memory, and programmable peripherals onto a single silicon chip. For instance, if an external hardware device triggers a type one interrupt, the 8086 reads vector table entry number one located at physical address 00004 hexadecimal to retrieve the four-byte segment and offset pointer of the designated service routine. In class exercise: Calculate the memory address in the interrupt vector table that corresponds to interrupt type 20 decimal.

title: Assignment 1: 8086 Assembly Programming and System Architecture
description: A comprehensive practical assignment covering address calculations, instruction coding, stack mechanics, and assembly programming.
content:
1. Given a Code Segment register value of 3050 hexadecimal and an Instruction Pointer value of 0210 hexadecimal, compute the exact 20-bit physical address in hexadecimal format. (4 marks)
2. Explain the step-by-step sequence of internal operations performed by the 8086 microprocessor when a CALL instruction is executed, detailing changes to the stack pointer and instruction pointer. (4 marks)
3. Write a well-commented 8086 assembly program segment that initializes the data segment, sets up a loop, and calculates the sum of an array of 5 word-sized integers stored in memory. (4 marks)
4. Describe the operational and architectural differences between a microprocessor-based system and a microcontroller-based system, referencing memory integration and peripheral support. (4 marks)
5. Given an array of 8 bytes stored consecutively in memory, write an assembly code snippet using base-plus-index addressing mode to copy all elements to a destination array. (4 marks)
Total marks: 20.
Submission instructions: Submit your complete solution as a single PDF document containing your written answers, calculations, and fully commented assembly code listings.

title: Lecture 1: Bus Timing and Memory Interfacing
description: This lecture explores processor read and write bus cycles, wait states, and address decoding techniques using logic gates and decoders.
content:
Learning objectives: understand bus cycle waveforms and calculate address decoding ranges.

When a CPU communicates with memory, it asserts address lines, control signals like read or write, and data lines within specific timing constraints. If memory response time is slower than the CPU clock, wait states must be inserted into the bus cycle by holding the ready input low to prevent data corruption. Address decoding maps physical memory chips into the processor's memory map. Full decoding uses all unused high-order address lines through logic gates or decoders to ensure each memory location responds to only one unique address, avoiding aliasing. Partial decoding ignores some high-order lines, resulting in multiple mirror images of the same memory block.

Worked example: Consider designing address decoding for an 8 KB memory chip using a 74LS138 3-to-8 decoder. An 8 KB chip requires 13 address lines (A0 to A12). Suppose we map this chip starting at base address hex 0000. The remaining address lines A13, A14, and A15 connect to the decoder inputs C, B, and A respectively. When A15, A14, and A13 are all low, output Y0 activates low, selecting the chip for addresses hex 0000 to hex 1FFF. The next chip can start at hex 2000, activated by Y1.

In class exercise: Calculate the exact address range for a memory chip connected to output Y3 of a 74LS138 decoder when A15 is high, A14 is low, and A13 is high.

title: Lecture 2: Parallel and Serial Communication
description: This lecture covers programmable parallel peripheral interfaces, universal asynchronous receiver-transmitters, and synchronous serial protocols.
content:
Learning objectives: configure parallel ports and distinguish between asynchronous and synchronous serial communication.

Parallel communication transfers entire bytes simultaneously using multiple data lines, managed efficiently by programmable peripheral interface chips like the 8255 which offer multiple ports with handshaking capabilities for reliable synchronization between devices of differing speeds. Serial communication transmits data bit by bit over a single line, reducing wiring complexity. Asynchronous serial communication, implemented via UARTs like the 8251, uses start and stop bits with configurable baud rates and voltage levels such as RS-232 to frame data without a shared clock. Synchronous protocols like SPI and I2C use a shared clock signal. SPI uses separate master out slave in, master in slave out, and clock lines along with individual chip select signals for high-speed full-duplex transfers. I2C uses only two shared lines, serial data and serial clock, relying on software addressing and pull-up resistors for half-duplex multi-master communication.

Worked example: Calculate the actual bit duration for a UART communication channel operating at a baud rate of 9600 baud. The bit duration is calculated as one divided by the baud rate, which equals 1 over 9600, resulting in approximately 0.104 milliseconds or 104.17 microseconds per bit.

In class exercise: Determine the total transmission time for an 8-bit ASCII character with one start bit, one parity bit, and two stop bits sent over a UART link at 4800 baud.

title: Lecture 3: Timers, Interrupts, and DMA
description: This lecture examines programmable interval timers, interrupt controllers, and direct memory access controllers for efficient system operation.
content:
Learning objectives: design pulse-width modulation signals, prioritize interrupts, and calculate direct memory access transfer rates.

Programmable interval timers like the 8253 or 8254 contain independent counter channels capable of generating accurate time delays, square waves, and pulse-width modulation signals for motor control by toggling output states upon reaching terminal count. Interrupt controllers like the 8259 manage multiple hardware interrupt requests from peripheral devices, prioritizing them and supplying appropriate vector addresses to the processor so it can suspend current execution and jump to the correct service routine. Direct memory access controllers like the 8237 bypass the processor during large block transfers between memory and I/O devices, taking over the system bus to move data at maximum hardware speeds, thereby freeing the central processing unit for computational tasks.

Worked example: Determine the output frequency of an 8254 timer counter initialized with an input clock frequency of 2 megahertz and a reload count value of 5000 in square wave mode. The output frequency is the input frequency divided by the count value, which is 2,000,000 divided by 5000, yielding exactly 400 hertz.

In class exercise: Calculate the reload count needed for a timer to generate a 1-kilohertz square wave given a 1-megahertz input clock.

title: Lecture 4: Analog Interfacing and Peripherals
description: This lecture focuses on analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog conversion, sensor conditioning, and human-machine interface peripherals.
content:
Learning objectives: compute converter resolution and design interface logic for keypads and displays.

Analog interfacing bridges the gap between digital processors and the physical world through analog-to-digital converters and digital-to-analog converters. Key performance metrics include resolution, which defines the smallest detectable change in analog voltage, and conversion time, which limits sampling bandwidth. Sensors convert physical phenomena like temperature or pressure into electrical signals, often requiring operational amplifiers for signal conditioning, while actuators translate control voltages or currents into mechanical movement. Human-machine interfaces involve multiplexed matrix keypads requiring row and column scanning algorithms, and alphanumeric or graphical displays driven through parallel or serial interfaces.

Worked example: Calculate the resolution of a 12-bit analog-to-digital converter that operates with a reference voltage of 3.3 volts. The number of quantization levels is 2 to the power of 12, which equals 4096. The resolution is the reference voltage divided by the number of levels, giving 3.3 divided by 4096, which is approximately 0.0008056 volts or 0.806 millivolts per step.

In class exercise: Find the digital output code produced by an 8-bit analog-to-digital converter with a 5-volt reference when an input analog voltage of 2.5 volts is applied.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Processor Interfacing Project
description: A comprehensive practical assignment covering address decoding, serial communication configuration, timer calculations, and analog conversion analysis.
content:
1. Design the complete address decoding logic for two separate 16 KB memory chips and one 8 KB peripheral block starting at base address hex 0000 using a 74LS138 decoder and standard logic gates. Provide the complete memory map and equations. (Marks: 5)
2. Configure an 8251 UART control word to initialize serial transmission for 19200 baud, 8 data bits, even parity, and 2 stop bits assuming an internal clock multiplier of 16. Show the exact binary byte value written to the control register. (Marks: 4)
3. Calculate the maximum throughput in bytes per second for a Direct Memory Access controller transferring blocks of data in single transfer mode, assuming a bus cycle takes 500 nanoseconds and every fourth cycle is stolen by the processor for refresh. (Marks: 4)
4. An industrial temperature monitoring sensor outputs an analog voltage from 0 to 5 volts corresponding to temperatures from -50 to plus 150 degrees Celsius. Calculate the digital output value and expected temperature reading for a 10-bit analog-to-digital converter with a 5-volt reference when the input voltage is 3.2 volts. (Marks: 4)
5. Explain why a high-speed data acquisition system requires Direct Memory Access rather than interrupt-driven input-output, detailing the overhead associated with each method during a 1 megabyte per second transfer. (Marks: 3)

Submission instructions: Submit your complete solutions as a single PDF document containing all calculations, circuit diagrams, and written explanations to the course portal before the deadline.

title: Lecture 1: Foundations and Taxonomies of Parallel Systems
description: This lecture introduces the fundamental limits of speedup and categorizes parallel computer architectures using Flynn's taxonomy.
content:
Learning Objectives: Understand Amdahl's law and Gustafson's law for theoretical performance limits. Classify architectures using Flynn's taxonomy. 

We begin by analyzing why throwing more processors at a problem has diminishing returns. Amdahl's law models speedup when the problem size remains fixed, bounded by the serial fraction. Suppose a program has a serial portion of 10 percent (0.1). If we use 9 processors (so p equals 9), the maximum theoretical speedup is calculated as 1 divided by (0.1 plus 0.9 divided by 9), which yields 1 divided by (0.1 plus 0.1), resulting in a speedup of exactly 5. Even as processors approach infinity, the speedup can never exceed 10. Conversely, Gustafson's law scales the problem size with the processor count, showing that larger workloads can achieve high parallel efficiency. To understand hardware execution, we use Flynn's taxonomy: SISD, SIMD like vector units, MISD, and MIMD like modern multicore clusters. 

In class exercise: Calculate the theoretical speedup using Amdahl's law for a program with a 20 percent serial fraction running on 4 processors, and explain how the result changes if the processor count approaches infinity.

title: Lecture 2: Parallel Algorithm Design and Shared-Memory Programming
description: This lecture covers Foster's methodology for algorithm design and practical multithreaded programming using OpenMP primitives.
content:
Learning Objectives: Apply Foster's design method for parallel algorithms. Write shared-memory parallel loops using OpenMP while avoiding synchronization pitfalls. 

Designing parallel software requires a structured approach. Foster's methodology outlines four steps: partitioning the computation and data, deciding on communication structures, agglomerating tasks to reduce overhead, and mapping tasks to physical processors. Once designed, we implement shared-memory parallelism using OpenMP directives. Consider a loop adding two vectors of size 1000. Without synchronization, race conditions occur if multiple threads update the same memory location. We use the reduction clause to safely accumulate results. For example, writing a parallel for loop with reduction(+:total) lets each thread maintain a private accumulator, combining them at the end. However, developers must watch out for false sharing, which happens when independent threads modify different variables residing on the same cache line, causing unnecessary cache invalidation traffic and performance degradation. 

In class exercise: Write an OpenMP parallel for loop to compute the dot product of two arrays of size 500, incorporating the correct reduction clause to sum the final scalar product.

title: Lecture 3: Distributed Memory and Message Passing
description: This lecture explores distributed memory architectures and explicit communication management using Message Passing Interface primitives.
content:
Learning Objectives: Implement point-to-point communication using MPI send and receive routines. Utilize collective operations for efficient data distribution and reduction. 

In distributed memory clusters, processors do not share a global address space, requiring explicit data transfer via message passing. The Message Passing Interface provides standard routines for this purpose. Point-to-point communication uses blocking or non-blocking send and receive functions, such as MPI_Send and MPI_Recv, where data is explicitly marshaled from a sender rank to a receiver rank. To simplify complex communication patterns, MPI provides collective operations that involve all processes within a communicator. For instance, broadcasting distributes data from a root process to all other processes, while a reduction operation combines data from all processes using an operator like addition or maximum and stores the result on the root. Consider summing 100 integers distributed across 4 processes. Each process computes a local sum of 25 numbers in local time proportional to 25. Then, an MPI_Reduce operation combines these four local sums into the global total with a logarithmic communication overhead proportional to the logarithm of 4, which is 2 steps. 

In class exercise: Sketch an MPI program where rank 0 sends an integer array to rank 1 using point-to-point communication, and explain how a collective broadcast would simplify the code if there were 8 recipient ranks.

title: Lecture 4: Accelerator Programming and Parallel Patterns
description: This lecture examines GPU architecture fundamentals, CUDA programming models, and classic parallel algorithmic patterns.
content:
Learning Objectives: Explain the CUDA execution hierarchy of threads, blocks, and grids. Implement fundamental parallel patterns such as map and scan. 

Modern parallel processing relies heavily on hardware accelerators like Graphics Processing Units, which feature thousands of arithmetic cores designed for data-parallel throughput. In the CUDA programming model, execution is structured hierarchically. Kernels are executed by grids of thread blocks, where threads within a block cooperate via shared memory and synchronization barriers. Memory management requires explicit data transfers between host system RAM and device global memory. Beyond hardware, parallel programming utilizes recurring algorithmic patterns. The map pattern applies a function independently to every element, such as scaling an array by a constant factor. The scan, or prefix sum, pattern computes running totals, which is essential for compaction and sorting algorithms. For example, performing an inclusive scan on the input array of integers 1, 2, 3, 4 yields the output array 1, 3, 6, 10. Stencil computations, common in physical simulations, update grid cells based on neighboring values using local shared memory to minimize slow global memory accesses. 

In class exercise: Write a simple CUDA kernel that performs a parallel vector addition for two arrays of floats, mapping each thread index directly to a distinct array element.

title: Assignment 1: Parallel Limits, OpenMP, and MPI
description: A comprehensive practical assignment covering theoretical speedup limits, OpenMP multithreading, false sharing mitigation, and MPI collective reduction.
content:
1. Amdahl's Law Analysis: Calculate and plot the theoretical maximum speedup for a program with a 5 percent serial fraction running on 1, 4, 16, 64, and infinity processors. Show all intermediate calculations. (Marks: 4)
2. OpenMP Reduction: Write a C program using OpenMP that finds the maximum value in an array of 10000 integers. Include the parallel pragma with an appropriate reduction clause and explain how thread-private variables are merged. (Marks: 4)
3. False Sharing Investigation: Explain why modifying adjacent elements of a shared array in separate concurrent threads degrades performance. Provide a code modification using local temporary variables to eliminate false sharing on a 64-byte cache line architecture. (Marks: 4)
4. MPI Vector Addition: Write a complete MPI C program where process 0 initializes a vector of 1000 elements, distributes chunks of 250 elements to 4 total processes, computes local vector scaling, and gathers the results back to process 0. (Marks: 5)
5. Algorithmic Complexity: Derive the time complexity of computing a parallel sum of n numbers using p processors, breaking down the cost into local computation phases and reduction communication phases. (Marks: 3)

title: Lecture 1: Foundations and Architectural Styles
description: This lecture introduces distributed system fundamentals, architectural patterns, and communication paradigms.
content: Learning objectives: Understand transparency goals in networked setups and evaluate client-server versus peer-to-peer topologies. Distributed systems connect independent computers via a network to present a single cohesive interface to end users. Achieving this requires masking complexities like location and migration transparency. For instance, in a microservices deployment handling e-commerce checkouts, the frontend gateway routes user requests across auth, inventory, and payment services transparently. Communication occurs through various mechanisms. A synchronous remote procedure call allows an application to invoke a function on a remote machine seamlessly. Suppose a client calls getStock(item_id=402) on a server. The local stub serializes the integer 402 into bytes, transmits it over TCP port 8080, and blocks until the server deserializes the request, queries the database, and returns the response integer 15. In contrast, asynchronous message queues decouple producers and consumers, enabling high elasticity under traffic spikes. In class exercise: Draw a sequence diagram illustrating a client placing an order via an API gateway that calls two microservices concurrently, and identify where network latency introduces potential partial failure points.

title: Lecture 2: Time, Ordering, and Synchronization
description: This lecture examines clock synchronization challenges, logical time formulations, and event causality tracking.
content: Learning objectives: Master physical time synchronization limitations and compute event ordering using Lamport and vector clocks. Because physical machines drift apart, distributed systems rely on logical clocks to establish a reliable happened-before relation. Consider a Lamport clock system with three processes. Process A initializes its counter to LA = 0. Process A executes a local event, incrementing LA to 1. Then, A sends a message containing timestamp 1 to Process B. Process B has its local clock at LB = 3 upon receiving this message. Process B computes its new clock as max(3, 1) + 1, resulting in LB = 5. While Lamport clocks capture causality, they cannot determine concurrency alone. Vector clocks extend this by maintaining an array of integer counters for every process in the system. If Process A has vector [1, 0, 0] and Process B has vector [0, 2, 0], neither dominates all indices, revealing that their respective local actions are concurrent. In class exercise: Given an execution trace with five messages exchanged between three nodes, construct the final vector clocks for each node step-by-step on the board.

title: Lecture 3: Coordination, Consensus, and Fault Tolerance
description: This lecture explores leader election, distributed mutual exclusion, consensus algorithms, and the CAP theorem tradeoffs.
content: Learning objectives: Analyze the CAP theorem constraints and trace consensus state transitions using Paxos or Raft. Distributed nodes must coordinate despite node crashes and network partitions. The CAP theorem states that a distributed data store can simultaneously provide at most two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance. Since network partitions are inevitable in WAN environments, designers must choose between CP and AP systems. For example, a banking ledger chooses CP: if network links split the cluster, the minority partition rejects writes to prevent double-spending anomalies. Consensus protocols like Raft ensure fault-tolerant state machine replication. In Raft, time is divided into arbitrary terms acting as logical epochs. When a follower node's randomized election timeout of 250 milliseconds expires without hearing from the current leader, it increments its term from 4 to 5, transitions to candidate status, votes for itself, and dispatches RequestVote RPCs to its peers. If it collects votes from a strict majority of nodes, it becomes the new leader and begins issuing AppendEntries heartbeats. In class exercise: Simulate a split-vote scenario in a 5-node Raft cluster and calculate the minimum number of active nodes required to elect a new leader successfully.

title: Lecture 4: Replication, Storage, and Distributed Computation
description: This lecture covers data replication strategies, distributed file systems, and large-scale batch processing paradigms.
content: Learning objectives: Implement quorum-based read-write consistency models and trace MapReduce data processing steps. High availability requires replicating data across multiple physical racks. Quorum systems guarantee strong consistency by enforcing the condition that read quorum size plus write quorum size exceeds total replica count, expressed mathematically as Vr + Vw > N. Consider a storage cluster with N = 5 replicas. If we configure a write quorum of Vw = 3 and a read quorum of Vr = 3, their sum equals 6, which is strictly greater than 5. This guarantees that any read operation will overlap with the most recent write operation on at least one common replica node. For large-scale data analysis, the MapReduce framework processes petabytes of unstructured records. Suppose we have a text dataset split across two chunks. The Map phase processes lines and emits intermediate key-value pairs like ("apple", 1) and ("apple", 1). The shuffle phase groups all values by key, sending them to reducers which sum the counts to output ("apple", 2). In class exercise: Compute the quorum intersection set for N = 7 replicas with Vw = 4 and Vr = 4, and explain what happens if two replica nodes fail simultaneously.

title: Assignment 1: Distributed Algorithms and Replication
description: This programming and analytical assignment evaluates student understanding of logical clocks, consensus mechanics, and quorum consistency models.
content:
1. Implement a Python function simulate_lamport_clock(events) that takes a list of local events and message passing actions across three processes, computes the final Lamport timestamp for each process, and returns the resulting dictionary of timestamps. (4 marks)
2. Write a Python script implementing vector clocks for a distributed system of four nodes. The script must process an input trace of ten events and output a boolean function is_concurrent(vc1, vc2) that accurately determines if two vector timestamps are causally unrelated. (4 marks)

4. Given a distributed key-value store with N = 9 storage nodes, calculate the minimum read quorum (Vr) and write quorum (Vw) required to guarantee strong consistency under quorum rules while minimizing read latency when read-to-write ratio is 9 to 1. Provide the mathematical proof. (4 marks)
5. Design and implement a fault-tolerant distributed locking service stub in Python using socket programming that handles node heartbeat failures gracefully within a 500 millisecond window. (4 marks)

title: Lecture 1: Foundations and Service Models
description: An introduction to cloud computing characteristics, service delivery models, and deployment strategies.
content: Learning objectives: Understand core cloud characteristics such as elasticity and measured service, and distinguish between IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS. Cloud computing delivers servers, storage, databases, networking, and software over the internet on a pay-as-you-go basis, eliminating the need to own physical datacenters. The NIST definition relies on five essential traits: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, and measured service. Service models divide responsibilities. For instance, consider hosting a student registration portal. If we choose IaaS, we rent raw virtual machines running Ubuntu, meaning our team manually installs the web server, patches the operating system, and configures the database. If we instead choose PaaS, such as a managed application platform, the cloud provider handles all OS patches and scaling infrastructure, allowing developers to focus solely on writing the application code. Deployment models further define where this infrastructure lives, ranging from single-tenant private clouds to multi-tenant public clouds and hybrid combinations. In class exercise: Draw a architectural diagram comparing the maintenance tasks your team must perform when deploying a legacy application on an IaaS virtual machine versus a PaaS managed database instance.

title: Lecture 2: Virtualization, Containers, and Orchestration
description: Exploring how hypervisors, containers, and orchestration tools abstract physical hardware for scalable deployments.
content: Learning objectives: Contrast hardware virtualization with containerization, and explain how Kubernetes manages container lifecycles. Virtualization uses a hypervisor to run multiple virtual machines on a single physical host, each with a full guest operating system. Containers, by contrast, share the host operating system kernel, making them lightweight and fast to start. Docker packages application code and its dependencies into a standard image. For example, building a microservice involves a Dockerfile containing instructions to copy Python scripts and install dependencies, resulting in a portable image of 150 megabytes that boots in under one second. When managing hundreds of these containers across multiple servers, container orchestrators like Kubernetes become essential. Kubernetes groups containers into pods, exposes them via services, and uses controllers to maintain desired states. Suppose we define a deployment configuration requiring a minimum of three replicas of our web server pod. If a physical node fails, the Kubernetes control plane automatically detects the lost pod and schedules a replacement instance on a healthy worker node within seconds, ensuring high availability without manual intervention. In class exercise: Write a basic Dockerfile snippet that uses an official python runtime image, sets a working directory, copies the current directory contents, and runs an application script.

title: Lecture 3: Storage, Scalability, and Distributed Architecture
description: Analyzing cloud storage tiers, database options, and architectural patterns for high availability and elastic scaling.
content: Learning objectives: Select appropriate cloud storage types and design stateless, horizontally scalable architectures using load balancers. Cloud storage falls into three primary categories: object storage for unstructured data accessible via REST APIs, block storage for raw disk volumes attached to virtual machines, and file storage for shared network file systems. Databases as a service provide managed relational and NoSQL engines with automated backups and replication. To handle traffic spikes, applications must be designed as stateless services. Imagine an e-commerce checkout service handling five thousand requests per minute. If user session data is stored locally in the server memory, routing requests across multiple backend instances will cause session loss errors. By decoupling state and storing user sessions in a distributed in-memory cache or a managed database, any backend container can handle any request. A load balancer distributes incoming network traffic across these stateless compute instances. During peak hours, an auto-scaling group monitors CPU utilization; if average utilization exceeds seventy percent for five minutes, the group automatically provisions four new container instances, scaling total capacity from two to six instances. In class exercise: Calculate the monthly cost of storing 500 gigabytes of object data at 0.023 dollars per gigabyte and performing 100000 PUT requests at 0.005 dollars per 1000 requests.

title: Lecture 4: Security, Compliance, and Cloud Operations
description: Mastering the shared responsibility model, identity management, encryption, and modern DevOps practices.
content: Learning objectives: Explain the cloud shared responsibility model and implement basic infrastructure automation and CI/CD pipelines. Security in the cloud is a collaborative effort between the provider and the customer. Under the shared responsibility model, the provider secures the underlying cloud infrastructure, including hardware, facilities, and virtualization software, categorized as security of the cloud. The customer remains responsible for security in the cloud, which encompasses configuring operating system patches, managing firewall rules, enforcing identity and access management policies, and encrypting data at rest and in transit. For example, storing sensitive student grades in an object storage bucket requires enabling server-side encryption and attaching an access policy that denies public read access while granting specific IAM role permissions to the grading service. Operations teams streamline these deployments using infrastructure as code tools, such as Terraform, which define cloud resources in declarative configuration files. A continuous integration and continuous deployment pipeline automatically tests code changes upon git commit, builds new container images, updates the infrastructure definition, and deploys the update with zero downtime. In class exercise: Write a pseudo-code IAM policy document in JSON format that grants a specific user read-only access to a designated cloud storage bucket.

title: Assignment 1: Cloud Architecture and Automation
description: A hands-on practical assignment covering containerization, infrastructure configuration, scaling, and security compliance.
content:
1. Containerize a simple web application by writing a valid Dockerfile that uses an official node runtime, installs dependencies from package.json, and exposes port 8080. (Marks: 4)
2. Write a Terraform configuration snippet to provision a private cloud storage bucket with versioning enabled and public access completely blocked. (Marks: 4)
3. Design a scalable architecture plan for a university grading portal expecting sudden traffic surges, detailing the role of the load balancer, stateless application design, and auto-scaling rules. (Marks: 4)
4. Explain the division of security responsibilities between the cloud provider and the customer when deploying a managed relational database service. (Marks: 4)
5. Write an Identity and Access Management policy in JSON that grants a specific reporting service read access to a specific database backup bucket while denying all other actions. (Marks: 4)

Submission instructions: Submit a single ZIP file containing your Dockerfile, Terraform configuration, architecture diagram image, and a PDF document answering the written questions.

title: Lecture 1: Design Patterns and System Architecture
description: This lecture explores how to structure large software systems using proven design patterns and decoupled architectural styles.
content:
Learning objectives: Understand how to select and implement creational, structural, and behavioural design patterns, and evaluate microservices versus clean architecture.

Software architecture defines the high-level structures of a system, guiding how components interact. Design patterns provide template solutions to recurring design problems. For instance, the Strategy pattern allows selecting an algorithm at runtime. Consider a shipping cost calculator where different rules apply based on the destination region. Instead of a large conditional statement, we define a ShippingStrategy interface with a calculate method, and concrete implementations like StandardShipping and ExpressShipping. The Order class holds a reference to this interface and executes it dynamically. When a new region is added, we simply implement a new strategy class without modifying the existing Order class logic, ensuring adherence to the open-closed principle.

At the architectural level, clean architecture organizes code in concentric circles, ensuring business logic remains independent of databases and frameworks. In contrast, microservices distribute business capabilities into loosely coupled, independently deployable services communicating over networks, which introduces trade-offs regarding network latency and data consistency.

In class exercise: Design a system using the Factory method pattern to instantiate different types of database connection objects based on a configuration string, and write the corresponding class diagram on the board.

title: Lecture 2: Code Quality, Refactoring, and Technical Debt
description: This lecture covers the identification of architectural decay, the quantification of code quality metrics, and systematic refactoring techniques.
content:
Learning objectives: Master the identification of code smells, calculate cyclomatic complexity, and manage technical debt through targeted refactoring.

Code quality directly influences maintainability. Technical debt represents the implied cost of choosing an easy, short-term software solution instead of a sustainable approach that takes longer. Left unmanaged, technical debt accumulates interest, making future changes slower and riskier. We measure code complexity using metrics such as cyclomatic complexity, which counts the linearly independent paths through a program's source code. For example, consider a method containing a conditional statement with three if-else branches and a loop: if the entry node is 1, and the graph has 4 decision points, the cyclomatic complexity is calculated as edges minus nodes plus two, yielding a value of 6. A complexity score above 10 indicates high risk.

Refactoring is the process of restructuring existing computer code without changing its external behavior to improve non-functional attributes. Common code smells include long methods, large classes, and duplicated code. By applying refactoring techniques such as extract method or replace conditional with polymorphism, developers systematically reduce cyclomatic complexity and pay down technical debt.

In class exercise: Analyze a provided code snippet with a cyclomatic complexity of 12, identify two code smells, and apply the extract method refactoring to bring the complexity below 8.

title: Lecture 3: Advanced Testing and Continuous Integration
description: This lecture examines modern testing methodologies and the automation pipelines required to deliver software reliably.
content:
Learning objectives: Implement test-driven development cycles, construct effective test doubles, and design automated continuous integration pipelines.

Advanced software testing ensures correctness and regression safety. Test-driven development follows a strict red-green-refactor cycle: write a failing automated test, write just enough production code to pass the test, and then refactor the codebase. When testing components that depend on external systems like databases or payment gateways, we use mocking frameworks to simulate dependencies and isolate unit behavior. For instance, to test a user registration service without hitting a live database, we create a mock repository object that returns a predefined boolean when saving a user.

Continuous integration automates the integration of code changes into a shared repository frequently. A typical CI pipeline consists of several sequential stages: compilation, static code analysis, unit testing, integration testing, and packaging. If any stage fails, the pipeline halts and notifies the development team, preventing broken builds from reaching production environments.

In class exercise: Write a test-driven development test case for a discount calculation function that applies a 20 percent discount for orders exceeding a numeric threshold of 100.

title: Lecture 4: Maintenance, Release Management, and Agile Metrics
description: This lecture details software maintenance categories, release versioning strategies, and agile project management metrics.
content:
Learning objectives: Classify software maintenance activities, apply semantic versioning rules, and interpret agile delivery metrics.

Software systems require ongoing management long after initial deployment. Maintenance is categorized into four types: corrective maintenance fixes discovered bugs; adaptive maintenance updates software to work in a new environment, such as a cloud migration; perfective maintenance improves performance or adds new user requested features; and preventive maintenance refactors code to prevent future failures. To manage software releases systematically, teams use semantic versioning, formatted as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. For example, version 2.1.4 indicates major version 2 with backward-incompatible API changes, minor version 1 with new backward-compatible functionality, and patch version 4 with backward-compatible bug fixes.

In agile project management, teams track velocity, which measures the amount of work completed during a sprint, typically represented in story points. A burndown chart visually displays the remaining work against the time left in an iteration, helping teams forecast whether they will meet their delivery goals.

In class exercise: Given a sprint backlog of 45 story points where the team has completed 30 points by day 7 of a 10-day sprint, calculate the current velocity-to-completion ratio and determine if the sprint goal is at risk.

title: Lecture 1: Foundations of Quality Management and Standards
courses: Quality Assurance of Information Systems and Programming
description: This lecture introduces core quality concepts, the distinction between quality assurance and quality control, and foundational industry standards.
content:
Learning objectives: Understand ISO 25010 quality characteristics and differentiate between quality assurance, quality control, and testing.

Quality assurance involves proactive process management to prevent defects, whereas quality control focuses on reactive product inspection to identify errors before release. Testing is a subset of quality control, executing software to discover discrepancies. System quality is evaluated using the ISO 25010 standard, which defines attributes such as reliability, maintainability, and security. For instance, in an online banking application, security ensures encrypted transactions, while reliability guarantees zero data loss during network interruptions. Organizations also adopt maturity models to systematically improve their processes. CMMI level 3, known as the Defined level, requires organizational standard processes to be documented, tailored, and deployed across all projects, moving away from ad-hoc execution.

In class exercise: Identify two ISO 25010 quality attributes for a hospital patient management system and explain how they conflict.

title: Lecture 2: Static Verification and Black-Box Testing Techniques
courses: Quality Assurance of Information Systems and Programming
description: This lecture explores early defect detection through reviews and systematic black-box test design techniques.
content:
Learning objectives: Conduct static reviews and derive test cases using equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis.

Static verification finds defects without executing code through walkthroughs, inspections, and formal code reviews guided by checklists. When testing functional behavior, black-box techniques eliminate bias by focusing purely on specifications. Equivalence partitioning divides input data into valid and invalid classes where all members are assumed to be processed identically. Boundary value analysis targets the edges of these partitions, where errors frequently occur. Consider a shipping calculator that accepts weight between 1 kilogram and 50 kilograms inclusive. Valid partitions yield typical inputs like 25. Boundary value analysis requires testing inputs 0, 1, 2, 49, 50, and 51. Testing the exact boundaries and their immediate offsets ensures arithmetic comparisons use correct operators like less-than-or-equal instead of strictly less-than.

In class exercise: Write the boundary test cases for a discount percentage field accepting integer values from 0 to 20 inclusive.

title: Lecture 3: White-Box Testing and Test Metrics
courses: Quality Assurance of Information Systems and Programming
description: This lecture covers structural code coverage criteria and quantitative quality metrics used to assess system reliability.
content:
Learning objectives: Calculate statement and branch coverage and compute standard software quality metrics.

White-box testing inspects internal program logic. Statement coverage measures the percentage of executed lines of code, while branch coverage measures the percentage of evaluated decision outcomes. Consider a function computing bonuses: if sales greater than 1000 and rating equals 5, bonus equals 500, else bonus equals 100. A test case passing sales equals 1500 and rating equals 5 executes all statements, achieving 100 percent statement coverage, but completely misses the false branch of the inner condition. To achieve branch coverage, a second test case with sales equals 500 and rating equals 3 must be executed. Quantitatively, quality is tracked using metrics such as defect density, computed as total defects divided by thousand lines of code, and mean time to failure, measuring operational reliability.

In class exercise: Draw a control flow graph for a simple loop and determine the minimum test cases required for 100 percent branch coverage.

title: Lecture 4: Test Planning, Defect Tracking, and Automation
courses: Quality Assurance of Information Systems and Programming
description: This lecture details comprehensive test planning, the defect lifecycle, and the role of continuous automated testing.
content:
Learning objectives: Design structured test documentation and manage the complete defect life cycle within automated pipelines.

Rigorous test planning organizes testing efforts, detailing scope, schedules, resources, and risk mitigation strategies in a master test plan. Individual test cases must specify prerequisites, input steps, and expected outputs. When execution fails, testers file a defect report containing steps to reproduce, severity, priority, and environment details. The defect lifecycle tracks an issue from New through Assigned, Resolved, Verified, and finally Closed. Modern software engineering integrates these testing activities into automated continuous integration pipelines. Automated test scripts run on every code commit, providing immediate feedback, reducing regression testing overhead, and ensuring that software continuously meets defined acceptance criteria prior to deployment.

In class exercise: Draft a concise defect report for a login screen that crashes when a user enters a password containing an ampersand.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Quality Assurance and Testing Project

content:
1. Quality Standards and Attributes (4 marks): Select three ISO 25010 quality attributes for an autonomous vehicle navigation system and write a specific, testable requirement for each.
2. Black-Box Test Design (4 marks): Design equivalence partitions and boundary value analysis test cases for a hotel booking system field that accepts stay durations from 1 to 30 nights inclusive. List all test inputs and expected results.

5. Defect Life Cycle and Reporting (4 marks): Write a complete defect report for a simulated payment processing failure, including steps to reproduce, expected behavior, actual behavior, severity, and priority, and map its lifecycle states.
