title: Lecture 1: Foundations of Human Factors and Interaction Principles
description: This lecture explores human cognitive limits, physical laws of movement, and core design principles to build intuitive interfaces.
content:
Learning objectives: Understand human memory constraints and Fitts's law, and apply Norman's design principles to everyday interactive systems.

Human factors dictate how effectively users interact with digital products. Our short-term memory is notoriously limited, famously described by George Miller as holding seven plus or minus two items. When designing navigation menus, keeping choices within this cognitive bound prevents overload. Physically, human movement is governed by Fitts's law, which states that the time to reach a target is a function of the distance to the target and the target's size. Mathematically, Movement Time equals a constant a plus b times the log base two of two D over W, where D is distance and W is width. For example, if a primary call-to-action button is placed far away in a corner and made tiny, the distance D is large and width W is small, resulting in a large logarithmic value and slow interaction times. To optimize this, critical actions should be placed near the natural resting position of the cursor with generous sizing.

To bridge the gap between user intent and system response, we rely on Donald Norman's principles. Consider volume control on a modern car dashboard: visibility is maintained through a glowing ring, feedback is instant via audio changes, physical constraints prevent turning it past maximum, and mapping is natural since rotating clockwise increases volume. 

In class exercise: In pairs, examine your current smartphone screen. Identify one interface element that violates Fitts's law due to its placement and propose a redesign with specific pixel dimensions.

title: Lecture 2: The User-Centred Design Process and Requirements Gathering
description: This lecture covers the iterative UCD lifecycle and practical methods for extracting accurate user requirements.
content:
Learning objectives: Master requirements gathering techniques, create actionable user personas, and structure the iterative design process.

User-centred design is an iterative framework that places the user at the center of every development phase: research, design, prototyping, and evaluation. Before writing a single line of code, we must gather requirements. This involves contextual inquiry, semi-structured interviews, surveys, and detailed task analysis. For instance, when designing an online library checkout system, observing a librarian reveals hidden workflows, such as manually checking physical logbooks for damaged books, which surveys alone would miss.

Once data is collected, we synthesize it into personas—archetypical users representing our target audience—and scenarios that narrate how a persona achieves a specific goal. Imagine persona Sarah, a busy working mother who exclusively browses on her mobile phone during her commute. A scenario details how Sarah opens the app, searches for a recipe, and saves it with three taps or fewer. This keeps the engineering team focused on real human needs rather than imagined features. The design process loops continuously; evaluation data feeds directly back into the research phase for refinement.

In class exercise: Draft a 50-word user persona for a university campus laundry room booking app, including one primary goal and one frustrating pain point.

title: Lecture 3: Prototyping Techniques and Heuristic Evaluation
description: This lecture details the spectrum of fidelity in prototyping and systematic methods for expert usability inspection.
content:
Learning objectives: Distinguish between low- and high-fidelity prototypes, and conduct a rigorous heuristic evaluation using Nielsen's principles.

Prototyping is the physical translation of abstract design ideas. We start with low-fidelity prototypes, such as paper sketches and structural wireframes, which are inexpensive, fast to produce, and excellent for testing early information architecture. As concepts stabilize, we transition to high-fidelity prototypes featuring realistic typography, color palettes, and functional interactivity using tools like Figma.

To evaluate these designs before involving real users, experts use heuristic evaluation against established guidelines like Jakob Nielsen's ten usability heuristics. Consider a checkout form that clears every input field when a user makes a single validation error on the password field. This directly violates heuristic five, error prevention, and heuristic nine, helping users diagnose and recover from errors. An expert evaluator would log this severity level four catastrophic error and recommend retaining valid inputs while highlighting only the erroneous field in red with a clear descriptive error message.

In class exercise: Review a provided screenshot of a login modal. Write down two specific Nielsen heuristic violations and rate their severity from zero to four.

title: Lecture 4: Usability Testing, Evaluation Methods, and Digital Accessibility
description: This lecture examines empirical usability testing methodologies, quantitative metrics, and WCAG compliance standards for inclusive design.
content:
Learning objectives: Plan and execute a think-aloud usability test, calculate SUS scores, and implement basic accessibility features.

Evaluating interactive systems requires both qualitative observation and quantitative metrics. In usability testing, the think-aloud protocol is the gold standard: participants verbalize their thoughts while attempting realistic tasks, exposing mental model mismatches. Quantitative assessment is often captured using the System Usability Scale, a ten-item questionnaire yielding a standardized score out of one hundred. For example, if five participants complete a task with an average completion time of forty-five seconds and a SUS score of seventy-two, the system demonstrates acceptable usability.

Inclusive design ensures accessibility for users with visual, auditory, motor, or cognitive impairments. Following the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines requires strict attention to contrast ratios, keyboard navigation, and screen reader compatibility. A button is truly accessible only if it has a minimum color contrast ratio of 4.5 to 1 against its background, is reachable via the tab key with a visible focus outline, uses semantic HTML elements, and includes an explicit aria-label for assistive technologies.

In class exercise: Test a partner on a simple website navigation task using the think-aloud method for three minutes, noting down two moments of hesitation.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Usability Audit and Prototyping Project
description: Students will evaluate an existing university portal, identify flaws using heuristics, design an improved wireframe, and outline a testing plan.
content:
Task 1: Perform a heuristic evaluation of the university portal homepage. Identify three distinct violations of Nielsen's heuristics, explain the user impact for each, and assign a severity rating from one to four. (5 marks)
Task 2: Calculate the theoretical Fitts's law movement time for a primary submit button versus a secondary cancel button, assuming given distance and width values, and explain how layout changes could improve interaction speed. (4 marks)
Task 3: Create two low-fidelity wireframe sketches (or digital wireframes) for a redesigned portal dashboard that resolves the heuristic violations found in Task 1. Include annotations pointing out design improvements. (5 marks)
Task 4: Plan a five-user usability test for your redesigned wireframe. Specify your recruitment criteria, define two concrete user tasks, and write a grading rubric for task completion success. (4 marks)
Task 5: Write a concise accessibility checklist verifying that your redesigned buttons meet WCAG 2.1 AA standards for contrast, keyboard focus, and screen reader support. (2 marks)

Total marks: 20.

Submission instructions: Submit your complete assignment as a single PDF document containing all written answers, wireframe images, and testing plans.

title: Lecture 1: Foundations of Systems and Discrete-Event Simulation
description: This lecture introduces the core taxonomy of simulation modeling, distinguishing between continuous dynamics and discrete-event state transitions.
content:
Learning objectives: Understand when to apply computer simulation versus analytical methods; define system entities, attributes, and events; master the mechanics of the simulation clock.

Simulation becomes necessary when analytical tractability fails due to high system complexity, stochastic dependencies, or non-linear interactions. A discrete-event simulation updates system states exclusively at countable points in time when events occur, skipping inactive idle intervals using a global simulation clock. The foundational components are entities representing active objects like customers, attributes describing their properties, events marking state changes, and the event list which acts as a chronological priority queue.

Consider a simple processing node. An arrival event schedules the entry of entity A at time 0.0 with a service duration of 3.0 minutes. The event list orders upcoming departures and arrivals. When the clock advances from 0.0 to 3.0, entity A departs, and the server state transitions from busy to idle if no other entity waits.

In class exercise: Trace the manual event list progression for three consecutive customer arrivals occurring at times 1.2, 2.5, and 3.1 with deterministic service times of 2.0 units.

title: Lecture 2: Stochastic Processes and Random Variate Generation
description: This lecture covers the mathematical foundations of pseudo-random number generation and techniques for sampling from arbitrary probability distributions.
content:
Learning objectives: Implement linear congruential generators for pseudo-random streams; apply the inverse transform method for non-uniform distributions; analyze basic queuing arrival processes.

Stochastic simulations rely on uniform pseudo-random numbers distributed evenly between 0 and 1. Linear congruential generators produce these values recursively using the formula X(i+1) = (a * X(i) + c) modulus m. To transform uniform variates into other distributions like the exponential distribution used for Poisson arrivals, we apply the inverse transform method. By setting the cumulative distribution function F(x) equal to a random number U, we solve for x in terms of U, yielding the explicit formula x = minus 1 divided by lambda times the natural logarithm of (1 minus U).

Suppose the arrival rate lambda is 0.5 customers per minute, and a generated random number U is 0.60. Using our formula, the time until the next arrival is calculated as minus 1 divided by 0.5 times the natural logarithm of 1 minus 0.60, which equals minus 2 times the natural logarithm of 0.40, resulting in approximately 1.83 minutes.

In class exercise: Derive and compute the exact inter-arrival time for a generated uniform value of U = 0.85 given an arrival rate lambda of 2.0.

title: Lecture 3: Queuing Theory and Monte Carlo Methods
description: This lecture explores analytical performance evaluation of service systems using M/M/1 queue formulas and static probabilistic estimation via Monte Carlo sampling.
content:
Learning objectives: Calculate steady-state operating characteristics of M/M/1 queuing systems; evaluate system utilization limits; apply Monte Carlo techniques to non-dynamic stochastic problems.

Queuing models provide rapid analytical approximations for congestion. For an M/M/1 system with Poisson arrivals at rate lambda and exponential service times at rate mu, traffic intensity rho is defined as lambda divided by mu. Provided rho is strictly less than 1, stability is guaranteed, and the expected number of customers in the system L is given by rho divided by (1 minus rho). Conversely, Monte Carlo simulation estimates deterministic mathematical quantities or static expectations by executing repeated random sampling without a dynamic time clock.

Imagine a technical support desk where calls arrive at lambda equal to 12 calls per hour, and the technician resolves calls at mu equal to 15 calls per hour. The utilization rho is 12 divided by 15, which equals 0.80. The average number of calls in the system L evaluates to 0.80 divided by (1 minus 0.80), yielding exactly 4.0 calls present on average.

In class exercise: Compute the traffic intensity and average system length for a checkout counter with an arrival rate of 15 customers per hour and a service rate of 20 customers per hour.

title: Lecture 4: Input Modeling, Output Analysis, and Model Validation
description: This lecture addresses the practical lifecycle challenges of fitting empirical data to theoretical distributions, managing warm-up bias, and validating simulation accuracy.
content:
Learning objectives: Fit input data distributions using goodness-of-fit tests; identify and mitigate transient initialization bias via warm-up periods; execute model verification and validation protocols.

Building a model is insufficient without rigorous statistical validation. Input modeling involves selecting appropriate statistical distributions for service and arrival times using historical data and chi-squared tests. Output analysis requires handling initialization bias, as starting simulations in an empty state distorts steady-state estimators. We implement warm-up periods using graphical inspection or Welch's method to truncate transient data. Finally, validation ensures the model accurately reflects the real-world system through operational validity techniques.

Suppose a simulation run produces raw waiting time observations across 5 independent replications. To construct a 95 percent confidence interval for the true mean waiting time, we calculate the sample mean and sample standard deviation across the replications, applying the student t-distribution critical value with 4 degrees of freedom.

In class exercise: Explain how you would determine the appropriate truncation point for a manufacturing simulation that starts with an empty factory floor.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Discrete-Event and Queuing Simulation
description: This assignment requires students to implement, analyze, and validate a complete discrete-event queuing model and a Monte Carlo estimator.
content:
1. Implement a linear congruential generator in Python using parameters m = 100, a = 13, c = 7, and seed X(0) = 4, generating the first 10 random integers and converting them to uniform decimals. (4 marks)
2. Apply the inverse transform method to generate 5 exponential inter-arrival times given lambda = 4.0 per hour, using the uniform decimals produced in task 1. Show all intermediate calculation steps. (4 marks)
3. Simulate a single-server M/M/1 queue by hand for the first 5 customer arrivals, assuming service rates mu = 6.0 per hour, and compute the total time each customer spends in the system. (4 marks)
4. Write a Python script using SimPy or pure Python logic to simulate 1,000 customers in an M/M/1 queue with lambda = 8 and mu = 10, measuring the average number of customers in the system and comparing it against the theoretical formula L = 4. (4 marks)
5. Describe a step-by-step validation plan for a real-world hospital emergency room simulation model, addressing data collection, face validity, and parameter calibration. (4 marks)

title: Lecture 1: Hardware Architecture and Safe Assembly
description: This lecture covers core physical components of personal computers and procedures for safe electrostatic-aware assembly.
content:
Learning objectives: identify motherboard form factors and CPU sockets, differentiate between volatile and non-volatile storage speeds, and execute an electrostatic discharge safe build.

Building a modern computer system requires precise matching of internal subsystems. The motherboard acts as the central nervous system, connecting the CPU, memory, and expansion cards. When selecting components, compatibility is critical. For instance, consider a workstation build utilizing an Intel Core i7 processor requiring an LGA 1700 socket motherboard paired with dual-channel DDR5 RAM running at 4800 megahertz and an NVMe M.2 solid-state drive communicating via PCIe 4.0 lanes offering read speeds up to 7000 megabytes per second. Power delivery must be calculated carefully; if your CPU draws a maximum turbo power of 125 watts and your graphics card consumes 250 watts under full load, a power supply unit rated at 650 watts with an 80 Plus Gold efficiency rating provides the necessary overhead without running near maximum thermal capacity. Technicians must always utilize anti-static wrist straps connected to a grounded chassis before handling sensitive silicon to prevent microscopic voltage spikes from destroying integrated circuits.

In class exercise: Inspect a provided motherboard layout, identify the primary 24-pin ATX power connector, locate the CPU fan header, and calculate total power consumption for a given hardware list.

title: Lecture 2: Initialization, Firmware, and OS Deployment
description: This lecture explores the boot process, UEFI configuration, and operating system installation workflows.
content:
Learning objectives: configure UEFI settings for secure boot, interpret power-on self-test error indicators, and deploy modern operating systems.

When a computer receives power, the Unified Extensible Firmware Interface initializes hardware components through the Power-On Self-Test. If a hardware fault occurs, such as a missing memory module, the system emits a specific series of acoustic tones, known as beep codes, to alert the technician. For example, a continuous pattern of three short beeps on an AMI BIOS typically points directly to a base memory initialization failure. Once hardware validation passes, the system reads the boot order sequence to locate a valid operating system loader. Deploying an operating system like Windows or Linux requires preparing an installation medium, configuring storage partitions using GUID Partition Table standards, and injecting necessary storage controller drivers during setup. Post-installation, verifying hardware stability involves installing vendor-specific chipset drivers and running Windows Update to ensure all hardware abstraction layer components communicate smoothly with the kernel.

In class exercise: Access the UEFI interface on a lab machine, alter the boot priority to place USB storage first, and document the current firmware version string.

title: Lecture 3: Troubleshooting Methodology and Fault Diagnostics
description: This lecture teaches systematic troubleshooting techniques for isolating and resolving hardware and software failures.
content:
Learning objectives: apply the six-step troubleshooting methodology to complex system faults, diagnose thermal and power anomalies, and analyze blue screen dump files.

Systematic troubleshooting separates amateur repair from professional computer maintenance. Technicians must follow a structured approach: identify the symptom, establish a theory of probable cause, test the theory, establish a plan of action, implement the solution, and verify full system functionality while documenting findings. Consider a diagnostic scenario where a desktop computer powers on for five seconds, displays no video output on the monitor, and then shuts down repeatedly. Following our methodology, we theorize a thermal cutoff or a poorly seated memory module. We test this by swapping out the power supply and reseating the dual inline memory modules. Suppose testing reveals that the CPU temperature reaches 100 degrees Celsius instantly due to a pump failure on an all-in-one liquid cooler; the plan involves replacing the cooling unit, applying thermal paste, and verifying that idle temperatures stabilize at 35 degrees Celsius.

In class exercise: Work in pairs to diagnose a deliberately misconfigured lab computer exhibiting a boot device not found error using the official six-step documentation template.

title: Lecture 4: Preventive Maintenance, Storage Health, and Networking
description: This lecture covers routine maintenance schedules, predictive disk monitoring, and basic network connectivity for workstations and peripherals.
content:
Learning objectives: interpret SMART disk health parameters, design preventive maintenance cleaning schedules, and configure basic TCP/IP settings and network printers.

Long-term reliability depends heavily on proactive maintenance and environmental management. Dust accumulation acts as a thermal blanket, raising internal component temperatures and accelerating hardware degradation. A robust preventive maintenance plan includes quarterly compressed air cleaning of heatsinks, bi-annual replacement of thermal interface material, and automated weekly system image backups. Storage maintenance relies on Self-Monitoring, Analysis, and Reporting Technology to predict impending drive failures before data loss occurs. If a mechanical hard disk reports a raw value of 5 for attribute 5, representing Reallocated Sectors Count, the technician must immediately migrate data to a new drive because the storage medium is actively failing. Furthermore, technicians must ensure network readiness by configuring static or DHCP IP addresses, verifying default gateway connectivity using command line ping utilities, and sharing network printers via Server Message Block protocols.

In class exercise: Run a SMART disk health diagnostic utility on your workstation, record the drive temperature, and map a shared network printer using its IP address.

content:
1. Component Compatibility and Power Calculation: Select a CPU with a 105 watt TDP, a GPU requiring 300 watts, and standard motherboard components. Calculate the minimum recommended power supply unit wattage, explain your safety margin, and list the correct power cables required. (Marks: 4)

Include how you would use MemTest86 to isolate the faulty component. (Marks: 6)
4. Storage Health and Backup Strategy: Analyze a provided text log of SMART attributes showing failing reallocated sectors. Recommend a data recovery and migration path, and outline a 3-2-1 backup strategy for a small business containing five workstations and one local file server. (Marks: 6)

title: Lecture 1: Media Types and Digitization
description: This lecture introduces the foundational concepts of converting continuous analog signals into discrete digital representations through sampling and quantization.
content: Learning objectives: Understand the process of analog-to-digital conversion, apply the Nyquist rate formula to audio and visual signals, and calculate raw uncompressed data rates. To digitize continuous phenomena like sound waves, we must perform sampling in the time domain and quantization in the amplitude domain. The Nyquist theorem states that to accurately reconstruct a signal without aliasing, the sampling frequency must be greater than or equal to twice the highest frequency component present in the original signal. For example, consider recording a sound wave with a maximum frequency of 10 kilohertz. According to the Nyquist criterion, the minimum required sampling rate is 2 times 10 kilohertz, which equals 20,000 samples per second or 20 kilohertz. If we use a bit depth of 16 bits per sample for a mono channel, the resulting bit rate is 20,000 samples multiplied by 16 bits, yielding 320,000 bits per second, or 40 kilobytes per second. In class exercise: Given a signal with a maximum frequency of 8 kilohertz sampled at 12 kilohertz, calculate the maximum frequency that can be represented without aliasing and determine if aliasing will occur.

title: Lecture 2: Visual Media and Compression Fundamentals
description: This lecture explores digital images, colour models, and the core principles of lossless and lossy data compression.
content: Learning objectives: Distinguish between various colour spaces and image formats, and evaluate the trade-offs between lossless and lossy compression methods. Visual media relies on digital grids of pixels, where each pixel's colour is defined using models such as RGB for displays, CMYK for printing, and YUV for broadcasting. Because raw images and videos demand immense storage, compression is mandatory. Lossless compression methods like Run-Length Encoding and Huffman coding reduce data size without discarding any information, making them ideal for text and technical drawings. Conversely, lossy techniques like JPEG achieve massive file size reductions by exploiting human visual perception. JPEG achieves this through the Discrete Cosine Transform and subsequent quantization, which discards high-frequency details that the human eye struggles to notice. For example, an uncompressed image of dimensions 1024 by 768 pixels with a 24-bit colour depth contains 1024 multiplied by 768 multiplied by 3 bytes per pixel, resulting in 2,359,296 bytes, or approximately 2.25 megabytes. Applying a lossy compression algorithm can reduce this file size significantly at the cost of imperceptible quality loss. In class exercise: Explain why a lossless algorithm like Huffman coding is poorly suited for compressing photographic noise.

title: Lecture 3: Audio and Video Architecture
description: This lecture details the temporal structures of digital audio and video, including frame types, container formats, and synchronization.
content: Learning objectives: Compute raw bitrates for audio and video streams, and analyze the function of different video frame types in temporal compression. Digital audio standards, such as compact discs, use a sampling rate of 44.1 kilohertz and a bit depth of 16 bits per sample across stereo channels. Video builds upon this by sequencing images at defined frame rates, utilizing spatial and temporal compression. Video streams incorporate three primary frame types to save bandwidth: Intra-coded frames, Predictive frames, and Bidirectional predictive frames. Intra-frames act as anchor points containing complete image data, while Predictive frames store only the changes relative to a preceding reference frame. Bidirectional frames reference both past and future frames for maximum compression efficiency. For example, consider an uncompressed audio stream with a 44.1 kilohertz sampling rate, 16 bits per sample, and 2 stereo channels. The bit rate is calculated as 44,100 samples per second multiplied by 16 bits multiplied by 2 channels, yielding 1,411,200 bits per second, or approximately 176.4 kilobytes per second. Multiplying this by 60 seconds gives a total file size of roughly 10.58 megabytes for one minute of audio. In class exercise: Calculate the raw size of a single uncompressed 720p video frame at 24-bit colour depth.

title: Lecture 4: Multimedia Networking and Delivery
description: This lecture covers the protocols, delivery mechanisms, and adaptive techniques used to stream multimedia content over packet-switched networks.
content: Learning objectives: Understand the mechanics of adaptive bitrate streaming, evaluate network buffering requirements, and define Quality of Service parameters. Delivering multimedia over the internet presents challenges due to packet loss, jitter, and bandwidth fluctuations. Traditional progressive download is often insufficient for live or high-definition content, necessitating streaming protocols. Modern streaming relies on adaptive bitrate technologies such as HTTP Live Streaming and Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP. These protocols chop media into short segments and encode them at multiple bitrates and resolutions. The client-side media player constantly monitors available network bandwidth and CPU load, dynamically switching to a higher or lower quality segment on the fly to prevent buffering pauses. For example, if a client experiences a drop in available bandwidth from 5 megabits per second down to 1.5 megabits per second, the adaptive streaming player will seamlessly transition from a 1080p stream down to a 720p stream without interrupting playback. Quality of Service mechanisms prioritize multimedia packets across routers to minimize latency. In class exercise: Discuss why TCP is generally avoided for real-time live video streaming compared to UDP-based transport.

content:
1. Calculate the exact uncompressed storage size in megabytes for a 30-second stereophonic audio recording sampled at 48 kilohertz with a 24-bit bit depth. (4 marks)
2. Determine the raw uncompressed data rate in megabytes per second for a video stream with a resolution of 1280 by 720 pixels, a frame rate of 60 frames per second, and a 24-bit colour depth. (4 marks)
3. Describe the distinct roles of I-frames, P-frames, and B-frames within an MPEG video compression sequence, explaining how motion compensation operates between them. (4 marks)
4. Compare and contrast lossless and lossy compression by identifying one practical use case where lossy compression is completely unacceptable and justifying your reasoning. (4 marks)
5. Explain how adaptive bitrate streaming handles sudden network congestion and describe the client-side decision-making process during playback. (4 marks)

title: Lecture 1: Emerging Technologies in Computing
description: This lecture introduces generative artificial intelligence, large language models, blockchain fundamentals, and quantum computing basics.
content: Learning objectives include understanding tokenization in language models, basic ledger immutability in cryptography, and qubit superposition principles. When a large language model processes text, it breaks sentences into smaller fragments called tokens before generating numerical vector representations. For example, consider processing the string data computing. If our vocabulary maps data to index 102 and computing to index 405, the input sequence becomes the vector [102, 405]. The model applies attention mechanisms to predict the next token probability distribution. In blockchain systems, data integrity is maintained using cryptographic hash functions. If a block contains the transaction record Alice pays Bob five dollars with a previous hash of 000a, and we append the nonce 45, the SHA-256 function computes a new hash output starting with four leading zeros, such as 0000abc123. Changing any single character in the transaction record invalidates the hash, preventing unauthorized alterations. Quantum computing utilizes qubits that exist in a linear combination of states zero and one, represented mathematically as the state vector psi equals alpha times state zero plus beta times state one, where the squared magnitude of alpha plus the squared magnitude of beta equals one. In class, write a simple Python script using a dictionary to map a five-word sentence to integer token IDs and calculate the vocabulary coverage ratio.

title: Lecture 2: Edge and Internet of Things Computing
description: This lecture examines decentralized data processing, latency reduction, and resource-constrained device management at the network edge.
content: Learning objectives involve contrasting centralized cloud architectures with edge paradigms, calculating transmission round-trip times, and implementing lightweight telemetry filters. Edge computing places computation closer to data generators to minimize bandwidth consumption and latency. Consider a smart factory sensor recording temperature readings every second, producing a floating-point value. Sending every single raw measurement to a distant cloud server over a cellular link introduces a network latency of 150 milliseconds per packet and high data transfer costs. If we deploy an edge gateway running a local aggregation script, we can compute a moving average over a sliding window of sixty samples. Suppose our sensor records 60 temperature values around 50 degrees Celsius with a single outlier spike of 95 degrees. A local threshold filter checking if absolute value of measurement minus mean is greater than 3 can immediately flag the anomaly locally within 2 milliseconds without wasting upstream bandwidth. The network transmission payload drops from 60 floating-point numbers down to a single alert flag and timestamp when an anomaly occurs. In class, calculate the total daily bandwidth in megabytes generated by 500 sensors transmitting a 64-byte JSON payload every 10 seconds, and compare it to an edge-filtered approach that only transmits updates when values change by more than 5 percent.

title: Lecture 3: DevOps and Cloud-Native Development
description: This lecture covers containerization, continuous integration and deployment pipelines, and microservices orchestration.
content: Learning objectives focus on writing deterministic container specifications, automating testing workflows, and managing service scalability. Cloud-native development relies on immutable infrastructure where applications run inside isolated user spaces called containers. A standard deployment configuration uses container images defined by a sequence of build instructions. For example, a multi-stage Dockerfile starts with a builder image containing a full software development kit to compile a web service binary, and then copies only the compiled binary into a lightweight alpine base image. Suppose our application compilation step produces a binary of size 45 megabytes. By using a multi-stage build, we exclude the 500 megabyte compiler toolchain from the final production image, reducing the attack surface and decreasing container startup time from 4.2 seconds down to 0.8 seconds. Continuous integration pipelines automate the validation of every code commit by executing unit tests, security scans, and container image builds before merging changes into the main branch. In class, draft a basic workflow configuration file that triggers a build job whenever a developer pushes code to the staging branch, runs a test suite containing 25 automated unit checks, and publishes the resulting artifact to a private registry only if all tests pass successfully.

title: Lecture 4: Cybersecurity Trends and Research Skills
description: This lecture explores modern threat landscapes, defensive engineering strategies, and academic literature review methodologies.
content: Learning objectives include identifying common vulnerability vectors, applying zero-trust principles, and systematically evaluating technical research papers. Modern cybersecurity shifts from perimeter-based defenses to a zero-trust model that continuously verifies identity and device health. Consider an enterprise access control system evaluating a login request from an employee. Instead of trusting the corporate local area network, the system checks three distinct signals: whether the user authenticated with multi-factor authentication, whether the device disk encryption is enabled, and whether the request originates from an approved geographic subnet. If the risk score calculated as the sum of weighted risk factors exceeds a threshold of 0.75, access is denied. When conducting computing research, reading academic literature requires a structured approach. To review a systems paper efficiently, students should extract the core problem statement, identify the novel architectural method, analyze the empirical evaluation metrics such as throughput or latency, and document any acknowledged limitations. In class, select a recent conference abstract on automated vulnerability patching, summarize the primary research question in one sentence, and list two quantitative evaluation metrics used by the authors to demonstrate improvement over baseline methods.

Zero-Trust Access Control Logic (4 marks): Implement a Python function evaluate_access(mfa_passed, device_secure, geo_match) that returns True if multi-factor authentication is passed and either the device is secure or the geographic match is true. Include three test cases demonstrating allowed and denied access scenarios.
4. Vulnerability Mitigation Analysis (4 marks): Given a web service vulnerable to SQL injection due to unescaped string concatenation like query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + user_input + "'", rewrite the query using parameterized statements. Calculate the percentage reduction in potential attack vectors if input sanitization and parameterized queries are fully adopted across an application containing 50 distinct database endpoints.
5. Academic Paper Review (4 marks): Read any peer-reviewed systems or artificial intelligence paper published within the last three years. Write a structured review of exactly five sentences covering the problem, the proposed method, the experimental setup, the primary quantitative result, and one limitation.

title: Lecture 1: Database Architecture and Entity-Relationship Modelling
description: This lecture introduces database management system concepts, the three-level architecture, and how to model real-world domains using ER diagrams.
content: Learning objectives: Understand data independence and the three-level architecture, translate conceptual requirements into entity-relationship diagrams, and map ER schemas into relational tables. To achieve physical data independence, the database uses a three-level architecture consisting of the internal, conceptual, and external levels. This separation ensures changes to physical storage do not affect application views. ER modeling captures domain semantics through entities, attributes, and relationships. Consider a university domain where a Student entity has attributes student_id and name, and a Department entity has dept_id and name. A Department offers many Students, forming a 1 to N relationship. To map this to tables, we create a Department table with dept_id as the primary key and a Student table containing student_id as the primary key and dept_id as a foreign key referencing Department. For an M to N relationship between Student and Course, we introduce a junction table, Enrollment, containing student_id, course_id, and grade as attributes, where the combination of student_id and course_id forms the primary key. In class exercise: Draw an ER diagram for a library system with Book, Member, and Borrow relationships, indicating cardinalities, and write down the corresponding relational schema tables with their primary and foreign keys.

title: Lecture 2: Relational Algebra and Relational Model Constraints
description: This lecture explores the theoretical foundations of the relational model, integrity constraints, and formal query manipulation through relational algebra.
content: Learning objectives: Master integrity constraints in the relational model, evaluate relational algebra expressions step by step, and understand the equivalence between algebra operators and declarative queries. The relational model organizes data into relations containing tuples and attributes governed by domain, entity, and referential integrity constraints. Foreign key constraints ensure referential integrity by restricting referencing values to existing referenced keys or null. Relational algebra provides procedural operators to query relations. The select operator sigma filters tuples based on a predicate, while the project operator pi extracts specific columns. Joins combine relations based on matching values. Suppose we have an Employee relation with columns id, name, and salary, and a Department relation with columns dept_id and name. To find the names of employees earning more than 50000 in the Sales department, we write the relational algebra expression pi_name(sigma_salary > 50000 and dept_name = 'Sales' (Employee bowtie Employee.dept_id = Department.dept_id Department)). Here, selection reduces the rows, joining aligns matching department names, and projection outputs only the name attribute. In class exercise: Given relations Sailor and Boat, write the relational algebra expression to find the names of sailors who have reserved a red boat.

title: Lecture 3: Structured Query Language and Database Normalization
description: This lecture covers advanced SQL querying techniques, data modification statements, functional dependencies, and normalization up to Boyce-Codd Normal Form.
content: Learning objectives: Construct complex SQL queries involving grouping, subqueries, and joins, analyze functional dependencies, and decompose relations to eliminate update anomalies. SQL serves as the standard language for querying relational databases. Aggregation groups rows to compute summaries, and the having clause filters grouped results. Normalization addresses redundancy and update anomalies such as insertion, deletion, and modification issues. A functional dependency X arrow Y implies that value X uniquely determines value Y. A relation is in third normal form if it is in second normal form and has no transitive dependencies where non-key attributes determine other non-key attributes. Consider a relation schema R(EmployeeId, Department, Budget) with functional dependencies EmployeeId arrow Department and Department arrow Budget. This relation is in second normal form but violates third normal form because Department, a non-key attribute, determines Budget. We decompose R into R1(EmployeeId, Department) and R2(Department, Budget) to remove the anomaly. In class exercise: Write an SQL query to find the department name and the maximum salary for departments where the average salary exceeds 60000, and normalize a given unnormalized table containing repeating groups.

title: Lecture 4: Transactions, Concurrency Control, and Performance Indexing
description: This lecture introduces transaction management, ACID properties, recovery concepts, and database indexing strategies to optimize query performance.
content: Learning objectives: Define the ACID properties of transactions, understand the role of commit and rollback operations, and analyze how indexing accelerates data retrieval. A transaction represents a logical unit of database work comprising multiple operations. To maintain database consistency, transactions must satisfy ACID properties: Atomicity ensures all or no operations execute; Consistency transitions the database from one valid state to another; Isolation ensures concurrent executions produce the same results as serial executions; Durability guarantees committed changes survive system failures. The commit operation saves changes permanently, while rollback undoes uncommitted modifications following a failure. Performance indexing reduces disk I-O by providing rapid access paths to data rows. B-Plus tree indexes organize keys hierarchically, allowing logarithmic search time complexity instead of full table scans. For instance, creating an index on a frequently filtered column like order_date transforms a linear scan of infinity rows into a targeted pointer lookup. In class exercise: Trace the execution of a bank transfer transaction involving debit and credit operations, explaining how atomicity and rollbacks handle a power failure midway through the execution steps.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Database Design and Querying
description: This assignment tests practical skills in ER modeling, relational algebra, advanced SQL querying, normalization, and transaction analysis.
content:
1. ER Modeling and Mapping. Design an ER diagram for a university hospital system with Patient, Doctor, and Treatment entities, including attributes and cardinalities. Map the diagram into a set of relational tables, clearly indicating primary keys and foreign keys. (Marks: 4)
2. Relational Algebra. Given relations Patient(patient_id, name, age) and Treatment(patient_id, doctor_id, diagnosis), write relational algebra expressions to retrieve: a) the names of all patients older than 50, and b) the patient IDs of individuals treated by doctor ID 105. (Marks: 4)
3. Advanced SQL Querying. Write an SQL query on a schema containing Employee(emp_id, name, salary, dept_id) and Department(dept_id, dept_name) to find the department name and total salary expenditure for each department, but only include departments with a total salary expenditure exceeding 150000, ordered descending by total salary. (Marks: 4)
4. Normalization. Consider a relation schema R(StudentID, CourseID, InstructorID, InstructorEmail) with functional dependencies StudentID, CourseID arrow InstructorID and InstructorID arrow InstructorEmail. Identify the primary key, determine the highest normal form of R, and perform a lossless decomposition into Boyce-Codd Normal Form if necessary. (Marks: 4)
5. Transactions and Indexing. Explain how the isolation property prevents dirty reads in a concurrent execution scenario, and describe how adding a B-Plus tree index on the salary column impacts the performance of both SELECT queries and INSERT updates. (Marks: 4)

title: Lecture 1: Storage, Indexing, and Query Processing
description: This lecture examines how database engines store records on disk and evaluate queries efficiently using cost-based optimization and physical operators.
content:
Learning Objectives:
1. Understand how pages and B+ trees organize data for rapid retrieval.
2. Analyze relational join algorithms and select optimal execution plans.

Explanation:
Database management systems store data in fixed-size pages organized inside heap files or index structures. A B+ tree index maintains sorted keys in leaf nodes connected as a doubly linked list, enabling both point queries and range scans in logarithmic time. When executing a query, the query optimizer translates declarative SQL into an execution plan composed of physical operators. Consider an inner join between a Department table with 1,000 pages and an Employee table with 10,000 pages on department_id. A block nested loop join loads pages of the outer relation into memory, reading the inner relation for each block. If memory holds 100 pages of Department, the total cost is 1,000 plus (10,000 times 10), yielding 101,000 page I/Os. Alternatively, a sort-merge join sorts both relations and merges them in a single pass over the sorted runs, significantly reducing I/O cost when input data is already ordered or indices are present. Cost estimation relies on table statistics such as number of tuples and distinct key counts.

In class exercise:
Calculate the cost of a nested loop join where relation R has 500 pages and relation S has 5,000 pages, assuming memory can hold 50 pages of R at a time.

title: Lecture 2: Transactions and Concurrency Control
description: This lecture explores ACID properties, serializability, two-phase locking protocols, and multiversion concurrency control mechanisms.
content:
Learning Objectives:
1. Differentiate between serializable schedules and anomalies caused by concurrent execution.
2. Apply the two-phase locking protocol and understand deadlock resolution strategies.

Explanation:
Concurrency control ensures database consistency when multiple transactions execute simultaneously. Without proper isolation, concurrent schedules can introduce phenomena such as dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and lost updates. The two-phase locking protocol guarantees conflict serializability by enforcing that all locks are acquired during the growing phase and released exclusively during the shrinking phase. However, strict two-phase locking can cause deadlocks when transactions request locks in conflicting orders. For example, transaction T1 holds an exclusive lock on resource A and requests resource B, while transaction T2 holds an exclusive lock on resource B and requests resource A. The database system resolves such deadlocks by detecting cycles in the wait-for graph and aborting one of the participating transactions. Modern database engines often implement Multiversion Concurrency Control, allowing readers to access older consistent snapshots of data without blocking writers, thereby dramatically increasing throughput for mixed read-write workloads.

In class exercise:
Draw a wait-for graph for transactions T1, T2, and T3 where T1 waits for T2, T2 waits for T3, and T3 waits for T1, and state the resolution.

title: Lecture 3: Recovery and Distributed Databases
description: This lecture covers failure recovery using write-ahead logging and the ARIES algorithm, alongside distributed database architecture and consensus.
content:
Learning Objectives:
1. Explain the three phases of the ARIES recovery algorithm.
2. Understand distributed database challenges including fragmentation, replication, and atomic commitment.

Explanation:
Database durability relies on the write-ahead logging protocol, which dictates that log records describing modifications must be flushed to non-volatile storage before the corresponding dirty data pages are written. When a system crashes, the ARIES recovery algorithm restores consistency through three sequential phases: Analysis, Redo, and Undo. During the Analysis phase, ARIES scans forward from the last checkpoint to identify active transactions and dirty pages. The Redo phase then repeats all actions historically, including those of uncommitted transactions, bringing the database to the exact state it was in at the time of the crash. Finally, the Undo phase rolls back actions of transactions that were active at crash time, writing compensation log records to ensure idempotency. In distributed environments, data is split across multiple nodes via horizontal fragmentation. Maintaining atomicity across these nodes requires protocols like two-phase commit, which coordinates commit decisions through a coordinator node across participant sites.

In class exercise:
Trace why the Redo phase in ARIES must process operations from the oldest unwritten log record identified in the analysis phase.

title: Lecture 4: Advanced SQL, NoSQL, and Data Warehousing
description: This lecture investigates analytical SQL window functions, NoSQL architectural trade-offs under the CAP theorem, and data warehousing principles.
content:
Learning Objectives:
1. Construct advanced analytical queries using window functions and common table expressions.
2. Evaluate NoSQL data models and assess CAP theorem trade-offs for distributed systems.

Explanation:
Modern data processing extends beyond basic relational queries. Advanced SQL features such as window functions allow computations across sets of table rows related to the current row without collapsing the result set. For instance, computing a running total or ranking records partitioned by a category uses syntax like RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC). Beyond relational models, NoSQL systems provide alternative paradigms tailored for horizontal scalability. Key-value stores prioritize extreme speed, document databases like MongoDB offer flexible schema evolution using JSON-like structures, and column-family stores optimize analytical scans. The CAP theorem states that a distributed data store can simultaneously provide at most two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance. Because network partitions are inevitable in real networks, systems must choose between consistency and availability. Data warehouses complement operational databases by utilizing star schemas, denormalized dimensions, and columnar storage optimized for Online Analytical Processing queries.

In class exercise:
Write an SQL window function query to calculate the moving average salary of employees over a window of the current row and the preceding row ordered by hire date.

content:

2. Provide an interleaving schedule involving two transactions, T1 and T2, that demonstrates the non-repeatable read anomaly, and explain how setting the isolation level to repeatable read prevents it. [Marks: 4]

3. Describe the exact sequence of log records written during a transaction update and subsequent system crash, and explain how the ARIES Undo phase processes this uncommitted change. [Marks: 4]

4. Given a distributed database with nodes N1 and N2, detail the two-phase commit protocol messages exchanged when participant N2 votes to abort due to a local disk failure during the prepare phase. [Marks: 4]

5. Analyze a scenario where an e-commerce application experiences high write contention on inventory counters, comparing how a relational database using row-level locking versus a distributed key-value store handles the workload under the CAP theorem. [Marks: 4]

title: Lecture 1: Storage Hardware and Physical File Organizations
description: This lecture connects physical storage characteristics like HDD latency and solid-state endurance directly to how records are laid out sequentially and hashed on disk.
content:
Learning objectives: Understand memory hierarchy trade-offs, compute disk access times, and compare fixed versus variable-length record formats.

Data storage begins with the physical medium. Hard disk drives require mechanical movement, incurring seek time and rotational latency, whereas solid-state drives rely on flash memory blocks with wear-leveling constraints. To minimize costly block reads, records are grouped into blocks. Consider a file containing fixed-length records of 100 bytes each, stored in a block size of 4096 bytes with a 96-byte block overhead. The usable space per block is 4000 bytes, allowing us to pack exactly 40 records per block. If a file has 10,000 records, it requires 250 blocks. For variable-length records, we must use delimiters or length fields, often pairing them with a slot-pointer directory inside each block to allow records to shift during updates without breaking external references. Sequential files store records in sort-order, making range scans efficient, while hashed files compute a bucket address directly from a search key using a hash function, achieving O(1) average lookup performance for exact matches.

In class exercise: Calculate the number of blocks needed for a file of 5,000 fixed-length records where each record is 250 bytes, given a block size of 2048 bytes with no overhead.

title: Lecture 2: Indexing Strategies and Tree Structures
description: Students will explore how primary, secondary, and dynamic tree indexes accelerate search operations while managing disk page splits.
content:
Learning objectives: Distinguish between primary and secondary indexes, analyze B+ tree fan-out, and explain how dynamic hashing adapts to data growth.

Sequential scans are too slow for large databases, necessitating indexes. A primary index is built on a sorted file's ordering key, whereas a secondary index provides a secondary access path using non-ordering fields. Because disk I/O is the primary bottleneck, databases favor B+ trees over binary search trees. A B+ tree keeps all data pointers in leaf nodes while internal nodes guide the search. Let us compute the fan-out of a B+ tree node. Suppose a disk block size is 4096 bytes, search keys take 8 bytes, and block pointers take 8 bytes. An internal node holds P pointers and P-1 keys, so P times 8 plus (P-1) times 8 must be less than or equal to 4096. Solving this yields 16 + 8P <= 4096, meaning 8P <= 4080, resulting in a maximum fan-out of 510 children per internal node. This massive fan-out allows a tree of height 3 to index over 130 million records. When static hashes overflow, structures like extendible hashing use a directory of pointers that doubles when a bucket overflows, avoiding massive re-rehashing operations.

In class exercise: Determine the maximum fan-out for a B+ tree node if the block size is 1024 bytes, key size is 12 bytes, and child pointer size is 8 bytes.

title: Lecture 3: Information Retrieval Models and Inverted Indexes
description: This lecture introduces text processing pipelines and mathematical ranking models used to score document relevance.
content:
Learning objectives: Construct an inverted index from raw text, apply stop word removal and stemming, and compute vector space similarity scores.

Unstructured data retrieval requires specialized text processing. Raw documents undergo tokenization, case-folding, stop-word removal, and stemming to extract core terms. These terms populate an inverted index, which maps each term to a posting list containing document IDs and term frequencies. For instance, consider document one containing 'data storage' and document two containing 'storage retrieval'. The term 'storage' appears in both, yielding a posting list of [doc1, doc2]. To score relevance, we use the vector space model with TF-IDF and cosine similarity. Suppose term T appears 2 times in a document of 100 terms (Term Frequency TF = 0.02). If the term appears in 10 out of 1,000 documents in the collection, its Inverse Document Frequency is the logarithm base 10 of (1000 divided by 10), which equals 2.0. The resulting TF-IDF weight is 0.02 multiplied by 2.0, giving 0.04. Documents and queries are represented as vectors of these weights, and their semantic alignment is measured by the cosine of the angle between them.

In class exercise: Compute the IDF of a term that appears in 5 documents within a total collection of 500 documents using base 10 logarithms.

title: Lecture 4: Evaluation Metrics and Modern Semantic Search
description: Students learn how to rigorously measure retrieval quality using standard metrics and transition from keyword matching to dense vector embeddings.
content:
Learning objectives: Calculate precision, recall, and F1-score, interpret ranking cutoffs, and understand how neural embeddings enable semantic search.

System performance must be evaluated quantitatively using test collections with known relevance judgments. Precision measures the fraction of retrieved documents that are relevant, while recall measures the fraction of all relevant documents that are successfully retrieved. Suppose a search query has a total of 15 relevant documents in the entire database. A retrieval system returns 10 documents, of which 6 are actually relevant. The precision is 6 divided by 10, which equals 0.60. The recall is 6 divided by 15, which equals 0.40. The F1-score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, computed as 2 times precision times recall divided by the sum of precision and recall, yielding 2 times 0.60 times 0.40 divided by 1.00, which equals 0.48. While traditional keyword systems rely on exact term matches, modern search engines utilize neural network embeddings. These models project words, sentences, or entire documents into dense vector spaces, allowing the system to retrieve results based on conceptual similarity rather than exact lexical overlap, measured via inner product or cosine similarity on high-dimensional vectors.

In class exercise: A system retrieves 8 documents for a query, and 4 of them are relevant. If there are 10 relevant documents in total, calculate the precision, recall, and F1-score.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Data Storage, Indexing, and Retrieval Project

content:
1. Block Allocation Analysis: Given a file of 12,000 fixed-length records where each record is 150 bytes, calculate the exact number of disk blocks required if the block size is 4096 bytes with a 96-byte block header. Show all steps. (Marks: 4)

3. title: Lecture 1: Foundations and Architecture
description: This lecture introduces the core principles of data warehousing by contrasting operational transaction processing with analytical processing and examining the end-to-end data flow architecture.
content:
Learning Objectives: Distinguish between operational and analytical workloads; trace data movement from source systems through staging and transformation to consumption layers.

Explanation: While online transaction processing systems are optimized for fast row-level insertions and updates to support daily business applications, online analytical processing systems are designed for complex read-heavy queries over massive historical datasets. The data warehouse architecture bridges this gap by decoupling analytics from source transactional databases. Raw data is first extracted from operational databases into a staging area for temporary storage and validation. During the extraction, transformation, and loading process, data is cleansed, reformatted, and integrated before being loaded into the enterprise data warehouse. For instance, consider a university where the transactional system stores student registrations across multiple campus databases with conflicting date formats. The staging area standardizes these dates to the ISO format, merges duplicate student records based on university ID, and loads the clean dataset into the warehouse.

In class exercise: Draw a diagram mapping an operational e-commerce database through a staging environment to a centralized data warehouse and a downstream business intelligence reporting tool, identifying where data transformation occurs.

title: Lecture 2: Dimensional Modeling and Schemas
description: This lecture explores dimensional modeling techniques, differentiating between facts and dimensions, and evaluating star versus snowflake schemas.
content:
Learning Objectives: Design star and snowflake schemas based on business requirements; define grain and select appropriate measures and contextual attributes.

Explanation: Dimensional modeling structures data to optimize user understanding and query performance. It centers around fact tables, which contain quantitative measurements resulting from a business process, and dimension tables, which provide descriptive context about the business process. The grain of a fact table defines the exact meaning of a single row. In a star schema, dimension tables are denormalized and connected directly to the central fact table. In a snowflake schema, those dimensions are further normalized into multiple related tables to reduce redundancy. Consider a university enrollment process where the fact table records every student enrollment. The fact table contains foreign keys to dimension tables for Student, Course, and Semester, along with additive measures like grade points equal to 12 and attendance percentage equal to 95. In a star schema, the Course dimension contains columns for course name and department in a single table. In a snowflake schema, the department details are split into a separate Department table linked by a department ID.

In class exercise: Determine the grain and list three measures and three dimensions for a hospital patient admission data warehouse.

title: Lecture 3: Slowly Changing Dimensions and ETL Operations
description: This lecture covers data evolution strategies through slowly changing dimensions and examines the mechanics of data cleansing, transformation, and loading pipelines.
content:
Learning Objectives: Implement type 1 and type 2 slowly changing dimensions; design robust data quality checks within extraction and transformation pipelines.

Explanation: Dimension attributes change over time, and data warehouses must handle these changes without breaking historical reporting. A type 1 slowly changing dimension simply overwrites the existing attribute value with the new one, which discards history and is used when historical accuracy is not required. A type 2 slowly changing dimension preserves history by creating a new dimension row with a new surrogate key, while updating effective start and end dates or current flags on the existing row. For example, if Professor Alice moves from the Mathematics department to the Computer Science department, a type 1 update changes her department attribute directly in the current record. A type 2 update expires her old record by setting an end date, and inserts a new record with a start date of today, pointing future enrollments to the new department while preserving past enrollments under Mathematics. ETL pipelines must validate data quality during this process by filtering out null keys and enforcing referential integrity.

In class exercise: Write a step-by-step logic description to detect an incoming address change for an employee dimension and process it as a type 2 update.

title: Lecture 4: OLAP Operations and Performance Optimization
description: This lecture investigates multidimensional data analysis operations and physical storage optimization techniques used to accelerate analytical queries.
content:
Learning Objectives: Apply OLAP operations to data cubes; configure performance tuning mechanisms such as indexing, partitioning, and materialized views.

Explanation: Data cubes organize data along multiple dimensions to allow rapid analytical querying through specialized operations. Roll-up aggregates data by moving up a dimension hierarchy, such as moving from daily sales to monthly sales. Drill-down performs the reverse operation to inspect finer details. Slice selects a single value for one dimension, while dice selects a sub-cube by specifying ranges across multiple dimensions. Pivot rotates the axes of the report to display data from a different perspective. To maintain high performance as data volumes grow, modern architectures employ physical tuning strategies. For instance, a university data warehouse containing billions of enrollment rows can be partitioned by semester, ensuring that queries filtering for the current semester scan only a fraction of the total storage blocks. Additionally, pre-calculating aggregate tables or materialized views for departmental summaries reduces query execution time from minutes to milliseconds.

In class exercise: Given a data cube of university enrollments across Course, Semester, and Department, write out the resulting subset when slicing the cube by Semester equals Fall 2023.

title: Lecture 1: Foundations of Business Intelligence and Data Architecture
description: This lecture introduces the end-to-end business intelligence lifecycle, data preparation techniques, and foundational metric design.
content:
Learning objectives: Understand the stages of the BI lifecycle from raw data to actionable insight. Master basic data preparation including cleaning and joining.

The business intelligence lifecycle begins by translating strategic business questions into measurable requirements. Once questions are defined, data collection gathers relevant information from diverse operational sources. However, raw data is rarely analysis-ready and requires rigorous preparation. Data preparation involves data cleaning to remove duplicates, resolving formatting inconsistencies, and handling missing values through imputation or deletion. Following cleaning, data transformation often requires joining separate relational tables using keys to create a unified analytical dataset.

Consider a university analyzing course enrollment. Suppose table A lists 100 student IDs and their department codes, while table B lists 100 student IDs and their final grades. An inner join on student ID merges these tables into a single dataset of 100 complete records. If 5 students have missing grade entries due to deferred exams, we handle this missing value by excluding them or imputing a placeholder, resulting in an active analysis set of 95 records. From this prepared data, we compute key performance indicators such as the course pass rate. For example, if 76 out of the 95 evaluated students passed, the pass rate formula is calculated as 76 divided by 95, yielding exactly 0.80 or 80 percent.

In class exercise: Given a dataset of 50 employee records with 3 missing salary values, write down the exact steps you would take to clean the data and compute the average salary.

title: Lecture 2: The Four Pillars of Analytics and Dashboard Design
description: Students will explore descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analytics alongside best practices in data visualization and dashboard design.
content:
Learning objectives: Categorize analytical problems into the four main analytics types. Design effective visual dashboards while avoiding common pitfalls.

Analytics maturity spans four progressive stages. Descriptive analytics answers what happened by summarizing historical data using metrics and aggregates. Diagnostic analytics examines why it happened by drilling down into root causes and correlations. Predictive analytics forecasts what will likely happen using statistical models and machine learning algorithms. Finally, prescriptive analytics recommends what action to take by optimizing decisions under given constraints.

Effective communication of these insights relies on deliberate dashboard design and visualization principles. Choosing the correct chart type is crucial for audience comprehension. For instance, to compare the average grades of four different university departments, a bar chart is ideal because it clearly displays discrete categorical comparisons. Conversely, line charts should be reserved for time-series trends. Analysts must actively avoid misleading charts, such as truncated vertical axes that exaggerate minor performance differences. A well-designed executive dashboard consolidates these visualizations alongside high-level scorecards, ensuring decision-makers can monitor core metrics at a glance without cognitive overload.

In class exercise: Identify whether determining last semesters dropout rate is descriptive or diagnostic analytics, and justify your answer in one sentence.

title: Lecture 3: Modern BI Tooling and Practical SQL and Python Implementation
description: This lecture covers the practical application of SQL and Python pandas for data extraction, manipulation, and analysis within standard BI pipelines.
content:
Learning objectives: Write efficient SQL queries for data aggregation. Utilize Python pandas for programmatic data manipulation and basic modeling.

Modern business intelligence relies heavily on robust software tools ranging from interactive visual platforms like Power BI and Tableau to programmatic languages like SQL and Python. SQL acts as the primary language for querying relational databases, allowing analysts to extract exact subsets of data using SELECT, WHERE, and GROUP BY clauses. Meanwhile, Python with the pandas library provides immense flexibility for advanced data wrangling and initial predictive modeling.

Let us look at a practical SQL aggregation example. Suppose we want to find the average grade per department from a table named grades. The SQL query is written as: SELECT department, AVG(grade) FROM grades GROUP BY department;
When executed on a database where the Engineering department has 10 student grades totaling 850 points, the database computes the average as 850 divided by 10, returning 85.0. In Python pandas, the equivalent operation is performed using the groupby method: df.groupby('department')['grade'].mean(). Both tools streamline the transition from raw transactional records to structured analytical inputs.

In class exercise: Write a SQL snippet that counts the total number of students enrolled in each course from an enrollment table containing student_id and course_id columns.

title: Lecture 4: Predictive Modeling, Data Governance, and Ethical Culture
description: This final lecture examines basic predictive modeling techniques, data-driven organizational culture, and critical data governance policies.
content:
Learning objectives: Apply basic predictive modeling concepts including regression and classification. Understand organizational data governance and privacy frameworks.

Predictive modeling enables organizations to look forward using historical patterns. Simple linear regression models the continuous relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent predictor variables, fitting a line of best fit to forecast future values. Classification models, such as logistic regression or decision trees, assign categorical labels to observations, such as predicting whether a student is at risk of failing based on attendance and past quiz scores. Forecasting models specifically analyze time-ordered data to predict seasonal trends, such as future university enrollment numbers.

Beyond technical modeling, successful business intelligence requires a sustainable data-driven culture supported by strict governance and privacy protocols. Data governance establishes internal standards for data quality, accessibility, and ownership. Privacy regulations mandate that personally identifiable information must be anonymized or securely encrypted, ensuring that analytical value generation never compromises individual user rights or legal compliance.

In class exercise: State whether predicting whether a customer will churn or not churn is a regression task or a classification task, and explain why.
