title: Lecture 1: Sinusoidal Steady State and AC Power Analysis
description: This lecture introduces phasor transformations, complex impedance, and AC power relationships for steady-state sinusoidal networks.
content: Learning objectives: Apply phasor analysis to solve AC circuits using nodal and mesh techniques, and compute average, reactive, and complex power. In the sinusoidal steady state, differential equations simplify to algebraic equations using phasors. Impedance is defined as Z = R + jX, extending Ohm's law to the frequency domain where resistors, inductors, and capacitors are represented as R, jomega L, and 1/(jomega C) respectively. AC power analysis requires evaluating instantaneous, average, and complex power. Complex power is expressed as S = V times I*, which combines real power P measured in watts and reactive power Q measured in volt-amperes reactive. For example, consider an AC voltage source of V = 120 angle 0 degrees volts operating at 60 radians per second connected in series with a resistance of 30 ohms and an inductive reactance of 40 ohms. The impedance is Z = 30 + j40 ohms, yielding a magnitude of 50 ohms and a phase angle of 53.13 degrees. The current is I = 120 angle 0 divided by 50 angle 53.13, which equals 2.4 angle -53.13 degrees amperes. The complex power is S = V times I* = (120 angle 0)(2.4 angle 53.13) = 288 angle 53.13 volt-amperes, resulting in P = 172.8 watts and Q = 230.4 volt-amperes reactive. In class exercise: Determine the input impedance and complex power delivered to a series combination of a 10 ohm resistor, a 20 mill Henry inductor, and a 50 micro Farad capacitor driven by a 50 volt, 500 radian per second source.

title: Lecture 2: Resonance, Magnetically Coupled Circuits, and Transformers
description: This lecture examines resonance phenomena in RLC circuits and analyzes circuits containing mutual inductance and ideal transformers.
content: Learning objectives: Calculate resonant frequencies, quality factors, and bandwidths, and analyze circuits with mutual inductance and impedance reflection. Resonance occurs in AC circuits when the imaginary part of the network input impedance becomes zero. For a series RLC circuit, resonance happens at a frequency f0 = 1 / (2 pi square root of L C), where the impedance reaches its minimum value equal to the resistance R. The quality factor Q determines the sharpness of the resonance peak and relates the maximum stored energy to dissipated energy, while the bandwidth is given by the resonant frequency divided by Q. When circuits feature coils placed in proximity, magnetic flux links them, introducing mutual inductance M. The dot convention dictates the sign of the induced voltage terms based on current directions entering or leaving the dot terminals. Ideal transformers scale voltage and current by the turns ratio N1 to N2 while reflecting impedances by the square of the turns ratio. For example, given an inductance L = 25 milli Henries and a capacitance C = 4 micro Farads, the resonant frequency is f0 = 1 / (2 pi square root of (0.025 times 4e-6)) = 1 / (2 pi times 3.162e-4) = 503.3 Hertz. In class exercise: Find the resonant frequency, quality factor, and bandwidth for a parallel RLC network where R = 1 kilo ohm, L = 10 milli Henries, and C = 100 nano Farads.

title: Lecture 3: Frequency Response, Passive Filters, and Bode Plots
description: This lecture covers network transfer functions, pole-zero analysis, asymptotic Bode plots, and the design of standard passive filter topologies.
content: Learning objectives: Derive transfer functions H of s, locate poles and zeros to sketch Bode magnitude and phase plots, and design basic passive filters. The frequency response of a linear time-invariant system is characterized by the transfer function H of s, defined as the ratio of the output response to the input excitation in the complex frequency domain. Roots of the numerator polynomial are called zeros, where the response drops to zero, and roots of the denominator polynomial are called poles, where the response approaches infinity. Bode plots graphically display magnitude in decibels and phase in degrees versus frequency on a logarithmic scale using straight-line asymptotic approximations. Passive filters constructed from resistors, capacitors, and inductors implement specific frequency selectivity functions including low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, and band-stop responses. For example, consider the transfer function H of s = 500 / (s + 50). This system has a pole at s = -50, corresponding to a corner frequency of 50 radians per second. The DC gain is 500 divided by 50, which equals 10, or 20 times the log base 10 of 10, giving 20 decibels. For frequencies well above 50 radians per second, the magnitude rolls off at a rate of -20 decibels per decade. In class exercise: Sketch the asymptotic Bode magnitude plot for the low-pass filter transfer function H of s = 1000 / (s + 200).

title: Lecture 4: Two-Port Networks and Network Synthesis
description: This lecture explores two-port network parameter representations and introduces passive network synthesis using Foster and Cauer realizations.
content: Learning objectives: Convert between Z, Y, h, and ABCD parameters, and synthesize LC driving-point impedance functions using Foster and Cauer forms. Two-port networks provide a black-box approach to analyzing electrical circuits by relating terminal voltages and currents using various parameter sets such as impedance Z parameters, admittance Y parameters, hybrid h parameters, and transmission ABCD parameters. These parameters facilitate the cascading of multiple sub-networks. Network synthesis is the reverse process of analysis: given a positive real driving-point impedance function, we construct a physical network realization. Foster's first and second forms realize driving-point functions through partial fraction expansion, resulting in series-connected parallel LC tanks or parallel-connected series LC branches. Cauer's first and second forms use continued fraction expansion to yield ladder network structures consisting of alternating series and shunt elements. For example, consider a simple series impedance Z connected between input and output ports. Its transmission parameters relate input voltage and current to output voltage and current. The ABCD matrix for a series impedance Z has A = 1, B = Z, C = 0, and D = 1. In class exercise: Derive the Y parameters for a two-port network defined by a single shunt admittance Y connected across the output terminals.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive AC Analysis, Filters, and Synthesis
description: This assignment covers phasor circuit calculations, AC power factor correction, resonant filter design, and two-port parameter derivations.
content:
Task 1: Calculate the nodal voltages for an AC circuit containing a 100 volt rms, 50 hertz source in series with a 20 ohm resistor, a 50 milli Henry inductor, and a 100 micro Farad capacitor. (4 marks)
Task 2: Determine the complex power supplied by the source in Task 1, and calculate the value of the parallel capacitor required to improve the power factor to unity. (4 marks)
Task 3: Design a series RLC band-pass filter with a center frequency of 1 kilo hertz and a bandwidth of 100 hertz, assuming a resistance of 50 ohms. Compute the required inductance and capacitance values. (4 marks)
Task 4: Derive the ABCD transmission parameters for a simple shunt admittance Y connected across a transmission line. (4 marks)
Task 5: Perform a Foster first-form realization for the driving-point impedance function Z of s = (s squared + 1) / (s times (s squared + 2)) and specify all component values. (4 marks)
Submission instructions: Submit a single compiled PDF document containing all analytical derivations, intermediate steps, and final calculated values.

title: Lecture 1: Introduction to Semiconductors and Diode Circuits
description: This lecture covers semiconductor physics fundamentals, the p-n junction, and fundamental diode applications including rectifiers and regulators.
content: Learning objectives: Understand charge carrier behavior in doped silicon, analyze diode circuits using the constant drop model, and apply Zeners for voltage regulation. Semiconductors form the foundation of modern electronics through silicon doping. Intrinsic silicon is a poor conductor, but adding pentavalent or trivalent impurities creates n-type and p-type materials. Joining these creates a p-n junction featuring a depletion region. When forward-biased, the diode conducts once overcoming the barrier potential. For our practical analysis, we adopt the constant drop model where a conducting silicon diode maintains a fixed 0.7 V drop. Consider a full-wave bridge rectifier connected to a 12 V peak AC source. Each path in the bridge contains two diodes in series, resulting in a total drop of 2 times 0.7 V, which equals 1.4 V. Subtracting this from the 12 V peak input yields a rectified output peak voltage of 10.6 V. Smoothing this output with a suitably sized filter capacitor reduces voltage ripple, providing a steadier DC supply. Furthermore, Zener diodes are operated in their reverse breakdown region to maintain a constant voltage across a load despite supply variations. In class exercise: Calculate the peak output voltage of a half-wave rectifier driven by a 15 V peak source using the constant drop model, assuming a single 0.7 V diode drop.

title: Lecture 2: Bipolar Junction Transistors and DC Biasing
description: This lecture explores BJT operation regions, DC biasing techniques, load line analysis, and small-signal parameters.
content: Learning objectives: Determine the operational region of a BJT, compute the DC operating Q-point using voltage-divider biasing, and derive small-signal parameters. The Bipolar Junction Transistor is a three-terminal device where a small base current controls a much larger collector current according to the relationship I_C equals beta times I_B. To function as a linear amplifier, the transistor must be biased into the active region. Voltage-divider biasing establishes a stable operating point that is relatively independent of beta variations. Consider a circuit with a 12 V supply, a collector resistor of 2 kilohms, and a voltage-divider network that establishes a base voltage of 2.0 V. Using a silicon base-emitter drop of 0.7 V, the emitter voltage is 1.3 V. If the emitter resistance is 1 kilohm, the emitter current is 1.3 V divided by 1 kilohm, which equals 1.3 milliamperes. The collector current is approximately equal to the emitter current, yielding 1.3 milliamperes. The collector-emitter voltage is then the supply voltage minus the drop across the collector and emitter resistors, which equals 12 V minus the product of 1.3 milliamperes and the sum of 2 kilohms and 1 kilohm, resulting in 8.1 V. This defines our Q-point at 1.3 milliamperes and 8.1 V. Small-signal analysis linearizes this operating point to find transconductance g_m as I_C divided by V_T, and input resistance r_pi as beta times V_T divided by I_C. In class exercise: Find the collector current if I_B is 25 microamperes and beta is 100.

title: Lecture 3: Field-Effect Transistors and Single-Stage Amplifiers
description: This lecture investigates MOSFET structure and operation, single-stage amplifier configurations, and terminal characteristics.
content: Learning objectives: Analyze MOSFET saturation characteristics, evaluate common-source and common-drain amplifiers, and determine voltage gain. Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistors control current through an insulated gate terminal via an electric field. In the saturation region, the drain current is given by one-half times the process transconductance parameter k multiplied by the square of the difference between gate-source voltage V_GS and threshold voltage V_t. Single-stage amplifiers utilize these devices to provide voltage gain, current gain, or impedance buffering. For instance, a common-source amplifier provides a large voltage gain determined by the transconductance multiplied by the effective drain resistance. In contrast, the common-drain configuration, also known as a source follower, provides a voltage gain close to unity and features a high input resistance and a low output resistance, making it an excellent voltage buffer. When analyzing these topologies, we replace the transistor with its small-signal equivalent circuit to systematically calculate input resistance, output resistance, and overall voltage gain. Impedance scaling and loading effects from subsequent stages must be carefully factored into the design to prevent signal degradation. In class exercise: Compute the saturation drain current for a MOSFET where k is 0.5 milliamperes per volt squared, V_GS is 3 V, and V_t is 1 V.

title: Lecture 4: Operational Amplifiers and Transistor Switches
description: This lecture examines operational amplifier ideal characteristics, feedback topologies, and the use of transistors as electronic switches.
content: Learning objectives: Calculate gains for inverting and non-inverting op-amp configurations, and design transistor switching circuits for loads. Operational amplifiers are high-gain differential amplifiers that simplify analog circuit design when combined with external feedback components. Using negative feedback, we can precisely set the closed-loop gain. For an inverting amplifier configuration, the closed-loop voltage gain is determined by the negative ratio of the feedback resistor R_f to the input resistor R_in, expressed as negative R_f divided by R_in. For example, if R_f is 100 kilohms and R_in is 10 kilohms, the voltage gain is negative 10. Applying an input voltage of 0.5 V results in an output voltage of negative 5.0 V. For a non-inverting amplifier, the gain is given by one plus the ratio of R_f to R_in, always yielding a positive gain greater than or equal to one. Beyond linear amplification, transistors serve as efficient digital switches in electronic systems. By driving a BJT or MOSFET between cutoff and saturation, the device acts as an open or closed switch to control heavy loads like relays, motors, or indicator LEDs. In saturation, the transistor drops a negligible voltage while passing the full load current determined by the external circuit parameters. In class exercise: Determine the output voltage of an inverting op-amp with an input of negative 0.2 V, an R_in of 5 kilohms, and an R_f of 50 kilohms.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Semiconductor Device and Circuit Design
description: This assignment assesses student mastery of diodes, BJT biasing, MOSFET saturation, and operational amplifier design through practical computational and design problems.
content:
1. Analyze a half-wave rectifier circuit powered by a 24 V peak sinusoidal source with a 0.7 V diode drop and a 100 ohm load resistor. Calculate the peak load voltage and the average DC current delivered to the load. (4 marks)
2. Determine the exact Q-point for a voltage-divider biased BJT circuit given a 15 V supply, a collector resistor of 3 kilohms, an emitter resistor of 1.5 kilohms, a beta of 120, and a base voltage set to 2.8 V. Compute I_C and V_CE. (4 marks)
3. Calculate the drain current and small-signal transconductance g_m for an n-channel MOSFET operating in saturation, given k equals 1.0 milliampere per volt squared, V_t equals 1.5 V, and V_GS equals 3.5 V. (4 marks)
4. Design an inverting operational amplifier circuit with an input resistance of 20 kilohms to achieve a closed-loop voltage gain of negative 15. Specify the required feedback resistor value and calculate the output voltage for an input of 0.4 V. (4 marks)
5. Design a BJT transistor switch to drive a 12 V, 240 ohm relay coil using a transistor with a minimum beta of 80. Calculate the required base current to ensure saturation, assuming a saturation V_BE of 0.8 V and a negligible V_CE saturation drop. (4 marks)
Submission instructions: Submit your complete solutions as a single PDF document showing all intermediate steps, formula derivations, and unit conversions clearly.

title: Lecture 1: Fundamental Semiconductor Physics and Transport
description: This lecture examines advanced carrier dynamics, energy band engineering, and statistical mechanics governing modern semiconductor materials.
content: Learning objectives: Derive carrier concentrations using Fermi-Dirac statistics, calculate drift-diffusion current densities, and analyze recombination mechanisms. Understanding the microscopic behavior of electrons and holes is critical for designing all subsequent device structures. We begin with the density of states and the Fermi-Dirac distribution function to determine the intrinsic carrier concentration ni. At thermal equilibrium, the product of electron concentration n and hole concentration p equals ni squared, regardless of doping. Consider a silicon sample at 300 Kelvin doped with a donor concentration of 10 to the 16th power per cubic centimeter. Given the intrinsic concentration ni equals 1.5 times 10 to the 10th power per cubic centimeter, the majority electron concentration n is approximately 10 to the 16th power per cubic centimeter, and the minority hole concentration p evaluates to ni squared divided by n, yielding 2.25 times 10 to the 4th power per cubic centimeter. Current flow consists of drift, driven by electric fields according to mobility, and diffusion, driven by spatial concentration gradients obeying Fick's first law and related via the Einstein relation. In class exercise: Calculate the diffusion current density for a hole concentration gradient of 10 to the 18th power per cubic centimeter across a one micrometer region, assuming a hole diffusion coefficient of 12 square centimeters per second.

title: Lecture 2: The p-n Junction and MOS Capacitors
description: This lecture explores junction electrostatics, capacitance-voltage characteristics, and the foundational physics of Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor structures.
content: Learning objectives: Evaluate depletion region widths under bias, interpret C-V curves for MOS capacitors, and determine threshold voltages. The abrupt p-n junction establishes a built-in potential barrier defined by thermal voltage multiplied by the natural logarithm of acceptor times donor concentrations divided by ni squared. Under reverse bias, the depletion region expands, modifying junction capacitance. For an asymmetrical p+-n junction with acceptor concentration Na equals 10 to the 18th power and donor Nd equals 10 to the 16th power per cubic centimeter, the built-in potential is approximately 0.81 volts. Applying a reverse bias voltage Vr of 5 volts across a relative permittivity of 11.8 for silicon yields a total depletion width W calculated as the square root of two times permittivity times the sum of potentials divided by elementary charge times the parallel combination of dopants, resulting in approximately 0.85 micrometers. Transitioning to the MOS capacitor, the threshold voltage Vt depends on the work function difference, oxide capacitance, surface potential, and body charge. In class exercise: Compute the maximum depletion width in a p-type silicon substrate with Na equal to 10 to the 17th power per cubic centimeter given that surface inversion occurs at twice the Fermi potential.

title: Lecture 3: Advanced Transistors and Short-Channel Physics
description: This lecture investigates MOSFET scaling limits, short-channel effects, and multi-gate architectures such as FinFETs and gate-all-around structures.
content: Learning objectives: Identify degradation mechanisms in scaled MOSFETs, quantify drain-induced barrier lowering, and compare FinFET performance metrics. As gate lengths shrink below 20 nanometers, classical drift-diffusion fails to capture ballistic transport and quantum confinement effects. Drain-induced barrier lowering occurs when the drain voltage modulates the source potential barrier, leading to subthreshold leakage current increases. For instance, a device experiencing a threshold voltage roll-off of 50 millivolts when scaling from 30 nanometers to 15 nanometers requires engineering solutions like high-k metal gates and ultra-thin body substrates. Gate-all-around nanowire transistors provide superior electrostatic control by surrounding the channel entirely, minimizing leakage paths. Consider a FinFET channel width defined by two times the fin height plus the fin thickness. If the fin height is 30 nanometers and the fin thickness is 8 nanometers, the effective drive width per fin equals 68 nanometers, directly influencing the on-state current capability. In class exercise: Estimate the subthreshold swing degradation factor for a device operating at 300 Kelvin with an oxide capacitance of 3.45 microfarads per square centimeter and a depletion capacitance of 1.15 microfarads per square centimeter.

title: Lecture 4: Compound Semiconductors, Power Devices, and Optoelectronics
description: This lecture covers wide bandgap materials, heterojunction devices, power switching components, and optoelectronic conversion efficiency.
content: Learning objectives: Analyze heterojunction bipolar transistors, evaluate silicon carbide power devices, and calculate solar cell output parameters. Compound semiconductors like Gallium Nitride and Gallium Arsenide offer high electron mobility and saturation velocity, making them ideal for high-frequency radio frequency power amplifiers. Heterojunctions create quantum wells that confine a two-dimensional electron gas in High Electron Mobility Transistors. In power electronics, Silicon Carbide devices leverage critical electric fields roughly ten times higher than silicon, permitting much thinner drift regions. For a SiC Schottky diode with a drift region doping of 10 to the 15th power per cubic centimeter and a breakdown electric field of 2.5 megavolts per centimeter, the theoretical breakdown voltage calculated by integrating the electric field triangle reaches approximately 1250 volts. In optoelectronics, a photodiode converts incident photon flux into photocurrent based on quantum efficiency. A solar cell illuminated with 100 milliwatts per square centimeter having a short-circuit current density of 35 milliamperes per square centimeter and an open-circuit voltage of 0.65 volts achieves a fill factor of 0.78, yielding an overall conversion efficiency of 17.7 percent. In class exercise: Calculate the maximum theoretical cut-off frequency for a HEMT given a gate length of 0.15 micrometers and an electron saturation velocity of 1.5 times 10 to the 7th centimeters per second.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Semiconductor Device Analysis
description: This assignment tests analytical and computational problem-solving skills across carrier transport, MOS electrostatics, scaling challenges, and power device limits.
content:
1. Calculate the intrinsic carrier concentration of silicon at 400 Kelvin given the effective density of states in the conduction band is 2.8 times 10 to the 19th power and in the valence band is 1.04 times 10 to the 19th power per cubic centimeter, with a bandgap energy of 1.12 electron-volts. (Marks: 4)

2. Determine the capacitance per unit area of an MOS capacitor with a silicon dioxide thickness of 3 nanometers, relative permittivity of 3.9, operating at flat-band conditions. (Marks: 3)

3. Analyze a short-channel MOSFET exhibiting drain-induced barrier lowering. If the threshold voltage shifts by 80 millivolts when drain bias changes from 0.1 volts to 1.2 volts, calculate the DIBL parameter in millivolts per volt. (Marks: 4)

4. Compute the on-resistance per unit area for a Silicon Carbide power MOSFET drift region designed for a 1200 volt rating, assuming a breakdown electric field of 2.0 megavolts per centimeter and electron mobility of 100 square centimeters per volt-second. (Marks: 5)

5. Derive and calculate the maximum open-circuit voltage for a gallium arsenide solar cell operating at 300 Kelvin with a reverse saturation current density of 10 to the minus 19th power amperes per square centimeter and a short-circuit current density of 30 milliamperes per square centimeter. (Marks: 4)

Submission instructions: Submit your complete derivations, step-by-step calculations, and final answers compiled into a single PDF document via the university portal.

title: Lecture 1: MOSFET Fundamentals and Current Mirrors
description: This lecture covers advanced MOSFET small-signal models, channel-length modulation, and the design of precision current mirrors for integrated circuits.
content:
Learning objectives: Understand channel-length modulation effects on output resistance, analyze cascode mirror topologies, and compute biasing errors.

In modern sub-micron CMOS processes, channel-length modulation significantly degrades the output resistance of a basic current mirror. The drain current of a saturated MOSFET is expressed as ID = 0.5 * mu * Cox * (W/L) * (VGS - Vth)^2 * (1 + lambda * VDS). The output resistance of a single transistor is approximately rO = 1 / (lambda * ID). To boost this resistance and achieve more stable biasing, we use cascode configurations. For example, consider a cascode current mirror where the reference branch supplies an ID of 100 microamperes, and the output transistor operates with an intrinsic rO of 50 kiloohms and an intrinsic gain (gm * rO) of 100. The effective output resistance of this cascode structure becomes roughly (gm * rO) * rO, which equals 100 * 50 kiloohms, yielding 5 megaohms. This drastically reduces current variation against changing drain-source voltages.

In class exercise: Calculate the output resistance of a cascade mirror if the transconductance is 2 millisiemens and the base output resistance is 25 kiloohms.

title: Lecture 2: Differential Amplifiers and Operational Amplifiers
description: This session explores differential pair operation, common-mode rejection, and the architecture of multi-stage operational amplifiers with frequency compensation.
content:
Learning objectives: Evaluate differential and common-mode gains, derive CMRR, and apply Miller compensation to prevent instability.

Differential amplifiers form the core of analog signal processing, rejecting common-mode noise while amplifying differential signals. The differential gain AD is given by gm * RD, and the common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR) depends heavily on tail current source impedance. When building multi-stage operational amplifiers, such as the classic two-stage CMOS op-amp, the second stage provides high voltage gain while the first stage establishes the differential input interface. However, multiple poles lead to severe phase shift at high frequencies. To ensure stability, we employ Miller compensation by placing a capacitor CC in feedback across the second stage. For instance, if the first stage output resistance is 1 megaohm, load capacitance is 5 picofarads, and we select a Miller capacitor CC of 2 picofarads, the dominant pole is pushed to a much lower frequency while the non-dominant pole is pushed out, guaranteeing a healthy phase margin above 60 degrees for unity feedback.

In class exercise: Determine the dominant pole frequency of an amplifier stage with an output resistance of 500 kiloohms and a total output capacitance of 4 picofarads.

title: Lecture 3: Frequency Response, Feedback, and Noise Analysis
description: Students will learn to analyze circuit frequency limitations, feedback stability criteria, and fundamental noise mechanisms in semiconductor devices.
content:
Learning objectives: Analyze closed-loop feedback stability, compute slew rate limits, and calculate thermal and flicker noise contributions.

Frequency response and feedback determine the speed and accuracy of analog blocks. Slew rate limits large-signal transient response, defined as SR = I_tail / CC. If a tail current of 20 microamperes charges a compensation capacitance of 2 picofarads, the resulting slew rate is 10 volts per microsecond. Beyond dynamics, intrinsic noise sets the lower limit of signal detection. Thermal noise from resistors and MOSFET channels is characterized by input-referred voltage noise spectra. The channel thermal noise spectral density of a MOSFET is given by v_n^2 = (8 * k * T * gamma) / (3 * gm), where k is Boltzmann constant, T is temperature in kelvin, and gamma is the excess noise factor, typically set to 2/3 for long-channel devices. Flicker noise, dominant at lower frequencies, adds an inversely proportional component 1/f to the total noise power spectral density.

In class exercise: Compute the thermal noise spectral density of a MOSFET with a transconductance of 4 millisiemens at room temperature assuming gamma equals 1.

title: Lecture 4: References, Switched-Capacitor Circuits, and Data Converters
description: This final lecture investigates voltage references, switched-capacitor techniques, and architectures of analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog converters.
content:
Learning objectives: Design bandgap voltage references, analyze switched-capacitor resistor equivalents, and compare ADC/DAC architectures.

Precision analog systems require temperature-independent references and sampled-data processing. Bandgap references achieve this by summing a proportional-to-absolute-temperature voltage with a complementary-to-absolute-temperature voltage, resulting in a stable output near 1.25 volts. In sampled systems, switched-capacitor circuits replace physical resistors with switched configurations, where equivalent resistance is Req = 1 / (f_s * C). For instance, if a clock frequency f_s is 1 megahertz and capacitance C is 5 picofarads, the equivalent resistance is 200 megaohms, enabling compact integrated implementations without large physical resistors. For data conversion, choices range from high-speed flash ADCs to high-resolution sigma-delta modulators. A successive approximation register (SAR) ADC uses binary search, taking N clock cycles for an N-bit conversion, balancing speed and power.

In class exercise: Calculate the equivalent switched-capacitor resistance for a clock rate of 500 kilohertz and a capacitor value of 2 picofarads.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Analog Integrated Circuit Design
description: This assignment tests students on current mirror design, differential pair analysis, op-amp compensation, and noise calculation through five structured computational problems.
content:
1. Design a simple cascode current mirror to deliver 50 microamperes. Calculate the required device widths if the process transconductance parameter is 200 microamperes per volt squared and overdrive voltage is 0.2 volts. (4 marks)
2. For a differential amplifier with a tail current of 100 microamperes and load resistors of 20 kiloohms, calculate the differential voltage gain assuming matching parameters. (4 marks)
3. A two-stage CMOS op-amp has an open-loop DC gain of 5000 and poles located at 10 kilohertz, 1 megahertz, and 10 megahertz. Determine the required Miller capacitance to place the dominant pole such that unity-gain bandwidth achieves safety margins. (4 marks)
4. Compute the output slew rate of an operational amplifier having a compensation capacitor of 3 picofarads and a maximum charging tail current of 60 microamperes. (4 marks)
5. Calculate the total input-referred thermal noise voltage in a 10 kilohertz bandwidth for a MOSFET having a transconductance of 2 millisiemens at 300 kelvin, assuming standard physical constants. (4 marks)

Submission instructions: Submit your complete derivation steps and numerical answers in a single PDF document through the university portal.

title: Lecture 1: CMOS Inverters and Static Behavior
description: This lecture covers the fundamental voltage transfer characteristics, noise margins, and sizing principles of the basic CMOS inverter.
content: Learning objectives: Understand how the NMOS and PMOS transistors operate in different regions to form an inverter, and calculate critical voltages like switching thresholds and noise margins. The CMOS inverter is the fundamental building block of modern digital systems, combining a pull-up network of PMOS transistors and a pull-down network of NMOS transistors. The voltage transfer characteristic maps input voltage to output voltage, displaying regions where both devices are off, linear, or saturated. The switching threshold occurs where input equals output voltage, heavily influenced by the ratio of electron to hole mobilities and transistor sizing. Noise margins quantify the circuit's immunity to spurious voltage fluctuations, defined by high and low noise margins derived from unity gain points on the transfer curve. Worked example: Consider an inverter with a switching threshold of 0.55 V operating at a supply voltage of 1.2 V. If the low noise margin is calculated as 0.35 V and the high noise margin as 0.40 V, any input noise below 0.35 V will be safely rejected, ensuring that a logical zero is not misinterpreted as a logical one by subsequent stages. In class exercise: Calculate the new switching threshold if the width of the PMOS transistor is doubled relative to the NMOS transistor, assuming mobility ratio is 2.5.

title: Lecture 2: Dynamic Power and Propagation Delay
description: This lecture analyzes the performance metrics of propagation delay and power dissipation in CMOS circuits.
content: Learning objectives: Derive the dynamic power equation, compute signal propagation delays using the RC delay model, and apply low-power optimization techniques. As transistors switch, energy is drawn from the power supply to charge and discharge load capacitances. Dynamic power is given by the product of switching activity factor, load capacitance, squared supply voltage, and clock frequency. Propagation delay is determined by the resistance of the conducting transistors and the capacitive load they must drive, often modeled using the Elmore delay approximation for multi-stage paths. Reducing supply voltage is a powerful method to cut power, but it comes at the penalty of increased transistor delay due to reduced overdrive voltage. Worked example: If a digital core operates at 1.2 V with a total switching capacitance of 2.0 nanofarads and a frequency of 500 megahertz, the dynamic power consumption is 1.44 watts. Reducing the supply voltage to 0.9 volts scales the power by the ratio of squared voltages, yielding 0.81 watts, which represents a power reduction of exactly 43.75 percent while sacrificing maximum operating frequency. In class exercise: Determine the dynamic power if the frequency is doubled and the capacitance is reduced by 30 percent at a constant 1.0 V supply.

title: Lecture 3: Combinational Logic and Sequential Circuits
description: This lecture explores the design of complex combinational networks using pull-up and pull-down structures alongside edge-triggered sequential elements.
content: Learning objectives: Design complex static CMOS gates using dual network topologies, evaluate logical effort, and prevent timing violations in sequential latches and flip-flops. Combinational gates implement Boolean functions where the pull-up network of PMOS transistors is the dual of the NMOS pull-down network. Logical effort normalizes the delay of a gate relative to a simple inverter, allowing designers to size logic paths for minimum delay. Sequential circuits store state and rely on clock signals to synchronize operations. Master-slave flip-flops and transparent latches require careful timing analysis to ensure data is stable before the clock edge arrives. Setup time is the duration data must be stable before the clock, while hold time is the duration data must remain stable after. Worked example: For a D flip-flop with a clock-to-Q delay of 150 picoseconds, a setup time of 50 picoseconds, and a clock period of 1000 picoseconds, the maximum combinational logic delay between registers running at this frequency with zero clock skew is 800 picoseconds. In class exercise: Design the transistor-level schematic for a complex static CMOS gate implementing the function Y equals not(A times B plus C) and identify the worst-case discharge path.

title: Lecture 4: Memories, VLSI Flow, and Testing
description: This lecture examines semiconductor memory architectures, the complete physical design flow, and design-for-testability methodologies.
content: Learning objectives: Differentiate between SRAM, DRAM, and non-volatile memories, trace the VLSI design flow from RTL to fabrication, and implement scan chains for testability. Semiconductor memories provide dense data storage, ranging from the six-transistor volatile static random-access memory cell to dynamic memory requiring periodic refreshing, and non-volatile flash storage. The VLSI design flow transforms architectural specifications into physical silicon through RTL coding, logic synthesis, floorplanning, placement, routing, and sign-off verification against manufacturing design rules. Physical layout translates schematics into geometric polygons adhering to strict spacing and width rules to ensure high fabrication yield. Because manufactured chips can contain defects, design-for-testability incorporates features like scan chains, which convert internal flip-flops into shift registers to apply test vectors and observe internal node responses. Worked example: A standard 6-transistor SRAM cell consists of two cross-coupled CMOS inverters forming a latch, connected to a pair of access NMOS transistors controlled by a word line to read and write differential voltages on the bit lines. In class exercise: Explain how a stuck-at-zero fault on a memory bit line can be detected using a simple write-and-read test pattern.

title: Assignment 1: CMOS Design, Power Analysis, and Timing Verification
description: A comprehensive practical assignment covering transistor-level logic design, dynamic power scaling computations, and sequential timing closure.
content:
1. Design the complete transistor-level schematic of a static CMOS complex gate that implements the Boolean function F equals not((A plus B) times C). Clearly label all PMOS and NMOS transistors. (4 marks)
2. Calculate the dynamic power consumption of a microprocessor block operating at 1.5 V with a switched capacitance of 800 picofarads and a clock frequency of 1.0 gigahertz. Then, calculate the new dynamic power if the voltage is scaled down to 1.0 V and frequency is reduced to 800 megahertz. (4 marks)
3. A critical path in a synchronous digital circuit has a register clock-to-Q delay of 120 picoseconds, a combinational logic delay of 650 picoseconds, and a register setup time of 80 picoseconds. What is the maximum allowable clock frequency for this path without causing a setup time violation? (4 marks)
4. Explain the physical mechanism of static leakage power in deep sub-micrometer CMOS technology and describe two circuit-level techniques used by designers to mitigate subthreshold leakage. (4 marks)
5. Draw the stick diagram for a two-input CMOS NAND gate, showing the proper placement of n-well, active areas, polysilicon gates, metal routing lines, and substrate contacts. (4 marks)

title: Lecture 1: Fundamental RF Concepts and Passive Networks
description: This lecture introduces scattering parameters, on-chip transmission lines, and classical impedance matching techniques using the Smith chart.
content: Learning objectives include mastering scattering parameters for two-port networks and applying L-networks for conjugate power transfer. When designing integrated circuits, distributed effects matter because dimensions are comparable to signal wavelengths. S-parameters characterize behavior under wave conditions rather than open or short circuits, mapping incident and reflected power waves. Impedance matching maximizes power delivery and minimizes reflections quantified by the reflection coefficient gamma. Consider matching a 50 ohm source impedance to a 10 ohm load resistance at two point four gigahertz using a discrete inductor and capacitor network. The quality factor equation Q equals the square root of the ratio of the source resistance to the load resistance minus one, yielding Q equal to the square root of five minus one, which calculates to roughly two point zero zero. The series reactance Xs equals Q multiplied by the load resistance, giving twenty ohms. The parallel susceptance Bp matches the source conductance, and the resulting component values are easily plotted on a Smith chart for verification. In class exercise: Determine the required series inductance to cancel out a capacitive load reactance of negative fifty ohms at five gigahertz.

title: Lecture 2: Receiver Noise and Nonlinearity Fundamentals
description: Students will explore noise figures, cascaded noise performance via Friis formula, and high-frequency distortion metrics like compression and intermodulation.
content: Learning objectives focus on evaluating system sensitivity through noise figure analysis and predicting distortion using third-order intercept points. Random thermal motion of electrons creates irreducible thermal noise, modeled as a voltage variance equal to four k T R B. When cascading stages, the total noise figure is heavily dominated by the input block because subsequent noise contributions are divided by the cumulative available power gain of all preceding stages. Nonlinearities produce harmonic distortion and intermodulation products that corrupt adjacent weak channels. For instance, consider an integrated receiver front-end with an LNA having a noise figure of two decibels, corresponding to a linear noise factor F1 of one point five eight, and a power gain of fifteen decibels, which is a linear gain G1 of thirty one point six two. Assume a second stage mixer with a noise figure of six decibels, giving an F2 of three point nine eight. Applying the Friis formula, the total system noise factor evaluates to F equals F1 plus the quantity F2 minus one divided by G1, resulting in one point five eight plus three point nine eight minus one divided by thirty one point six two, yielding a total noise factor of one point six seven, or two point two two decibels. In class exercise: Calculate the cascaded noise factor if the first stage gain drops to ten decibels.

title: Lecture 3: Active RF Blocks - Low-Noise Amplifiers and Mixers
description: This session covers active circuit topologies including inductive source degeneration for LNAs and the operation of active versus passive mixers.
content: Learning objectives involve designing narrowband low-noise amplifiers for optimal input matching and analyzing frequency translation in mixers. Low-noise amplifiers require simultaneous noise and input impedance matching, typically achieved via inductive source degeneration. The input impedance of a degenerated common-source FET features a real part proportional to the transconductance and the gate-source capacitance, allowing real impedance matching to fifty ohms without adding resistive thermal noise. Mixers perform frequency translation by multiplying the incoming radio frequency signal with a local oscillator waveform, generating sum and difference frequencies. Conversion gain measures the efficiency of this translation process. Suppose an inductive degeneration LNA operates at five gigahertz with a transconductance of twenty milliSiemens and a gate-source capacitance of zero point five picoFarads. With an on-chip gate inductor of ten nanoHenries, the series resonance sets the input matching frequency accurately. The real part of the input impedance equals g m times L s divided by C g s, which evaluates to twenty milliSiemens multiplied by ten nanoHenries divided by zero point five picoFarads, resulting in four hundred ohms before external tuning networks are applied. In class exercise: Estimate the gate-source voltage swing required to maintain linear operation in a passive switching mixer.

title: Lecture 4: Oscillators, Synthesizers, and Power Amplifiers
description: The final lecture examines LC oscillators, phase-noise mechanisms, phase-locked loops, and high-efficiency power amplifier classes.
content: Learning objectives encompass analyzing phase noise in LC oscillators and distinguishing power amplifier efficiency classes from A through E. Oscillators rely on positive feedback around an active amplifier combined with a frequency-selective LC tank to sustain continuous sinusoidal signals. Phase noise describes short-term frequency fluctuations, degrading spectral purity and increasing bit error rates in digital communications. Power amplifiers trade linearity for dc-to-rf conversion efficiency. Class A offers high linearity but low theoretical efficiency capped at fifty percent, whereas switch-mode topologies like Class E shape voltage and current waveforms to theoretically achieve one hundred percent efficiency by eliminating simultaneous high voltage and current states. Consider an LC tank operating at two gigahertz using a one nanoHenry inductor and a six point three three picoFarad capacitor. The oscillation frequency formula one divided by two pi times the square root of L C gives exactly two gigahertz. The Leeson phase noise model predicts that phase noise degrades quadratically with offset frequency and inversely with the carrier power and loaded quality factor squared. In class exercise: Calculate the theoretical maximum drain efficiency of a Class B power amplifier driven by an ideal sinusoidal input.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive RF Integrated Circuit Analysis and Design
description: This assignment evaluates student proficiency in impedance matching, noise calculations, linearity analysis, and amplifier topology selection.
content:
Task 1: Design an L-network to match a source impedance of twenty five ohms to a load resistance of one hundred ohms at a frequency of three gigahertz. Compute the exact component values for both series and parallel reactive elements. (4 marks)
Task 2: A three-stage receiver cascade consists of a filter with zero decibel insertion loss, an LNA with a three decibel noise factor and twelve decibel gain, and a mixer with an eight decibel noise factor and ten decibel conversion gain. Calculate the overall system noise figure in decibels using the Friis equation. (4 marks)
Task 3: An amplifier has a measured input-referred third-order intercept point of minus ten dBm and a small-signal gain of fifteen decibels. Determine the output-referred third-order intercept point in dBm and estimate the input power level where third-order intermodulation distortion equals the fundamental output power. (4 marks)
Task 4: Derive the real input impedance expression for a common-source amplifier with inductive source degeneration and explain why this topology avoids thermal noise degradation compared to a simple resistive termination. (4 marks)
Task 5: Compare and contrast Class A, Class B, and Class E power amplifiers in terms of conduction angle, theoretical maximum efficiency, and harmonic filtering requirements. Present your comparison in a structured format. (4 marks)
Total marks: 20.

title: Lecture 1: System-Level Architecture and Mixed-Signal Interfacing
description: This lecture covers top-level electronic system partitioning, power budgeting, and the conversion of physical phenomena into digital data streams.
content: Learning objectives: Understand how to construct a complete signal chain from a physical sensor to a digital processor, and calculate total system power consumption. Modern electronics require a holistic approach where system-level design dictates component selection. The signal chain typically starts at a transducer, passes through analog conditioning, gets sampled by an Analog-to-Digital Converter, and enters a processor. Consider a battery-powered temperature monitor utilizing a thermistor. If the sensor draws 100 microamps at 3.3 volts, the analog front-end consumes 1.5 milliamps, and the microcontroller operating in active mode uses 10 milliamps at 1.8 volts, we must evaluate the power budget carefully. For active mode duration of 10 milliseconds every second, the average current is calculated as (0.1 milliamperes plus 1.5 milliamperes plus (10 milliamperes multiplied by 0.01)) yielding 1.76 milliamperes of average current. Accounting for a sleep current of 5 microamps for the remaining 990 milliseconds, the total average current is approximately 1.765 milliamperes. In class exercise: Draw a complete block diagram for a digital weight scale, labeling the voltage rails, signal types, and expected data rates at each interface between the load cell and the microcontroller.

title: Lecture 2: Consumer Audio, Video, and Display Technologies
description: This lecture explores high-efficiency audio amplification, image capture mechanics, and modern flat-panel display driving techniques.
content: Learning objectives: Analyze the operational efficiency of switch-mode audio amplifiers and contrast the pixel-level driving mechanisms of LCD and OLED screens. Audio output stages in portable devices rely on Class D amplifiers, which modulate audio signals into high-frequency pulse width modulation square waves. Because the output transistors operate strictly as switches rather than in their linear region, power dissipation is drastically minimized. For instance, delivering 5 watts of audio power into an 8 ohm speaker using a Class D amplifier with 92 percent efficiency results in a total power consumption of 5 divided by 0.92, yielding 5.435 watts, meaning only 0.435 watts is lost as heat. In contrast, older linear Class A or B topologies would dissipate significantly more thermal energy under identical output conditions. For visual output, LCDs utilize a passive backlight with liquid crystal light valves, whereas OLEDs feature emissive organic compounds where each subpixel generates its own illumination, enabling infinite contrast ratios and faster response times. Image sensors complement this by using CMOS technology to convert photon counts into electrical charges via active pixel sensors. In class exercise: Calculate the thermal dissipation of a Class D amplifier delivering 10 watts to a 4 ohm load at an efficiency of 88 percent, and explain where the lost energy goes.

title: Lecture 3: Highly Integrated Consumer Devices and Power Management
description: This lecture examines system-on-chip architectures, power management integrated circuits, and advanced battery charging strategies.
content: Learning objectives: Evaluate the architectural benefits of System-on-Chip integration in smartphones and design basic power management strategies including energy harvesting. Modern consumer electronics demand extreme miniaturization and high computational density, achieved by combining central processing units, graphics processing units, digital signal processors, and multi-mode radio frequency transceivers onto a single silicon die. This integration reduces parasitic inductance on high-speed buses and shrinks board footprint. Power Management Integrated Circuits coordinate these complex subsystems by supplying multiple regulated voltage domains through low-dropout regulators and high-efficiency DC-DC step-down converters. Furthermore, battery management systems protect lithium-ion cells by enforcing strict constant-current and constant-voltage charging profiles. Suppose a single-cell lithium-ion battery with a capacity of 3000 milliamp-hours is charged at a 1C rate using a constant current phase up to 4.2 volts, followed by a constant voltage taper until the current drops to 0.05C. The initial constant current phase takes approximately 1 hour to reach 4.2 volts, while the saturation taper phase adds roughly 45 minutes, bringing the total rapid charge duration to 1.75 hours under ideal thermal constraints. In class exercise: Outline the power state transitions of a smartphone SoC when waking from deep sleep to handle a push notification.

title: Lecture 4: Embedded Processing, Reliability, and Emerging Trends
description: This lecture investigates programmable logic, system reliability standards, electromagnetic compatibility, and edge artificial intelligence accelerators.
content: Learning objectives: Compare microprocessor versus FPGA flexibility, identify common electromagnetic compatibility mitigation techniques, and understand edge AI processing paradigms. While microcontrollers execute sequential instructions, Field Programmable Gate Arrays implement hardware parallelism, making them ideal for deterministic real-time control and custom protocol handling. As electronic systems grow denser, electromagnetic compatibility becomes paramount; engineers employ ground planes, differential signaling, and ferrite beads to suppress conducted and radiated emissions. Reliability testing must account for thermal stress and signal integrity degradation over time. Looking toward current trends, edge AI accelerators are increasingly integrated into modern electronic systems to process neural network inference locally rather than relying on cloud servers. Consider an edge vision processor running a lightweight convolutional neural network that processes 30 frames per second. If each inference operation requires 15 million multiply-accumulate operations, the processor must sustain 450 million operations per second. Operating at a power efficiency of 10 tera-operations per watt, the inference engine consumes a mere 0.045 watts, illustrating why localized hardware acceleration is essential for battery-operated smart devices. In class exercise: Propose two specific hardware mitigation techniques to reduce electromagnetic interference radiated from a high-speed clock trace on a four-layer printed circuit board.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Electronic System Design and Analysis
description: Students will complete practical design calculations, signal chain mapping, power budgeting, and EMC mitigation analysis for a modern portable IoT device.
content:
1. Signal Chain Architecture: Draw and describe the complete signal chain for a wearable heart-rate monitor, detailing the transducer, analog front-end filtering, Analog-to-Digital Converter resolution requirements, and communication bus. [4 marks] 
2. Power Budget Calculation: A portable sensor node operates on a 3.7 volt lithium battery. The microcontroller draws 5 milliamps active for 50 milliseconds out of every second, and 2 microamps in sleep mode for the remaining 950 milliseconds. The sensor subsystem draws 1.2 milliamps continuously. Calculate the average current consumption and estimate the battery life in days for a 2000 milliamp-hour capacity cell. [4 marks] 
3. Audio Efficiency Analysis: Determine the total power drawn from the supply and the thermal dissipation in watts for a Class D audio amplifier delivering 2.5 watts into an 8 ohm speaker with an operating efficiency of 89 percent. Show all intermediate formulas and steps. [4 marks] 
4. SoC and Memory Interconnects: Explain why modern smartphones utilize System-on-Chip architectures instead of discrete processor, memory, and logic chips, specifically addressing board space, power consumption, and high-speed signal integrity. [4 marks] 
5. Electromagnetic Compatibility Mitigation: A prototype multi-layer printed circuit board fails radiated emissions testing due to high-frequency harmonic noise generated by a 100 megahertz clock line. Propose four distinct layout or component-level engineering modifications to resolve this compliance issue. [4 marks]

title: Lecture 1: Foundations of Signals, Systems, and LTI Analysis
courses: Analysis of Continuous and Discrete-Time Signals
description: This lecture introduces the core taxonomy of signals and tests fundamental system properties before developing the convolution sum.
content:
Learning objectives: Distinguish continuous from discrete signals, verify system linearity, and compute discrete convolution.

Signals are categorized as continuous-time or discrete-time, periodic or aperiodic, and classified by energy or power. Systems process these signals. We test properties like linearity and time-invariance to determine if standard mathematical tools apply. A linear and time-invariant (LTI) system is fully characterized by its impulse response, denoted as h(t) or h[n]. When an arbitrary input x[n] excites an LTI system, the output y[n] is computed via the discrete convolution sum y[n] = sum over k of x[k]h[n-k]. 

Worked Example: Let the input be x[n] = {1, 2} starting at n = 0, and the impulse response be h[n] = {1, 1, 1} starting at n = 0. We compute y[n] = x[n] * h[n]. By flipping and shifting h[n], we find y[0] = 1*1 = 1. For n = 1, y[1] = 1*1 + 2*1 = 3. For n = 2, y[2] = 0*1 + 2*1 = 2. For n = 3, y[3] = 0. Thus, the resulting output sequence is y[n] = {1, 3, 2, 0}.

In class exercise: Determine if the system described by y(t) = t times x(t) is time-invariant. Test it by applying a time shift to the input and comparing it to a shifted output.

title: Lecture 2: Frequency Domain Representations with Fourier and Laplace
courses: Analysis of Continuous and Discrete-Time Signals
description: This lecture expands signal analysis into the frequency domain using Fourier series, Fourier transforms, and Laplace transforms.
content:
Learning objectives: Calculate frequency spectra, apply transform properties, and analyze poles and zeros for stability.

While time-domain differential or difference equations describe systems, frequency domains offer deeper insight. Periodic signals are decomposed into harmonic components via Fourier series. Aperiodic signals use the continuous Fourier transform to reveal continuous frequency spectra. To handle a broader class of signals that lack pure Fourier transforms, we use the bilateral or unilateral Laplace transform. The resulting transfer function H(s) provides poles and zeros in the complex plane. For a causal system to be stable in the bounded-input bounded-output sense, all poles of H(s) must lie strictly in the left half of the complex plane, meaning they have negative real parts.

Worked Example: Consider the frequency response of an RC low-pass filter given by H(j omega) = 1 / (1 + j omega RC). Suppose R = 1 kiloohm and C = 1 microfarad, yielding an RC product of 0.001 seconds. At a frequency where omega = 1000 radians per second, the denominator becomes 1 + j(1000)(0.001) = 1 + j1. The magnitude response is 1 divided by the square root of (1 squared plus 1 squared), which equals 1 over the square root of 2, or approximately 0.707, representing the cutoff frequency.

In class exercise: Find the poles of the transfer function H(s) = 5 / (s squared + 3s + 2) and determine if the system is stable.

title: Lecture 3: Discrete-Time Systems and the Z-Transform
courses: Analysis of Continuous and Discrete-Time Signals
description: This lecture covers discrete-time system analysis through linear constant-coefficient difference equations and the Z-transform.
content:
Learning objectives: Solve difference equations, compute Z-transforms, and map regions of convergence.

Computers and digital signal processors process information in discrete steps. Discrete-time linear time-invariant systems are mathematically modeled by linear constant-coefficient difference equations. To solve these equations efficiently without recursive time-domain iteration, we apply the Z-transform. The Z-transform converts difference equations into algebraic polynomials in terms of the complex variable z. The region of convergence is critical because it dictates whether the inverse Z-transform exists and whether the discrete system is causal and stable. Poles inside the unit circle of the z-plane guarantee discrete BIBO stability.

Worked Example: Consider the simple difference equation y[n] = 0.5 y[n-1] + x[n] with zero initial conditions. Taking the Z-transform of both sides gives Y(z) = 0.5 z to the power of negative 1 times Y(z) + X(z). Rearranging terms yields the transfer function H(z) = Y(z) over X(z) = 1 / (1 - 0.5 z to the power of negative 1). This has a single pole at z = 0.5. Since the pole has a magnitude less than 1 and lies inside the unit circle, the system is stable.

In class exercise: Compute the Z-transform of the finite signal x[n] = {2, 4, 6} starting at n = 0.

title: Lecture 4: Sampling Theory and State-Space Representations
courses: Analysis of Continuous and Discrete-Time Signals
description: This lecture bridges continuous and discrete worlds via the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem and introduces state-space modeling.
content:
Learning objectives: Apply the sampling theorem, prevent aliasing, and formulate state-space matrices for linear systems.

Converting continuous-time physical signals into digital data requires proper sampling. The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem states that to avoid information loss and aliasing, a bandlimited signal with maximum frequency component f max must be sampled at a rate strictly greater than twice that maximum frequency, meaning f s must be greater than 2 times f max. If this condition is violated, high-frequency components fold over into lower frequencies. Additionally, complex multi-input multi-output systems are compactly modeled using state-space representations, which track internal state variables using matrix differential equations.

Worked Example: Suppose an analog audio signal contains frequency components up to 4 kilohertz. According to the sampling theorem, the minimum sampling frequency required for perfect reconstruction is 2 times 4 kilohertz, which equals 8 kilohertz. Therefore, the sampling period T s must be less than or equal to 1 over 8000 seconds, which is 0.125 milliseconds.

In class exercise: Calculate the minimum sampling rate for a sensor signal containing frequency components up to 4 kilohertz.

content:
Task 1: Compute the discrete convolution of the signal x[n] = {1, 0, 2} and the impulse response h[n] = {3, 1} assuming both start at index n = 0. Show all intermediate steps. (4 marks)

Task 2: Test the system defined by the input-output relationship y(t) = cos(x(t)) for both linearity and time-invariance. Provide mathematical proofs for your conclusions. (4 marks)

Task 3: For an RC low-pass filter with a time constant RC = 0.002 seconds, calculate the exact magnitude of the frequency response H(j omega) at an angular frequency of omega = 500 radians per second. (4 marks)

Task 4: Given the causal discrete-time system described by the difference equation y[n] - 0.4 y[n-1] = x[n], find its transfer function H(z) and determine if the system is stable by checking its pole location. (4 marks)

Task 5: An analog signal is given by x(t) = cos(2 times pi times 300 times t) + sin(2 times pi times 900 times t). State the maximum frequency present in the signal and compute the minimum required sampling rate to prevent aliasing. (4 marks)

title: Lecture 1: Discrete-Time Signals, Sampling, and Z-Transforms
courses: Introduction to Digital Signal Processing Applications
description: This lecture introduces the fundamentals of discrete-time representation, the transition from continuous signals via sampling, and analysis using the Z-transform.
content:
Learning objectives: Master the sampling process and Nyquist criterion, compute Z-transforms, and evaluate system stability using pole locations.

To bridge the analog world into digital computation, continuous signals are sampled at a rate exceeding twice the highest frequency component, known as the Nyquist rate. Once in the discrete domain, we analyze sequences using the Z-transform. For example, consider the causal step sequence x[n] = u[n]. Its Z-transform is defined as X(z) = sum from n equals zero to infinity of x[n] z to the power of negative n. Substituting the step sequence, this evaluates to X(z) = 1 + z to the negative 1 + z to the negative 2 plus infinity, which sums to the closed form 1 divided by (1 - z to the negative 1) for the region of convergence magnitude of z greater than 1. System stability is strictly determined by the location of the system function poles. If all poles lie strictly inside the unit circle in the complex z-plane, the system is bounded-input bounded-output stable. Conversely, a pole on or outside the unit circle indicates instability or marginal stability.

In class exercise: Determine the Z-transform and the region of convergence for the finite sequence x[n] = {2, 3, 1} starting at n equals zero.

title: Lecture 2: Fourier Analysis and the Fast Fourier Transform
courses: Introduction to Digital Signal Processing Applications
description: This lecture explores frequency-domain analysis through the DTFT, DFT, and the computational efficiency of the Fast Fourier Transform alongside windowing techniques.
content:
Learning objectives: Calculate discrete Fourier transforms, understand spectral leakage and windowing, and apply the Fast Fourier Transform algorithm.

While the Z-transform handles general analysis, frequency-domain characteristics are evaluated using the Discrete-Time Fourier Transform and the Discrete Fourier Transform. Direct computation of an N-point DFT requires order N squared operations, which becomes computationally prohibitive for large datasets. The Fast Fourier Transform exploits symmetry and periodicity to reduce this complexity to order N log N. When analyzing finite segments of continuous signals, truncating the data introduces spectral leakage due to abrupt boundary discontinuities. Applying smooth tapering windows, such as the Hamming or Hann windows, mitigates this leakage by smoothing the edges of the time-domain frame before transformation. For instance, computing the 4-point DFT of the impulse sequence x[n] = {1, 0, 0, 0} using the analysis equation yields X[k] = sum from n equals 0 to 3 of x[n] e to the power of negative j 2 pi k n divided by 4. Evaluating this for k equals 0, 1, 2, and 3 results in the constant frequency spectrum {1, 1, 1, 1}.

In class exercise: Compute the 4-point DFT of the shifted impulse sequence x[n] = {0, 1, 0, 0} and interpret the resulting phase.

title: Lecture 3: Digital Filter Design: FIR and IIR Architectures
courses: Introduction to Digital Signal Processing Applications
description: This lecture covers the design methodologies for both Finite Impulse Response and Infinite Impulse Response digital filters.
content:
Learning objectives: Design linear-phase FIR filters using windows, and transform analog prototype filters into digital IIR filters using the bilinear transform.

Digital filters shape frequency spectra by modifying signal components. FIR filters possess strictly finite impulse responses, are inherently stable, and can easily be designed to exhibit exact linear phase, preventing phase distortion. The window method achieves this by truncating an ideal impulse response with a window function. IIR filters, conversely, provide sharper magnitude responses with fewer coefficients by utilizing feedback loops, though they lack inherent linear phase. Standard IIR design maps classical analog prototypes, such as Butterworth or Chebyshev filters, into the digital domain via the bilinear transform, which substitutes s with 2 times (1 - z to the negative 1) divided by (T times (1 + z to the negative 1)) to prevent aliasing of the frequency axis. For example, a simple 3-point moving average filter defined by y[n] = (x[n] + x[n-1] + x[n-2]) divided by 3 has filter coefficients h[n] = {1/3, 1/3, 1/3}, realizing a low-pass frequency response.

In class exercise: Find the difference equation and transfer function H(z) for a 2-point moving average filter.

title: Lecture 4: Multirate Signal Processing and Practical Applications
courses: Introduction to Digital Signal Processing Applications
description: This lecture investigates multirate systems involving decimation and interpolation, and surveys real-world applications in audio, biomedical, and communications engineering.
content:
Learning objectives: Implement decimation and interpolation operations, avoid aliasing during sampling rate conversion, and identify real-world DSP system requirements.

Multirate digital signal processing alters sampling rates dynamically within a system using decimation to decrease the rate and interpolation to increase it. Decimation by a factor M involves low-pass filtering the input signal to remove high-frequency components that would otherwise alias, followed by retaining every M-th sample. Interpolation by a factor L inserts L minus 1 zero-valued samples between each original sample and applies an anti-imaging low-pass filter to smooth the waveform. These operations underpin complex applications such as audio effects, noise cancellation, electrocardiogram filtering, and modern software-defined radios. Implementing these algorithms efficiently requires specialized hardware platforms like Digital Signal Processors, or rapid prototyping environments using Python and MATLAB. For instance, decimating a 48 kilohertz audio stream by a factor of 2 requires an anti-aliasing filter with a cutoff frequency below 12 kilohertz to protect the new 24 kilohertz Nyquist limit.

In class exercise: Outline the processing steps required to convert a signal sampled at 8 kilohertz up to 12 kilohertz using rational resampling.

title: Lecture 1: Communication Models and Spectral Analysis
description: This lecture introduces the foundational components of communication systems and applies Fourier analysis to determine signal bandwidth.
content:
Learning objectives: Understand the roles of transmitters, channels, and receivers, and apply Fourier transforms to compute signal spectra and bandwidth.

At the core of any communication system, an information source generates a message that a transmitter converts into a transmittable waveform. The physical medium, or channel, introduces impairments such as additive white noise and linear distortion before the signal reaches the receiver. To analyze these waveforms, we rely on spectral analysis. The Fourier transform maps time-domain signals into the frequency domain, revealing the range of frequencies occupied by the signal, which defines its bandwidth. For instance, consider a baseband rectangular pulse signal with a duration of two milliseconds. The first null in its sinc frequency spectrum occurs at the inverse of the pulse duration, which is 500 hertz. Consequently, the essential transmission bandwidth required to pass this signal without severe degradation is 500 hertz.

In class exercise: Calculate the first null bandwidth of a rectangular pulse with a duration of 0.5 milliseconds, and explain how channel noise degrades the received spectrum.

title: Lecture 2: Analog Modulation Techniques
description: This lecture covers amplitude and angle modulation schemes, detailing mathematical representations, detection methods, and bandwidth requirements.
content:
Learning objectives: Distinguish between various amplitude modulation variants and apply Carson's rule to compute angle modulation bandwidth.

Analog modulation shifts baseband information to higher frequencies for efficient propagation. Amplitude modulation includes double sideband with large carrier, double sideband suppressed carrier, and single sideband, which reduces bandwidth by half. Envelope detectors provide low-cost demodulation for amplitude modulation containing a carrier. Conversely, angle modulation varies the carrier phase or frequency, encompassing phase modulation and frequency modulation. Bandwidth calculation for frequency modulation is governed by Carson's rule, which states that the transmission bandwidth is approximately equal to two times the sum of the peak frequency deviation and the maximum modulating frequency. For example, in commercial broadcast frequency modulation, if the peak frequency deviation is 75 kilohertz and the maximum audio frequency is 15 kilohertz, the required bandwidth is computed as two times the sum of 75 and 15, yielding 180 kilohertz.

In class exercise: Using Carson's rule, calculate the transmission bandwidth for a frequency modulation signal with a peak frequency deviation of 50 kilohertz and a modulating frequency of 10 kilohertz.

title: Lecture 3: Receivers, Sampling, and Pulse Code Modulation
description: This lecture examines superheterodyne receiver architecture, the sampling theorem, and quantization noise in pulse code modulation systems.
content:
Learning objectives: Explain superheterodyne frequency conversion and calculate the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio for pulse code modulation.

Practical receivers utilize the superheterodyne architecture to translate incoming radio frequencies to a fixed intermediate frequency using a local oscillator and a mixer, simplifying filtering and amplification. Moving to digital conversion, the sampling theorem dictates that a continuous-time bandlimited signal must be sampled at a rate strictly greater than twice its highest frequency component to prevent aliasing. Once sampled, pulse code modulation converts these samples into binary digits through quantization. Each additional bit in the quantization process substantially improves signal fidelity. Specifically, the theoretical signal-to-quantization-noise ratio in decibels is approximated by multiplying the number of bits per sample by 6.02 and adding 1.76. For an 8-bit pulse code modulation system, multiplying 8 by 6.02 yields 50.16, and adding 1.76 gives a total signal-to-quantization-noise ratio of approximately 51.92 decibels.

In class exercise: Calculate the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio for a 12-bit pulse code modulation system and state the minimum sampling rate for a signal bandlimited to 4 kilohertz.

title: Lecture 4: Digital Modulation and System Performance
description: This lecture explores basic digital modulation schemes, thermal noise limits, and channel multiplexing strategies.
content:
Learning objectives: Compare digital modulation formats and compute thermal noise power alongside multiplexing capacities.

Digital modulation conveys binary data by altering the amplitude, frequency, or phase of a carrier, leading to amplitude shift keying, frequency shift keying, and phase shift keying. Performance in these systems is ultimately bounded by noise. Thermal noise power is modeled as the product of Boltzmann's constant, absolute temperature, and system bandwidth, expressed as kTB. To accommodate multiple users over a single shared physical medium, multiplexing is deployed. Frequency division multiplexing separates users by assigning non-overlapping frequency bands, whereas time division multiplexing allocates distinct time slots to each user within a shared frame. For instance, if a channel with a total bandwidth of 100 kilohertz hosts individual sub-channels each requiring 10 kilohertz with a 2 kilohertz guard band, system design must carefully balance capacity and interference.

In class exercise: Compute the thermal noise power in a 1 megahertz bandwidth system operating at standard room temperature where the product of Boltzmann's constant and temperature is approximately 4 times 10 to the negative 21 joules.
