title: Lecture 1: Foundations of Entropy and Mutual Information
description: This lecture introduces the core measures of uncertainty and dependency, including entropy, joint entropy, and mutual information.
content:
Learning objectives: Define entropy and conditional entropy for discrete random variables, and compute mutual information to measure shared randomness between two variables. 

Entropy measures the average uncertainty of a random variable. Given a discrete random variable X with probability mass function p(x), the entropy is defined as H(X) = minus sum over x of p(x) log2 p(x) bits. When we extend this to two variables, we define joint entropy H(X,Y) and conditional entropy H(X given Y), leading to the chain rule H(X,Y) = H(X) plus H(Y given X). Mutual information I(X;Y) quantifies the reduction in uncertainty of X due to knowing Y, expressed as I(X;Y) = H(X) minus H(X given Y), which is always greater than or equal to zero.

Consider a concrete example where X and Y are binary random variables representing a noisy transmission. Let X be uniformly distributed with p(X=0) = 0.5 and p(X=1) = 0.5, so H(X) = 1 bit. Suppose Y is equal to X with probability 0.8 and flipped with probability 0.2. The conditional entropy H(X given Y) is calculated using the binary entropy function h(p) = minus p log2 p minus (1 minus p) log2 (1 minus p). Here, h(0.2) is approximately 0.722 bits. Thus, the mutual information is I(X;Y) = 1 minus 0.722 = 0.278 bits.

In class exercise: Calculate the mutual information I(X;Y) when X is a fair coin flip and Y is an independent coin flip, explaining why the resulting value matches intuition.

title: Lecture 2: Source Coding Theorems and Practical Compression
description: This lecture explores lossless data compression limits and practical algorithms like Huffman and arithmetic coding.
content:
Learning objectives: Apply Shannon's source coding theorem to optimal codeword lengths and construct efficient prefix codes using Huffman coding. 

Source coding addresses how to represent data compactly without losing information. Shannon's source coding theorem states that the expected codeword length L for a source with entropy H(X) can be made arbitrarily close to H(X), satisfying H(X) less than or equal to L less than H(X) plus 1. The Kraft inequality establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of prefix-free codes given a set of codeword lengths. Huffman coding achieves optimal prefix-free source coding by bottom-up merging of the two lowest probability nodes until a single tree is formed.

Let us work through a numerical example. Consider a discrete source emitting symbols A, B, C, and D with probabilities 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, and 0.1 respectively. The entropy is H(X) = -(0.4 log2 0.4 + 0.3 log2 0.3 + 0.2 log2 0.2 + 0.1 log2 0.1) = 1.846 bits. To build a Huffman code, we combine C (0.2) and D (0.1) into a node with probability 0.3. Next, we combine B (0.3) and this new node (0.3) to get 0.6. Finally, we combine A (0.4) and 0.6 to form the root. Assigning bits 0 and 1 down the branches gives codewords: A=0, B=10, C=110, D=111. The expected length is L = 0.4(1) + 0.3(2) + 0.2(3) + 0.1(3) = 1.9 bits, which is very close to the entropy.

In class exercise: Construct a Huffman code for probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125 and compute its average length.

title: Lecture 3: Channel Capacity and Discrete Memoryless Channels
description: This lecture investigates reliable communication over noisy channels, defining channel capacity and analyzing the binary symmetric channel.
content:
Learning objectives: Formulate the capacity of discrete memoryless channels and calculate capacities for standard models like the binary symmetric channel. 

A communication channel is characterized by input alphabet X, output alphabet Y, and conditional transition probabilities p(y given x). The channel capacity C is defined as the maximum mutual information between the input and output over all possible input probability distributions, maximizing over p(x) of I(X;Y). For a binary symmetric channel (BSC), the input is flipped with crossover probability p. The capacity of a BSC is given by C = 1 minus h(p), where h(p) is the binary entropy function.

Let us calculate the capacity for a BSC with crossover probability p = 0.11. First, compute the binary entropy function for p = 0.11: h(0.11) = minus 0.11 log2 0.11 minus 0.89 log2 0.89. Calculating the terms, 0.11 multiplied by log2(0.11) is approximately minus 0.354, and 0.89 multiplied by log2(0.89) is approximately minus 0.158, yielding h(0.11) equal to approximately 0.512 bits. Therefore, the channel capacity is C = 1 minus 0.512 = 0.488 bits per transmission. This means no matter how clever our encoding scheme is, we cannot reliably transmit more than 0.488 bits per channel use over this noisy medium.

In class exercise: Determine the capacity of a BSC where the crossover probability is 0.5, and interpret the physical meaning of the result.

title: Lecture 4: Continuous Channels and Advanced Topics
description: This lecture extends information theory to continuous alphabets, examining the AWGN channel capacity and rate-distortion theory basics.
content:
Learning objectives: Compute differential entropy for continuous variables, derive the AWGN channel capacity formula, and introduce rate-distortion tradeoffs for lossy compression. 

Extending to continuous variables requires differential entropy, defined with an integral rather than a sum. The additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel models physical communication links where signal is corrupted by Gaussian noise of variance N and constrained by average power P. Shannon's famous formula states that the capacity of an AWGN channel with bandwidth B is C = B log2(1 plus P divided by N), where P divided by N represents the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Rate-distortion theory addresses lossy compression by finding the minimum rate required to represent a source within a specified distortion bound.

Consider an AWGN channel with a bandwidth of 4 kilohertz and a signal-to-noise ratio of 7. The capacity is calculated as C = 4000 multiplied by log2(1 plus 7). Since log2(8) equals 3, the capacity evaluates to 4000 multiplied by 3 = 12000 bits per second. If we increase the bandwidth or power, the capacity scales accordingly, highlighting the logarithmic trade-off between power and bandwidth in power-limited regimes.

In class exercise: Calculate the capacity of an AWGN channel with a bandwidth of 1 megahertz and an SNR of 15.

title: Lecture 1: Evolution of Public Switched Telephone Networks and Switching Fundamentals
description: This lecture explores the traditional PSTN architecture, local loops, switching techniques, and the transition from analog hierarchies to digital exchanges.
content:
Learning objectives: Understand the hierarchy of central offices and trunks, and differentiate between circuit switching and digital time-division switching mechanisms.

The Public Switched Telephone Network relies on a hierarchical structure connecting subscriber local loops to local central offices, which then route calls through tandem offices and high-capacity trunks. Historically, switching was mechanical, but modern systems utilize digital exchanges capable of handling multiple simultaneous channels. Circuit switching establishes a dedicated, guaranteed physical or logical path for the duration of the connection, ensuring constant bandwidth. Consider a scenario where a central office manages 30 concurrent digital channels on a multiplexed link, requiring space-division matrices to route physical paths and time-division switches to reorder time slots between incoming and outgoing streams. To compute traffic volume, if a local exchange observes 150 calls per hour with an average holding time of 2 minutes, the offered traffic intensity is calculated as 150 multiplied by (2 divided by 60), yielding 5 Erlang of traffic.

In class exercise: Calculate the traffic intensity in Erlangs for a business trunk group that processes 300 calls per hour, where each call lasts an average of 4 minutes.

title: Lecture 2: Signaling, Traffic Engineering, and Digital Telephony Standards
description: This lecture covers subscriber and network signaling, Erlang traffic engineering formulas, and the principles of pulse code modulation and digital transmission frames.
content:
Learning objectives: Master the application of Erlang B for grade of service estimations and analyze the framing structure of E1 digital transmission links.

Signaling ensures control information flows accurately through the network. Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency handles analog subscriber dialing, while Signalling System 7 manages out-of-band network messaging for call setup and teardown. In digital telephony, analog voice is sampled at 8 kHz and quantized to 8 bits per sample, resulting in the standard Pulse Code Modulation rate of 64 kbps. Multiplexing multiple channels creates transmission hierarchies such as the European E1 standard. An E1 frame operates at 2.048 Mbps and is divided into 32 distinct time slots of 64 kbps each. Specifically, slot 0 is dedicated to frame synchronization and alarms, slot 16 carries common-channel signaling, and the remaining 30 time slots are allocated for user voice or data channels. Traffic engineering utilizes the Erlang B formula to determine the probability of call blocking given a specific number of trunk circuits and offered traffic load.

In class exercise: Verify the total bit rate of an E1 system by multiplying the number of channels by the bit rate per channel, and explain the specific utility of time slot 16.

title: Lecture 3: Voice over IP Architectures, Protocols, and Quality of Service
description: This lecture investigates modern packet-switched voice communication, focusing on SIP signaling, RTP media transport, audio codecs, and QoS mechanisms.
content:
Learning objectives: Contrast circuit-switched paradigms with packet-switched VoIP, and analyze the roles of Session Initiation Protocol and Real-time Transport Protocol.

Voice over IP converts analog audio into digital packets transmitted over IP networks, fundamentally departing from dedicated circuit paths. Session Initiation Protocol manages endpoint registration, invitation, and session teardown using text-based messages like INVITE and ACK. Once a session is established, Real-time Transport Protocol encapsulates the audio stream, utilizing codecs such as G.711 which samples at 64 kbps or compressed variants like G.729 operating at 8 kbps. Because IP networks do not guarantee bandwidth, packets encounter jitter, delay, and loss. Quality of Service configurations, including differentiated services code point marking and queue management, are essential to prioritize real-time voice packets over standard data traffic. For example, a G.711 codec generating a 20-millisecond packet payload produces a 160-byte payload, which grows to 200 bytes when adding IP, UDP, and RTP headers.

In class exercise: Compare the packet overhead percentage for a VoIP stream using G.711 versus a compressed codec over an Ethernet network.

title: Lecture 4: Telecommunications Standards, Regulation, and Spectrum Management
description: This lecture examines global telecommunications standardization bodies, national regulatory frameworks, spectrum licensing, and consumer protection policies.
content:
Learning objectives: Identify the jurisdictions of major international standards organizations and understand the regulatory responsibilities of national telecommunications authorities.

Global telecommunications operate under strict regulatory and standards frameworks defined by international bodies. The International Telecommunication Union standardizes telecommunications infrastructure globally, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers develops local and metropolitan area network protocols, the 3rd Generation Partnership Project specifies mobile communication standards, the European Telecommunications Standards Institute drives European norms, and the Internet Engineering Task Force oversees internet protocols. At the national level, regulators such as the National Telecommunication Regulatory Authority in Egypt manage domestic spectrum licensing, numbering plans, interconnection agreements, and type approval processes for telecommunications equipment. Spectrum management ensures that wireless frequencies are allocated efficiently without interference, while numbering plans guarantee unique global identification for subscribers. Type approval mandates that all hardware connected to the public network meets safety, electromagnetic compatibility, and interoperability standards before commercial deployment.

In class exercise: Outline the distinct responsibilities of the ITU and the IETF in shaping modern converged communication networks.

title: Lecture 1: IoT Architecture and Embedded Platforms
description: This lecture introduces the foundational layers of IoT systems and examines the hardware constraints of microcontrollers.
content: Learning objectives: Understand the end-to-end data pipeline from physical sensors to the cloud, and evaluate microcontroller power consumption profiles. The architecture of the Internet of Things spans five distinct layers: physical perception devices, edge gateways, transmission networks, cloud storage and analytics platforms, and end-user applications. Sensors capture physical phenomena, actuators execute physical changes, and microcontrollers orchestrate localized operations. When building battery-powered sensor nodes, hardware selection dictates longevity. Consider an ESP32 microcontroller powered by a 2000 milliamp-hour lithium-ion battery. In active transmission mode, the module draws 160 milliamperes at 3.3 volts. If the device wakes up every 60 seconds for 100 milliseconds to read a temperature sensor and transmit the value via Wi-Fi, the average current draw calculates to approximately 0.37 milliamperes. Assuming a realistic battery capacity depletion limit of 80 percent, the estimated operating lifespan reaches roughly 4300 hours or approximately 179 days before battery exhaustion. Optimizing this lifespan requires shifting from active Wi-Fi states to ultra-low-power deep sleep modes, where current draw drops to 15 microamperes. In class exercise: Calculate the theoretical battery lifetime in days for a sensor node that consumes 50 milliamperes for 2 seconds every 15 minutes, powered by a 1000 milliamp-hour battery.

title: Lecture 2: Wireless Connectivity and Trade-offs
description: This lecture explores the fundamental trade-offs between communication range, power consumption, and data rate across various wireless protocols.
content: Learning objectives: Compare short-range and long-range IoT radio technologies, and match application requirements to appropriate network topologies. Selecting a wireless protocol involves balancing three competing engineering constraints: communication range, energy consumption, and payload throughput. Short-range protocols like Bluetooth Low Energy and Zigbee operate in the 2.4 gigahertz ISM band, offering data rates up to 1 megabit per second with minimal power consumption, making them ideal for personal area networks and mesh smart homes. Conversely, cellular IoT technologies like Narrowband IoT and long-range wide area networks operate over sub-gigahertz frequencies to achieve transmission distances exceeding 10 kilometers at the expense of constrained data rates ranging from 300 bits to 50 kilobits per second. For example, deploying a remote agricultural monitoring network across a 15 square kilometer farm requires long-range wide area network technology using a frequency of 868 megahertz. With a transmission power of 14 dBm and a spreading factor of 12, the link budget allows a path loss of up to 140 decibels. This configuration yields a data rate of 292 bits per second, which easily accommodates a 20-byte sensor payload transmitted once every hour while ensuring a multi-year battery operational window. In class exercise: List the primary wireless protocol choice for a smart water meter located inside a basement, and justify your selection based on signal penetration and power availability.

title: Lecture 3: Lightweight Messaging Protocols and Edge Data Handling
description: This lecture covers application layer communication protocols optimized for constrained devices and the role of edge computing.
content: Learning objectives: Implement publish-subscribe messaging patterns using MQTT, and explain how edge processing reduces cloud bandwidth overhead. Efficient machine-to-machine communication relies on lightweight protocols designed to operate over unstable, high-latency networks. Message Queuing Telemetry Transport uses a publish-subscribe architecture centered on a broker, decoupling publishers from subscribers through hierarchical topics. To guarantee message delivery across unreliable links, Message Queuing Telemetry Transport provides three Quality of Service levels. Quality of Service 0 represents at most once delivery with no confirmation. Quality of Service 1 ensures at least once delivery using a acknowledgement handshake. Quality of Service 2 guarantees exactly once delivery through a four-step handshake mechanism. For instance, an industrial vibration sensor monitoring a pump motor samples data at 1000 hertz. Transmitting raw time-series data directly to the cloud saturates available bandwidth and incurs heavy cloud ingestion costs. By implementing edge processing on the local microcontroller, root mean square calculations are performed locally, reducing the outbound payload to a single summary floating-point value transmitted every minute to the topic factory/assembly/motor4/rms. In class exercise: Design a three-level MQTT topic structure for a smart office building that monitors temperature and occupancy in multiple rooms across different floors.

title: Lecture 4: IoT Security and Real-World Applications
description: This lecture examines critical security vulnerabilities in connected systems and analyzes deployments across various industry domains.
content: Learning objectives: Identify major security attack vectors in IoT deployments, and design mitigation strategies incorporating encryption and authentication. Security in Internet of Things deployments is frequently compromised by constrained processing power, default credentials, unencrypted communication channels, and physical tampering vulnerabilities. Protecting device ecosystems requires mutual Transport Layer Security authentication using X.509 digital certificates, hardware-based secure elements for cryptographic key storage, and robust over-the-air firmware update pipelines with cryptographic signature verification. Consider a connected healthcare deployment where wearable cardiac monitors transmit patient heart rate data to a hospital server. If the wireless link uses unencrypted plain-text communication, an attacker can intercept the packets, perform a man-in-the-middle attack, and inject false medical alerts, endangering patient safety. Implementing end-to-end Transport Layer Security version 1.3 encryption ensures confidentiality and integrity of the physiological data stream. Across industry verticals, applications like smart cities leverage similar secure architectures for intelligent traffic light control, waste management optimization, and environmental pollution tracking. In class exercise: Propose two specific defense mechanisms to prevent an unauthorized device from publishing malicious sensor readings to a public MQTT broker.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive IoT System Design and Implementation

Task 1: System Architecture and Hardware Selection. Draw a complete block diagram of an IoT environmental monitoring system for a remote greenhouse. Task 3: MQTT Protocol Configuration and QoS Analysis. Design the MQTT topic hierarchy for monitoring temperature, humidity, and soil moisture across three distinct greenhouse zones. (Marks: 4)
Task 4: Edge Filtering Algorithm and Code Logic. Write a pseudocode or Python function running on the edge microcontroller that reads a raw temperature value every second. (Marks: 4)
Task 5: Security Vulnerability Assessment. Identify three distinct security risks applicable to this greenhouse IoT deployment. For each risk, propose a concrete technical countermeasure to protect the integrity, confidentiality, or availability of the system. (Marks: 4)

title: Lecture 1: Vector Calculus and Static Fields
description: This lecture reviews spatial differential operators and static electromagnetic field laws in various coordinate systems.
content:
Learning objectives: Master gradient, divergence, and curl operations; apply Gauss's and Ampere's laws to symmetric charge and current distributions.

Explanation: Electromagnetic fields vary across space and time, requiring robust mathematical tools. Vector calculus lets us analyze these variations. The gradient maps scalar potential fields to vector fields, showing the direction of steepest ascent. Divergence measures the net outward flux per unit volume from a point, underpinning Gauss's law for electric fields, which states that the total electric flux through a closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by the permittivity. Curl quantifies rotational vector fields, forming the foundation of Ampere's law, where the line integral of a magnetic field around a closed loop equals the enclosed current scaled by permeability. In cartesian coordinates, divergence operates via partial derivatives along x, y, and z axes. Boundary conditions dictate how electric and magnetic fields behave across interfaces separating different media, ensuring tangential electric fields and normal magnetic flux densities remain continuous where appropriate.

Worked example: Consider a point charge Q = 5 nanocoulombs at the origin. Using spherical coordinates, compute the electric field magnitude at a radial distance r = 0.1 meters in free space (permissivity epsilon_0 equals 8.854 times 10 to the power minus 12 farads per meter). Applying Gauss's law, the electric field E equals Q divided by (4 times pi times epsilon_0 times r squared). Substituting the values: E equals (5 times 10 to the power minus 9) divided by (4 times pi times 8.854 times 10 to the power minus 12 times 0.01), which evaluates to approximately 4496 volts per meter.

In class exercise: Calculate the divergence of the vector field F equals x squared i plus y squared j plus z squared k at the point (1, 2, 3).

title: Lecture 2: Maxwell's Equations and Wave Equations
description: This lecture formulates Maxwell's complete equations and derives the fundamental wave equation for source-free media.
content:
Learning objectives: Translate physical electromagnetic principles into differential and integral Maxwell equations; derive the vector wave equation.

Explanation: James Clerk Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism by introducing the displacement current density into Ampere's law, resolving an inconsistency involving time-varying charge conservation. In differential form, Maxwell's equations consist of Gauss's law for electricity, Gauss's law for magnetism showing the non-existence of magnetic monopoles, Faraday's law of induction linking changing magnetic fields to electric fields, and the modified Ampere-Maxwell law linking changing electric fields and conduction currents to magnetic fields. By taking the curl of Faraday's law and substituting the curl of the magnetic field from Ampere's law, we eliminate one field variable to derive the Helmholtz wave equation for propagating electromagnetic fields. This equation governs wave propagation speeds, showing that the wave velocity in a vacuum equals the inverse square root of the product of permeability and permittivity, which matches the speed of light.

Worked example: For a source-free, lossless dielectric medium with relative permittivity epsilon_r equal to 4 and relative permeability mu_r equal to 1, determine the phase velocity of the electromagnetic wave. The speed of light in vacuum c is 3 times 10 to the power 8 meters per second. The phase velocity v equals c divided by the square root of (epsilon_r times mu_r). Thus, v equals (3 times 10 to the power 8) divided by the square root of 4, which yields 1.5 times 10 to the power 8 meters per second.

In class exercise: State the physical significance of the displacement current term included by Maxwell.

title: Lecture 3: Plane Waves, Lossy Media, and Power Flow
description: This lecture examines uniform plane wave propagation characteristics, material losses, and electromagnetic power transmission.
content:
Learning objectives: Analyze intrinsic impedance and skin depth in lossy conductors; compute power flow using the Poynting vector.

Explanation: Uniform plane waves possess fields that are constant in any transverse plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation. The ratio of the electric field amplitude to the magnetic field amplitude defines the intrinsic impedance of the medium, which is 377 ohms for free space. When waves travel through lossy media such as damp earth or metals, finite conductivity causes attenuation. The skin depth quantifies how deeply electromagnetic fields penetrate a conductor before decaying to about 37 percent of their surface value. Because of this phenomenon, high-frequency alternating currents are restricted to a thin layer near the conductor surface, increasing effective resistance. Energy transport is quantified by the Poynting vector, defined as the cross product of the electric field vector and the magnetic field vector, representing directional power flow per unit area.

Worked example: Calculate the skin depth delta for copper at a frequency f of 1 megahertz (10 to the power 6 hertz). Given permeability mu equals 4 pi times 10 to the power minus 7 henries per meter and conductivity sigma equals 5.8 times 10 to the power 7 Siemens per meter. The formula is delta equals 1 divided by the square root of (pi times f times mu times sigma). Substituting values: delta equals 1 divided by the square root of (pi times 10 to the power 6 times 4 pi times 10 to the power minus 7 times 5.8 times 10 to the power 7), which evaluates to approximately 6.6 times 10 to the power minus 5 meters, or 66 micrometers.

In class exercise: Determine the intrinsic impedance magnitude for a medium where relative permittivity is 9 and relative permeability is 1.

title: Lecture 4: Boundary Conditions, Reflections, and Applications
description: This lecture investigates wave reflection at material interfaces and explores modern industrial and wireless applications.
content:
Learning objectives: Compute reflection and transmission coefficients for normal incidence; survey modern engineering applications like wireless power and EMC shielding.

Explanation: When an electromagnetic wave traveling in one medium encounters a boundary with a different medium, impedance mismatches cause partial reflection and partial transmission. Applying tangential and normal boundary conditions for electric and magnetic fields at the interface yields explicit formulas for the voltage reflection and transmission coefficients. These coefficients depend directly on the intrinsic impedances of the two contiguous media. For normal incidence, the reflection coefficient is the difference of the second and first impedances divided by their sum. Beyond classical boundary problems, electromagnetic theory drives modern technology. Wireless power transfer relies on resonant inductive coupling. Radio Frequency Identification systems use near-field electromagnetic coupling for tracking. Electromagnetic compatibility and shielding prevent unwanted interference in sensitive electronics by exploiting reflection and absorption losses in metallic enclosures.

Worked example: Find the normal-incidence power reflection coefficient for an electromagnetic wave traveling from air (impedance Z_1 equals 377 ohms) into a glass medium with a refractive index n equal to 1.5. The intrinsic impedance of glass is Z_2 equals 377 divided by 1.5, which is approximately 251.33 ohms. The electric field reflection coefficient gamma equals (Z_2 minus Z_1) divided by (Z_2 plus Z_1), which equals (251.33 minus 377) divided by (251.33 plus 377), yielding minus 0.200. The power reflection coefficient is the square of the magnitude of gamma, which is (minus 0.200) squared, equaling 0.040, meaning 4 percent of the incident power is reflected.

In class exercise: Explain why microwave ovens operate effectively around 2.45 gigahertz for heating water molecules.

title: Lecture 1: Modern Antenna Elements and Array Principles
description: This lecture examines microstrip patch antennas, bandwidth enhancement techniques, and phased array beamforming fundamentals.
content:
Learning objectives: Understand patch antenna resonance principles, evaluate bandwidth improvement methods, and calculate phased array factor steering.

The microstrip patch antenna is popular due to its low profile, but it suffers from narrow bandwidth. Bandwidth can be enhanced by introducing stacked patches, cutting U-slots, or using thick substrates with low dielectric constants to reduce the quality factor. For instance, a rectangular patch designed on a substrate with dielectric constant 2.2 and thickness 1.52 mm resonates at 2.45 GHz with a modest 2 percent bandwidth. By adding a parasitic stacked patch above the driven element, the resonant modes split slightly, increasing the impedance bandwidth to 12 percent, which fully covers the 2.4 GHz industrial, scientific, and medical band.

Moving to arrays, phased array systems achieve electronic beam steering without mechanical movement. The array factor for a uniform linear array of isotropic elements is given by the summation of weighted exponential phase terms. Consider a uniform linear array with 8 elements spaced at half-wavelength distance. To steer the main beam to an angle of 30 degrees off boresight at 5 GHz, the required progressive phase shift between adjacent elements is calculated as minus 2 times pi times element spacing times sine of the angle, resulting in a phase increment of approximately 1.81 radians or 103.8 degrees.

In class exercise: Calculate the progressive phase shift needed for a 16-element linear array with 0.4 wavelength spacing to steer the beam to 45 degrees at 10 GHz.

title: Lecture 2: Advanced Radiating Structures and Metamaterials
description: This lecture covers reconfigurable antennas, mutual coupling in MIMO configurations, millimeter-wave on-chip designs, and metasurface applications.
content:
Learning objectives: Analyze mutual coupling mechanisms in MIMO systems, evaluate mmWave on-chip challenges, and apply metasurface concepts to gain enhancement.

As wireless systems demand higher data rates, multi-input multi-output configurations become essential. However, closely spaced antenna elements suffer from mutual coupling, which degrades channel capacity and correlation coefficients. Consider two half-wave dipoles separated by a distance of 0.1 wavelength on a crowded smartphone board. The mutual impedance can be high, causing severe port mismatch. To mitigate this, defected ground structures or neutralization lines are introduced. For instance, placing a lumped capacitive-inductive decoupling network between the two feed ports can lower the S21 transmission parameter from minus 5 dB down to minus 25 dB across the operating band.

At millimeter-wave frequencies, on-chip antennas face high substrate losses due to low-resistivity silicon. Designers utilize artificial magnetic conductors and metasurfaces, which are two-dimensional periodic structures engineered to manipulate electromagnetic waves. A metasurface antenna can transform a spherical wave from a simple patch feed into a highly directive planar phase front. For example, a metasurface consisting of 10 by 10 unit cells operating at 28 GHz can achieve an antenna gain of 18 dBi while maintaining a total thickness of less than a quarter wavelength, significantly outperforming conventional horn antennas in mobile terminals.

In class exercise: Determine the required element separation in terms of free-space wavelength to keep mutual coupling below minus 15 dB for two parallel dipoles without decoupling networks.

title: Lecture 3: High-Power Microwave Generation and Vacuum Tubes
description: This lecture investigates vacuum electronic devices and solid-state power amplifiers used for generating high microwave power.
content:
Learning objectives: Contrast the operating mechanisms of klystrons and traveling-wave tubes, analyze magnetron parameters, and evaluate GaN HEMT solid-state devices.

High-power microwave systems require specialized sources that exceed the capabilities of standard semiconductor devices. Vacuum tubes remain dominant for ultra-high power applications such as particle accelerators and radar transmitters. A klystron uses velocity modulation of an electron beam passing through input and output resonant cavities. In contrast, a traveling-wave tube utilizes a continuous interaction between an electron beam and a slow-wave structure along the entire length of the tube, yielding a much wider operating bandwidth. Consider a standard cavity magnetron operating in a domestic appliance: it typically generates an output power of 1 kilowatt continuous wave at 2.45 GHz with an overall direct current to radio frequency conversion efficiency of 70 percent, driven by an anode voltage of 4 kilovolt and an anode current of 350 milliamperes.

Solid-state power amplifiers have advanced rapidly, especially with gallium nitride high electron mobility transistors. A single GaN HEMT device can deliver hundreds of watts at S-band frequencies with high power-added efficiency. For radar transmitters, engineers now compare vacuum tube reliability against modular solid-state arrays. While a single travelling-wave tube can output 20 kilowatts peak power, combining forty 500-watt GaN amplifier modules through a corporate combiner provides graceful degradation if individual modules fail.

In class exercise: Calculate the input DC power required for a magnetron operating at 70 percent efficiency if it delivers 1500 watts of microwave output power.

title: Lecture 4: Antenna Measurement Techniques and System Applications
description: This lecture explores anechoic chamber measurement methodologies, near-field to far-field transformations, numerical simulation software, and safety exposure limits.
content:
Learning objectives: Distinguish between near-field and far-field measurement ranges, set up electromagnetic simulation tools, and assess radio frequency safety compliance.

Accurate characterization of advanced antennas requires specialized testing facilities. Anechoic chambers are lined with radio frequency absorber cones to eliminate unwanted reflections, simulating free-space conditions. When testing electrically large base station arrays, measuring directly in the far-field is impractical due to the required distance boundary, defined as 2 times the maximum dimension squared divided by the wavelength. For an antenna array with a dimension of 1.5 meters operating at 6 GHz, the far-field boundary is 180 meters. Therefore, engineers use near-field measurement systems, scanning the electromagnetic field close to the antenna on a planar, cylindrical, or spherical grid, and applying mathematical near-field to far-field transformation algorithms.

Numerical simulation tools such as Ansys HFSS and CST Studio Suite are vital before physical fabrication. These solvers use finite element method or finite integration technique to solve Maxwell equations. For safety and regulatory compliance, engineers must evaluate specific absorption rate and power density limits near high-power transmitting antennas. For instance, the maximum permissible exposure for the general public in the frequency range from 1.5 GHz to 100 GHz is 10 watts per square meter averaged over 6 minutes.

In class exercise: Calculate the minimum far-field distance for an antenna with a maximum aperture of 0.8 meters operating at a frequency of 28 GHz.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Antenna Array and High-Power Microwave Analysis
description: This assignment evaluates student competency in phased array design, microstrip bandwidth calculations, vacuum tube performance, and simulation workflows.
content:
1. Microstrip Patch Design: Design a rectangular microstrip patch antenna on FR4 substrate with a relative permittivity of 4.4 and thickness of 1.6 mm to operate at a center frequency of 5.8 GHz. Calculate the patch width and effective length. Marks: 4.

2. Phased Array Steering: Consider a linear array of 12 isotropic elements spaced by 0.5 wavelengths. Compute the exact progressive phase shift required to steer the main beam to 22 degrees off broadside. Sketch the expected array factor normalized magnitude versus angle from minus 90 to 90 degrees. Marks: 4.

3. Mutual Coupling Analysis: A two-element MIMO antenna array has an S-parameter matrix where S11 is minus 15 dB and S21 is minus 6 dB. Calculate the total reflected power fraction and the power coupled to the second port assuming an incident available power of 2 watts at port 1. Marks: 4.

4. High-Power Microwave Source: A pulsed klystron operates at 9.3 GHz with a beam voltage of 50 kV and a beam current of 120 A. If the interaction efficiency is 45 percent, determine the peak RF output power and the average power assuming a pulse repetition frequency of 400 Hz and a pulse width of 5 microseconds. Marks: 4.

5. Safety and Measurement: An outdoor cellular base station sector antenna radiates an equivalent isotropically radiated power of 1000 watts. Calculate the radial distance from the antenna where the power density drops to the general public safety limit of 10 watts per square meter, assuming free-space propagation. Marks: 4.

Submission instructions: Submit your complete solutions as a single PDF document containing all mathematical derivations, intermediate calculation steps, annotated sketches, and simulation screenshots where applicable.

title: Lecture 1: Introduction to Embedded Systems and Hardware Architecture
description: This lecture introduces embedded system constraints and explores internal microcontroller architectures.
content: Learning objectives: Understand key embedded characteristics including real-time demands and resource limits, and identify core components of microcontrollers. Embedded systems combine dedicated hardware and software to execute specific tasks under strict physical limitations such as constrained memory, strict timing, and low power consumption. Unlike general-purpose computers, a microcontroller integrates a CPU core, flash memory for non-volatile code storage, SRAM for runtime data, and various hardware peripherals onto a single silicon die. For example, consider an ARM Cortex-M processor running at 72 MHz with 64 kilobytes of flash and 20 kilobytes of SRAM. Calculating instruction cycles reveals that a single instruction executes in approximately 13.88 nanoseconds, meaning high-speed calculations must be carefully planned to fit within tight power and timing budgets. To interact with the physical world, software directly accesses memory-mapped registers. For instance, configuring a specific pin involves writing to a directional register, and setting bit 5 of port register PORTB using the C statement PORTB |= (1 << 5) drives that output pin high, while clearing it via PORTB &= ~(1 << 5) drives it low. In class exercise: Write a C code snippet that configures bit 2 of a hypothetical output data register to high without altering the states of any other bits in that register.

title: Lecture 2: Low-Level Programming and Peripheral Interfacing
description: This lecture covers Embedded C techniques and fundamental hardware communication peripherals.
content: Learning objectives: Master bit manipulation in C and configure standard communication and timing peripherals. Writing efficient embedded software requires direct hardware control using pointers and bitwise operations. The volatile keyword is mandatory for variables modified asynchronously, such as inside an interrupt service routine, because it instructs the compiler to read the variable from memory on every access rather than caching it in a CPU register. Peripherals bridge the digital processor to external sensors and actuators. Timers utilize internal clock sources and prescalers to generate precise delays or Pulse Width Modulation signals. For example, using a 16 megahertz timer clock with a prescaler of 16 and a period register value of 1000 yields a PWM frequency of 16000000 divided by (16 multiplied by 1000), which equals 1000 hertz, producing a stable 1 kHz signal. Communication interfaces vary by topology: UART provides asynchronous point-to-point serial data transfer, SPI offers high-speed synchronous full-duplex communication using separate data lines and a chip select, and I2C enables multi-device communication over just two shared lines using device addressing. In class exercise: Calculate the reload value for a timer running at 8 megahertz to generate an exact interrupt interval of 1 millisecond.

title: Lecture 3: Interrupts, Concurrency, and Real-Time Operating Systems
description: This lecture examines interrupt-driven design paradigms and preemptive real-time operating system concepts.
content: Learning objectives: Compare polling with interrupt architectures and understand task scheduling within an RTOS. Polling continuously checks peripheral status flags in a CPU-intensive loop, which wastes processing cycles and increases power consumption. Conversely, interrupt-driven designs allow peripherals to signal the CPU asynchronously via Interrupt Service Routines, ensuring rapid response times to external events. However, shared resources between the main thread and ISRs demand careful synchronization to avoid race conditions. As system complexity grows, bare-metal super-loops become difficult to maintain, making a Real-Time Operating System necessary. An RTOS manages multitasking through deterministic task schedulers, such as priority-based preemptive scheduling or rate monotonic scheduling, which assigns higher execution priorities to tasks with shorter periods. Inter-task communication relies on primitives like semaphores for mutual exclusion and message queues for safely transferring data buffers between concurrent tasks. For example, in FreeRTOS, a queue of length 10 holding integer sensor readings allows a producer task to safely pass data to a consumer display task without risking memory corruption. In class exercise: Explain why a low-priority task holding a shared resource can temporarily block a high-priority task, and name the phenomenon.

title: Lecture 4: System Reliability, Power Management, and Development Tools
description: This lecture focuses on extending battery life, ensuring fault tolerance, and mastering debugging workflows.
content: Learning objectives: Implement power-saving strategies, configure watchdog timers, and utilize hardware debuggers. Embedded devices often operate on battery power, requiring aggressive power management techniques. Processors can dynamically scale voltage and frequency, or enter sleep and deep-sleep modes where high-frequency clocks are halted until an external interrupt wakes the system. To guarantee reliability in unattended environments, watchdog timers provide hardware-level fault recovery. If software crashes or enters an infinite loop and fails to refresh or pet the watchdog within a specified window, the timer resets the microcontroller automatically. Developing and verifying this software requires specialized toolchains, including cross-compilers that generate target-specific machine code from host development machines. Debugging relies on hardware interfaces like JTAG or Serial Wire Debug, allowing developers to set breakpoints, inspect memory-mapped registers, and step through code execution line by line. Software simulation and hardware-in-the-loop testing complete the verification cycle. In class exercise: Describe the sequence of events that occurs when a watchdog timer expires while a microcontroller is executing a corrupted firmware routine.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Embedded Firmware Development
description: This assignment tests practical skills in bit manipulation, timer configuration, ISR synchronization, and state machine design.
content:
1. Bit Manipulation and Memory-Mapped I/O: Write an embedded C function that initializes a control register by setting bits 3 through 6 while clearing bits 0 and 1, leaving all other bits unaffected. Provide the exact bitwise expression. (4 marks)
2. Timer and PWM Generation: Calculate the prescaler and auto-reload register values required to generate a 500 Hz PWM signal with a 25 percent duty cycle using a timer driven by a 16 MHz clock source. Write the configuration sequence in C. (4 marks)
3. Interrupts and Volatile Variables: Design an interrupt service routine for an external button press that increments a shared step counter. Explain why the counter variable must be declared volatile and write the safe retrieval function for the main application loop. (4 marks)
4. RTOS Task Communication: Write a short FreeRTOS application snippet featuring two tasks: a sensor reading task that posts data to a queue every 50 milliseconds, and an actuator task that blocks on that queue and processes incoming data. Include queue creation and task instantiation calls. (4 marks)
5. Power Saving and Watchdog Configuration: Write a routine that configures a watchdog timer with a 2-second timeout window and places the microcontroller into a low-power sleep mode while awaiting external sensor interrupts. (4 marks)
Submission instructions: Submit your complete solutions compiled into a single PDF document containing all code snippets, calculations, and explanations.

title: Lecture 1: System Modelling and Block Diagrams
description: This lecture covers the fundamentals of mathematical modelling for electrical and mechanical systems and system representation using block diagrams.
content:
Learning objectives: Derive transfer functions for basic physical systems and simplify multi-loop block diagrams.

In control engineering, accurate mathematical models are essential for predicting system behavior. We begin by applying physical laws, such as Kirchhoff's laws for electrical circuits and Newton's laws for mechanical systems, converting differential equations into the Laplace domain to find the transfer function G(s) = Output(s) over Input(s).

Consider an RL series circuit with resistance R = 5 ohms and inductance L = 2 henries driven by a voltage source V(s). The governing differential equation is v(t) = Ri(t) + L di(t)/dt. Taking the Laplace transform with zero initial conditions yields V(s) = (R + Ls)I(s). The transfer function relating current to voltage is therefore I(s)/V(s) = 1 / (5 + 2s), which can be rewritten in standard time-constant form as 0.2 / (1 + 0.4s). For mechanical rotational systems, torque balances inertia, damping, and stiffness analogously.

Block diagram algebra allows us to combine multiple subsystems. When two blocks with transfer functions G1(s) and G2(s) are in cascade, the overall transfer function is their product. For a feedback loop with forward path G(s) and feedback path H(s), the closed-loop transfer function is G(s) / (1 + G(s)H(s)).

In class exercise: Find the equivalent transfer function of two cascaded blocks where G1(s) = 3 / (s + 1) and G2(s) = 2 / (s + 4), and determine the closed-loop transfer function assuming unity feedback.

title: Lecture 2: Time Response and Stability Analysis
description: Students will analyze first- and second-order transient responses and evaluate system stability using the Routh-Hurwitz criterion.
content:
Learning objectives: Calculate key transient performance metrics and apply the algebraic Routh-Hurwitz stability criterion.

The time response of a control system reveals how it reacts to inputs like steps or ramps. For a standard second-order system characterized by natural frequency omega_n and damping ratio zeta, the poles dictate the transient shape. If zeta = 0.6 and omega_n = 5 radians per second, the closed-loop poles are complex conjugates at -3 plus or minus j4. The percent overshoot is given by exp(-pi * zeta / sqrt(1 - zeta squared)) multiplied by 100, which evaluates here to roughly 9.5 percent. The settling time for a 2 percent criterion is approximately 4 divided by the product of zeta and omega_n, yielding 1.33 seconds.

While transient analysis tells us how fast a system responds, stability tells us if it will remain bounded. Absolute stability requires all roots of the characteristic equation to lie in the open left-half of the complex plane. Instead of factoring high-order polynomials, we use the Routh-Hurwitz criterion. Given a characteristic equation like s cubed + 3 s squared + 5 s + K = 0, we construct a Routh array. The first column elements must all be positive for stability. Row entries for s to the power of 1 yield (15 - K) / 3, meaning K must be strictly greater than 0 and less than 15 for the system to remain stable.

In class exercise: Construct the Routh array for the polynomial s cubed + 2 s squared + 4 s + 8 = 0 and determine the exact number of right-half plane poles.

title: Lecture 3: Root Locus and Frequency Response Methods
description: This lecture explores graphical design techniques including root locus sketching and frequency response analysis via Bode plots.
content:
Learning objectives: Sketch root locus plots to observe pole migration and interpret gain and phase margins from Bode diagrams.

Root locus analysis shows how closed-loop poles move in the complex plane as a parameter, typically loop gain K, varies from zero to infinity. Rules for sketching include finding the starting points at open-loop poles, ending points at open-loop zeros, and calculating asymptotes that intersect the real axis at a centroid given by the sum of poles minus the sum of zeros divided by the number of poles minus zeros.

Frequency response methods evaluate steady-state responses to sinusoidal inputs. A Bode plot displays magnitude in decibels and phase in degrees versus frequency on a logarithmic scale. Consider a plant with transfer function G(s) = 10 / (s(s + 2)). The magnitude plot starts with a slope of -20 dB per decade due to the pole at the origin. The phase crossover frequency is where the phase angle reaches -180 degrees. If the magnitude at this frequency is -6 dB, the gain margin is +6 dB, indicating the system has adequate relative stability.

In class exercise: For a system with open-loop poles at s = 0, -1, and -5, calculate the centroid of the asymptotes and determine the number of root locus branches going to infinity.

title: Lecture 4: Controller Design and State-Space Methods
description: The final lecture covers classical PID controller tuning, lead-lag compensation, and modern state-space representations.
content:
Learning objectives: Design PID controllers for performance specifications and formulate state-space models with pole placement.

Classical controller design relies on shaping the loop transfer function. A Proportional-Integral-Derivative controller has the transfer function C(s) = K_p + K_i/s + K_d s. The proportional term reduces overall error, the integral term drives steady-state error to zero for step inputs by acting as a type-1 integrator, and the derivative term introduces predictive damping to improve phase margin. If steady-state error persists, adding integration eliminates it completely, though it typically reduces relative stability.

Modern control shifts to state-space representations using matrices A, B, C, and D. For a system dx/dt = A x + B u and y = C x + D u, we examine structural properties. Controllability ensures we can drive the state vector to any desired location using input u, verified by checking if the controllability matrix [B AB A^2 B] has full rank. Observability ensures we can reconstruct internal states from output measurements. Using full-state feedback u = -K x, we can place closed-loop poles at arbitrary locations by matching coefficients of det(sI - (A - B K)) with desired polynomial roots.

In class exercise: Given a system matrix A = [[0, 1], [-2, -3]] and input vector B = [[0], [1]], compute the controllability matrix and verify if the system is completely controllable.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Control Systems Analysis and Design
description: A comprehensive practical assignment covering system modelling, stability criteria, root locus, Bode analysis, and PID controller tuning.
content:
1. Derive the transfer function V_out(s) over V_in(s) for an operational amplifier differentiator circuit with input resistor R_1, feedback capacitor C, and a small parasitic feedback resistor R_2 in parallel with C. [4 marks]

2. Given the closed-loop characteristic polynomial P(s) = s to the power of 4 + 5 s cubed + 7 s squared + 25 s + K = 0, use the Routh-Hurwitz criterion to determine the exact range of real parameter K for which the system is stable. [4 marks]

3. Sketch the root locus for a unity feedback system with open-loop transfer function G(s) = K / (s (s + 3) (s + 6)). Calculate all break-away points on the real axis and find the exact value of gain K where the locus crosses the imaginary axis. [4 marks]

4. A plant has the frequency response function G(j omega) = 5 / (j omega (0.5 j omega + 1)). Construct the theoretical Bode magnitude and phase curves on semi-log paper, and compute the exact gain margin and phase margin. [4 marks]

5. Design a parallel PID controller with K_p = 4, K_i = 2, and K_d = 0.5 for a second-order plant G(s) = 1 / (s squared + 2 s + 5). Write a Python script using the control library to simulate the closed-loop step response and compute the resulting percent overshoot and settling time. [4 marks]

title: Lecture 1: Foundations of Optimal Control and Calculus of Variations
description: This lecture introduces the mathematical foundations of optimal control, focusing on performance indices, the calculus of variations, and Pontryagin's minimum principle.
content: Learning objectives: Understand how to formulate control problems as optimization tasks and apply necessary conditions for optimality. In optimal control, we seek a control input trajectory that minimizes a chosen cost function while satisfying system dynamics. The performance index typically integrates running costs on states and control inputs over a time horizon. To solve this, the calculus of variations uses the Euler-Lagrange equations, while Pontryagin's minimum principle generalizes this by introducing costates or adjoint variables, establishing that the Hamiltonian of the system must be minimized over the admissible control set at every time instant. For example, consider a simple scalar system defined by the differential equation dx/dt = u(t) with the initial state x(0) = 1 and terminal time T = 1. We wish to minimize the cost functional J = integral from 0 to 1 of (0.5 x squared + 0.5 u squared) dt. Using the Hamiltonian H = 0.5 x squared + 0.5 u squared + p u, where p is the costate, the optimality condition dH/du = 0 yields u = -p. Coupled with the costate equation dp/dt = -dH/dx = -x, and the state equation, we obtain a two-point boundary value problem whose solution governs the optimal feedback trajectory. In class exercise: formulate the Hamiltonian for a vehicle moving in one dimension with state dynamics x dot = v and v dot = u, aiming to minimize control effort subject to a final position constraint.

title: Lecture 2: Linear Quadratic Regulators and Model Predictive Control
description: This lecture covers state-feedback optimal control through the Linear Quadratic Regulator and introduces constrained horizon optimization via Model Predictive Control.
content: Learning objectives: Derive the algebraic Riccati equation for LQR and understand constraint handling in Model Predictive Control. The Linear Quadratic Regulator provides a mathematically tractable solution for linear systems with quadratic cost functions. By solving the algebraic Riccati equation, we determine the optimal feedback gain matrix K that minimizes state deviations and control energy. For instance, consider a discrete plant with state matrix A = 1.1 and input matrix B = 1, where the weighting matrices are chosen as Q = 2 and R = 1. Solving the scalar algebraic Riccati equation P = A squared P - (A P B)(R + B squared P inverse)(B P A) + Q yields a steady-state positive root P approximately equal to 1.83. Consequently, the optimal feedback gain K = (R + B squared P inverse) inverse B P A calculates to approximately 0.72, ensuring stable closed-loop pole placement at 1.1 - (1)(0.72) = 0.38. However, real-world systems operate under strict physical limits on actuators and states, which LQR cannot directly enforce. Model Predictive Control addresses this limitation by solving a finite-horizon open-loop optimal control problem at each sampling instant, applying only the first computed control action, and repeating the optimization at the next step to incorporate receding horizon feedback and constraints. In class exercise: compute the open-loop prediction vector for a 2-step horizon using the given plant matrices.

title: Lecture 3: Fuzzy Logic and Neural Network Control Systems
description: This lecture explores intelligent control methodologies that mimic human reasoning and biological learning through fuzzy logic controllers and neural network architectures.
content: Learning objectives: Design fuzzy rule bases and membership functions, and understand neural network system identification. Fuzzy logic controllers translate linguistic rules into precise numerical control actions through fuzzification, rule evaluation, and defuzzification. They do not require an exact mathematical model of the plant, making them robust for nonlinear environments. For example, to control a heating element based on temperature error and error rate, we define triangular membership functions for error labeled Negative, Zero, and Positive. If the error is Positive and the error rate is Zero, a typical fuzzy rule states that the heater power output should be Medium. The linguistic outputs are then aggregated and defuzzified using the centroid method to yield a crisp control voltage. Complementing rule-based systems, neural network control leverages universal function approximation properties. In direct or indirect adaptive control, a multilayer perceptron is trained offline or online using backpropagation through time to identify unknown plant dynamics or act directly as a neuro-controller. The network weights are adjusted iteratively to minimize the squared error between the plant output and the reference model output. In class exercise: sketch the membership functions and write three IF-THEN rules for an automated cruise control braking system.

title: Lecture 4: Evolutionary Optimization and Reinforcement Learning for Control
description: This lecture examines advanced tuning and decision-making techniques using evolutionary algorithms and reinforcement learning frameworks for complex control tasks.
content: Learning objectives: Apply evolutionary algorithms to controller parameter tuning and understand the basics of reinforcement learning in control loops. Traditional tuning methods often fail in highly complex or time-varying systems. Evolutionary techniques, such as genetic algorithms and particle swarm optimization, search large parameter spaces globally by mimicking natural selection or social behavior. For instance, to tune a proportional-integral-derivative controller, a genetic algorithm initializes a population of candidate gain triplets (Kp, Ki, Kd). Each candidate is evaluated by running a simulation of the closed-loop system and calculating a fitness score based on the integral of time-weighted absolute error. Selection, crossover, and mutation operators generate successive generations until optimal gains are found. Beyond optimization of static parameters, reinforcement learning addresses sequential decision-making under uncertainty. An agent interacts with the control environment, observing states, taking actions, and receiving numerical rewards or penalties. Through algorithms like Q-learning or policy gradients, the agent learns a policy that maximizes cumulative discounted rewards over infinity without requiring an explicit analytical model of the plant dynamics. In class exercise: define the state space, action space, and reward function structure for a reinforcement learning agent tasked with balancing an inverted pendulum.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Optimal and Intelligent Control Design
description: This assignment tests student proficiency across analytical LQR design, model predictive constraint formulation, fuzzy rule construction, and evolutionary controller tuning.
content:
Task 1: Given a continuous-time linear system with A = 0 and B = 1, formulate the Hamiltonian and derive the Euler-Lagrange equations for minimizing the cost index J = integral from 0 to infinity of (4 x squared + u squared) dt. (4 marks)
Task 2: Solve the algebraic Riccati equation for the system in Task 1 to find the positive definite matrix P, and calculate the optimal LQR feedback gain K. (4 marks)

Task 5: Outline the pseudocode for a genetic algorithm used to tune the proportional and derivative gains of a controller, explicitly defining the fitness evaluation step using the integral of absolute error metric. (4 marks)

title: Lecture 1: Measurement and Final Elements in Process Dynamics
description: This lecture covers physical process variables, 4 to 20 mA signal conversion, control valves, and first-order plus dead time mathematical models.
content:
Learning objectives: Understand field instrumentation signals, calculate valve flow responses, and interpret first-order plus dead time parameters.

Process control begins with accurately measuring physical variables like temperature, pressure, level, and flow. Industrial sensors convert these into standard 4 to 20 milliamp current loops. The base value of 4 milliamps represents zero percent of the calibrated span, while 20 milliamps represents one hundred percent. This current standard resists electrical noise over long distances and allows loop-powered device diagnostics. If a transmitter has a calibrated span from 0 to 10 bars and outputs 12 milliamps, the measured pressure is exactly 5 bars, calculated using linear interpolation where (12 - 4) / (20 - 4) multiplied by the span of 10 bars equals 5 bars. Final control elements, primarily control valves, manipulate the mass or volumetric flow rate. Their inherent flow characteristics, such as linear or equal percentage, dictate how valve stem position relates to flow capacity. Valve sizing ensures the valve takes a significant pressure drop from the system. Process dynamics describe how outputs respond to inputs over time. Most industrial processes are effectively modeled as a first-order plus dead time system, defined by process gain, time constant, and dead time. When a step change of magnitude 2 is applied to a process with a gain of 3, the final steady-state change in output reaches 6.

In class: Calculate the current output for a temperature transmitter scaled from 50 to 250 degrees Celsius when the measured temperature is 150 degrees Celsius.

title: Lecture 2: Advanced Control Strategies and PID Tuning
description: This lecture explores feedback PID control, advanced configurations like cascade and feedforward, and systematic tuning using Ziegler-Nichols methods.
content:
Learning objectives: Compare single-loop and advanced control architectures, apply feedforward principles, and execute the Ziegler-Nichols tuning method.

Feedback control loops measure the controlled variable, compare it to a setpoint, and compute an error. The Proportional-Integral-Derivative algorithm applies corrective action based on current error, accumulated past error, and the rate of future error change. While standard feedback handles many loops, disturbances can cause large upsets before correction occurs. To improve performance, advanced strategies are deployed. Cascade control uses two nested loops where a secondary inner loop addresses intermediate disturbances before they affect the primary outer loop. Feedforward control measures a major disturbance directly and takes corrective action before it impacts the controlled variable. Ratio control keeps two flows at a fixed proportion, and split-range control uses a single controller output to operate multiple final elements. When configuring a PID controller, proper tuning is essential. The Ziegler-Nichols closed-loop ultimate gain method provides a systematic starting point. By increasing the proportional gain until the system sustains stable, continuous oscillations, the ultimate gain and the ultimate oscillation period are recorded. For a classic PID controller, the proportional gain is set to 0.6 times the ultimate gain, the integral time is set to 0.5 times the ultimate period, and the derivative time is set to 0.125 times the ultimate period.

In class: Determine the PID tuning parameters using Ziegler-Nichols rules if an ultimate gain of 4 and an ultimate period of 6 minutes are observed.

title: Lecture 3: P&ID Diagrams and Industrial Automation Networks
description: This lecture details Piping and Instrumentation Diagrams, standard instrumentation symbols, and industrial communication networks for plant integration.
content:
Learning objectives: Read and interpret P&ID symbology, understand SCADA and HMI integration, and compare industrial network protocols.

Piping and Instrumentation Diagrams serve as the master blueprint for chemical and manufacturing plants. They illustrate the physical sequence of equipment, piping, and the automation instrumentation required to operate the process safely. Standard ISA-5.1 symbols define instrument identities through circular bubbles containing function letters and loop numbers. For example, a tag reading TIC-101 designates a Temperature Indicating Controller in loop 101. Lines connecting equipment denote process piping, pneumatic signals, electric signals, or data links. Modern plants integrate these field devices with Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition systems and Human Machine Interfaces to provide operators with centralized monitoring and control dashboards. Underpinning this plant-wide integration are robust industrial communication networks. Traditional serial protocols like Modbus RTU communicate via master-slave request-response polling over RS-485 physical layers. Modern systems leverage industrial Ethernet protocols such as Profibus, Profinet, and Ethernet/IP to handle high-speed deterministic data exchanges. These networks ensure that critical interlock signals and high-resolution process data move reliably between programmable logic controllers, drives, and control rooms without packet collisions or unacceptable latency.

In class: Draw the ISA-5.1 symbol and label for a pressure transmitter connected to a shared control display in loop 205.

title: Lecture 4: PLC Architecture, Programming, and Ladder Logic
description: This lecture examines programmable logic controller hardware architecture, the execution scan cycle, IEC 61131-3 languages, and discrete ladder logic programming.
content:
Learning objectives: Describe the PLC scan cycle, write IEC 61131-3 structured or ladder code, and implement interlocking start-stop logic with timers.

Programmable Logic Controllers automate industrial machinery through a solid-state computer architecture consisting of a central processing unit, memory, power supply, and modular input and output cards. The operation of a PLC relies on a strict repetitive operating sequence known as the scan cycle. During the first phase, the CPU reads the state of all physical input terminals and updates the input image table. During the second phase, the processor executes the user control program line by line from top to bottom, resolving ladder rungs or software instructions using the input and internal memory states. During the third phase, the CPU writes the resulting output states from the output image table to the physical output terminals. Programming follows the IEC 61131-3 international standard, supporting graphical languages like ladder diagram and function block chart, as well as text-based languages like structured text. Ladder logic emulates historical relay schematic diagrams using normally open contacts, normally closed contacts, and output coils. Sequential control often requires memory latching. For instance, to keep a motor running after a momentary push button is released, a seal-in contact wired in parallel with the start button ensures the rung remains true: Motor equals the logical sum of Start and current Motor status, combined with the inverted Stop condition.

In class: Write the ladder logic boolean expression for a conveyor belt that must run only when a safety gate interlock is closed and either a manual or automatic run command is active.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Process Control and PLC Programming
description: This assignment tests student competency in process calculations, advanced control selection, PID tuning, P&ID interpretation, and PLC ladder logic design.
content:
1. Transmitter Scaling: A level transmitter is calibrated for a range of 0 to 5 meters. Calculate the expected current output in milliamps if the measured tank level is 3.75 meters. (4 marks)

2. PID Tuning: A closed-loop test on a flow control loop yields an ultimate gain of 5.0 and an ultimate oscillation period of 2 seconds. Compute the proportional gain, integral time, and derivative time constants for a standard PID controller using the Ziegler-Nichols tuning formulas. (4 marks)

3. Control Strategy Selection: A large distillation column suffers from severe feed temperature disturbances that disrupt the bottom product composition long before feedback control can react. Propose an advanced control strategy to counteract this specific issue and explain how it improves disturbance rejection compared to a single-loop feedback configuration. (4 marks)

4. P&ID Interpretation: Identify and describe the functions of the following three standard ISA-5.1 instrumentation tags found on a P&ID: PIT-102, FIC-201, and LSH-305. (4 marks)

5. PLC Ladder Logic Design: Design a complete start-stop motor control circuit in ladder logic that includes a thermal overload trip contact to stop the motor, and an on-delay timer (TON) set for 10 seconds that illuminates a running indicator lamp only after the motor has successfully run continuously for 10 seconds. Provide the complete rung layout or boolean representation. (4 marks)

title: Lecture 1: Mathematical Foundations and Kinematics
description: This lecture introduces vector algebra and the equations governing motion in one and two dimensions.
content: Learning objectives: Master vector components alongside dot and cross products, and apply kinematic equations to linear and projectile trajectories. We begin with mathematical tools. Vectors possess magnitude and direction. The dot product yields a scalar measuring alignment, while the cross product generates a perpendicular vector measuring rotational tendency. Kinematics describes motion without referencing forces. For constant acceleration, velocity evolves as v = v0 + at, and position changes according to x = x0 + v0t + 0.5at^2. Combining these yields v^2 = v0^2 + 2a times delta x. Consider a projectile launched from ground level at 25 meters per second at an angle of 30 degrees above the horizontal. The initial vertical velocity component is v_y = 25 times sin(30 degrees), which equals 12.5 meters per second. Using the acceleration due to gravity g = 9.8 meters per second squared, the time to reach the apex is t_apex = 12.5 divided by 9.8, resulting in approximately 1.28 seconds. The total flight time is double this value, giving 2.56 seconds. The horizontal component is v_x = 25 times cos(30 degrees) equals 21.65 meters per second, producing a total horizontal range of 21.65 multiplied by 2.56, which equals approximately 55.42 meters. In class exercise: Calculate the final velocity of a car accelerating from rest at 3 meters per second squared over a distance of 50 meters.

title: Lecture 2: Dynamics and Circular Motion
description: This lecture connects force interactions to translational and rotational acceleration using Newton's laws.
content: Learning objectives: Construct free body diagrams to solve Newton's second law problems and analyze centripetal forces in uniform circular motion. Dynamics explains why objects move. Newton's first law establishes inertial frames, the second law dictates that the net force equals mass times acceleration, F = ma, and the third law states that forces occur in equal and opposite action reaction pairs. Contact forces include normal forces and friction, where kinetic friction is modeled as f = mu times N. When analyzing curved paths, objects experience centripetal acceleration directed toward the center of curvature, given by a_c = v^2 divided by r. Consider a 2 kilogram mass attached to a string of length 0.5 meters, swung in a horizontal circle at a constant speed of 4 meters per second. The tension in the string provides the necessary centripetal force. We compute the acceleration as a_c = 4 squared divided by 0.5, which equals 16 divided by 0.5, yielding 32 meters per second squared. The required tension force is then mass times acceleration, F_t = 2 times 32, resulting in 64 Newtons. In class exercise: Determine the maximum speed a car can negotiate a flat curve of radius 40 meters if the static coefficient of friction between tires and road is 0.4.

title: Lecture 3: Work, Energy, and Momentum
description: This lecture explores conservation principles through work-energy theorems and collision dynamics.
content: Learning objectives: Compute work done by variable forces, apply energy conservation laws, and solve collision problems using momentum conservation. Work is defined as the dot product of force and displacement, W = F dot d. The work-energy theorem states that net work equals the change in kinetic energy, where kinetic energy is 0.5mv^2. Conservative forces, such as gravity and springs, possess associated potential energies of mgh and 0.5kx^2 respectively. Total mechanical energy remains constant in systems lacking non-conservative forces like friction. Power measures the rate of doing work, expressed as P = dW/dt. Momentum, p = mv, is conserved in isolated systems during collisions. In a perfectly inelastic collision, objects stick together, losing kinetic energy to internal thermal or deformation energy. Consider a 3 kilogram cart moving at 4 meters per second colliding with a stationary 2 kilogram cart, sticking together post-impact. Initial momentum is 3 times 4 equals 12 kilogram meters per second. The combined mass is 3 plus 2 equals 5 kilograms. The final velocity is 12 divided by 5, resulting in 2.4 meters per second. In class exercise: Find the compressed length of a spring with constant 500 Newtons per meter required to stop a 1 kilogram ball rolling at 6 meters per second.

title: Lecture 4: Rotation and Oscillations
description: This lecture examines rotational dynamics, angular momentum, and periodic oscillatory systems.
content: Learning objectives: Calculate torque and rotational inertia, apply angular momentum principles, and determine the period of simple harmonic oscillators. Rotation parallels linear motion. Torque is the cross product of lever arm and force, tau = r cross F. Newton's second law for rotation states that net torque equals moment of inertia multiplied by angular acceleration. Angular momentum is conserved in the absence of external torques. Rolling motion combines translation and rotation without slipping. Oscillations occur when a restoring force pulls a system toward equilibrium. Simple harmonic motion describes systems where acceleration is proportional to displacement. The period of a mass-spring system depends on mass and stiffness. Consider a mass of 0.5 kilograms attached to a spring with a spring constant of 50 Newtons per meter. The angular frequency is the square root of k over m, which is the square root of 50 divided by 0.5, yielding the square root of 100, or 10 radians per second. The period T equals 2 times pi divided by angular frequency, giving T = 2 times 3.1416 divided by 10, which equals approximately 0.628 seconds. In class exercise: Calculate the moment of inertia of a solid cylinder of mass 4 kilograms and radius 0.2 meters rotating about its central symmetry axis.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Physics Problem Set
description: A graded problem set covering kinematics, dynamics, conservation laws, and rotational mechanics.
content:
Task 1: A ball is thrown horizontally off a cliff that is 45 meters high with an initial speed of 12 meters per second. Calculate the total time of flight and the horizontal distance it travels before hitting the ground. (4 marks)
Task 2: A 10 kilogram crate rests on a rough horizontal floor where the coefficient of static friction is 0.5 and kinetic friction is 0.3. If a horizontal pull of 40 Newtons is applied, find the resulting acceleration of the crate. (4 marks)
Task 3: An elevator with a mass of 500 kilograms ascends from rest with a constant acceleration of 2 meters per second squared for 4 seconds. Compute the total work done by the tension force in the cable during this time interval. (4 marks)
Task 4: A bullet of mass 0.02 kilograms traveling at 300 meters per second embeds itself into a stationary wooden block of mass 1.98 kilograms resting on a frictionless surface. Determine the final velocity of the block-bullet system and the fraction of initial kinetic energy lost. (4 marks)
Task 5: A uniform disk of mass 3 kilograms and radius 0.4 meters rolls without slipping down an inclined plane of height 2 meters. Calculate the linear speed of the disk's center of mass when it reaches the bottom of the incline. (4 marks)
