title: Lecture 1: Wireless Propagation and Channel Characteristics
description: This lecture examines how electromagnetic waves travel through space, analyzing path loss, shadowing, and multi-path fading metrics.
content: Learning objectives: Understand large-scale path loss models and compute received power, and analyze small-scale fading parameters like coherence bandwidth and coherence time. Wireless signals attenuate as they propagate through environments due to distance and obstacles. The free-space path loss model expresses attenuation based on carrier frequency and distance. For example, considering a transmission frequency of 2.4 GHz over a distance of 100 meters, the free-space path loss formula yields approximately 80 dB of attenuation, assuming unity antenna gains. In real urban environments, buildings cause log-distance path loss and log-normal shadowing. Furthermore, multi-path propagation causes frequency-selective or flat fading depending on the relationship between the channel delay spread and the signal bandwidth. Similarly, motion induces Doppler spread, which determines the coherence time of the channel. Engineers use these fading statistics to design robust modulation schemes that combat signal dropouts. In class exercise: Calculate the free-space path loss in decibels for a communication link operating at 5 GHz over a distance of 200 meters, assuming isotropic antennas, and state how doubling the distance impacts the total path loss value.

title: Lecture 2: Cellular Architecture and Multiple Access Techniques
description: This lecture explores cellular system design principles, frequency reuse strategies, and methods for sharing radio resources among users.
content: Learning objectives: Evaluate the trade-offs in cellular cluster sizing and differentiate between various multiple access schemes. Cellular networks divide geographic areas into cells to reuse available frequency spectra efficiently. The cluster size dictates how frequently frequencies can be reused without causing unacceptable co-channel interference. A smaller cluster size packs cells closer together, which increases system capacity per unit area but simultaneously elevates co-channel interference levels for users near the cell edges. To manage this resource sharing, systems employ multiple access techniques. Frequency Division Multiple Access assigns distinct frequency bands to users, while Time Division Multiple Access divides the channel into time slots. Code Division Multiple Access separates users using orthogonal spreading codes across the exact same frequency and time resources. Modern broadband systems utilize Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access, which allocates a grid of orthogonal subcarriers to multiple users simultaneously to maximize spectral efficiency and mitigate inter-symbol interference. Network operators also use cell splitting and sectoring to handle high traffic congestion in urban hotspots. In class exercise: Discuss why decreasing the cluster size from seven to three improves capacity while simultaneously degrading the signal-to-interference ratio at the cell boundary.

title: Lecture 3: Diversity, MIMO, and Link Budget Analysis
description: This lecture covers spatial and temporal diversity techniques, multiple-input multiple-output systems, and practical link budget calculations.
content: Learning objectives: Design reliable communication links using diversity techniques and perform a complete link budget calculation for a cell edge user. Fading severely degrades wireless reliability, but diversity techniques provide independent signal paths to combat this issue. Time and frequency diversity transmit redundant information across different time slots or frequency channels, whereas spatial diversity uses multiple antennas to achieve Maximal Ratio Combining, effectively boosting the signal-to-noise ratio by coherently combining received branches. Multiple-Input Multiple-Output systems extend spatial techniques to deliver multiplexing gains, increasing data rates, or diversity gains, improving link robustness. To ensure a wireless link closes successfully, engineers construct a link budget. The fundamental link budget equation states that received power equals transmit power plus transmitter and receiver antenna gains minus all path, cable, and fading losses. For instance, if a transmitter outputs 40 dBm, adds a 15 dBi antenna gain, subtracts 80 dB of free-space path loss, and subtracts 5 dB of miscellaneous losses, the resulting received power is negative 30 dBm. If this value exceeds the receiver sensitivity threshold, the link is viable. In class exercise: Compute the received power in dBm given a transmit power of 30 dBm, a transmitter gain of 10 dBi, a receiver gain of 5 dBi, and a total path loss of 95 dB.

title: Lecture 4: Evolution of Cellular Generations and Advanced Technologies
description: This lecture traces the evolution of mobile networks from early analog and digital standards up to 5G New Radio and emerging 6G paradigms.
content: Learning objectives: Contrast the technological advancements across 2G, 3G, 4G, and 5G networks, and explain advanced physical layer concepts like beamforming and cognitive radio. Cellular evolution spans from circuit-switched voice in 2G GSM and packet-switched data in 3G UMTS to the all-IP broadband architecture of 4G LTE. 5G New Radio significantly expands capabilities by introducing massive MIMO, millimeter-wave propagation, and network slicing to support diverse applications like ultra-reliable low-latency communication and massive machine-type communication. Looking toward 6G, research focuses on integrating artificial intelligence, terahertz communications, and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces. Alongside these cellular generations, advanced physical layer techniques enhance performance. Cognitive radio allows secondary users to dynamically sense and utilize vacant spectrum bands without interfering with primary license holders. Cooperative relaying uses intermediate nodes to forward signals, extending coverage and creating virtual spatial diversity. Furthermore, beamforming focuses electromagnetic energy in a specific direction using antenna arrays, which is crucial for overcoming high path loss at millimeter-wave frequencies. In class exercise: Identify the three primary use cases defined for 5G networks and explain how network slicing addresses their conflicting performance requirements.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Wireless System Design and Link Analysis
description: This assignment tests students' ability to compute path loss, analyze cellular reuse, evaluate link budgets, and design multi-antenna diversity configurations.
content:
1. Path Loss and Fading: Calculate the free-space path loss at a carrier frequency of 3.5 GHz over a distance of 500 meters. Express your answer in decibels and explain how log-normal shadowing modifies this deterministic value in a suburban environment. (4 marks)
2. Cellular Planning: A cellular operator uses a cluster size of 7. If the cluster size is reduced to 4 to increase capacity, calculate the theoretical percentage change in co-channel reuse distance relative to cell radius, assuming a hexagonal geometry. (4 marks)
3. Link Budget Analysis: A base station transmits with a power of 43 dBm. The transmitter has a 12 dBi antenna gain and 2 dB cable loss. The propagation path loss is 110 dB, and the mobile station has a 0 dBi antenna gain with 1 dB receiver loss. Compute the total received power in dBm and determine if the link succeeds given a receiver sensitivity of negative 75 dBm. (4 marks)
4. Diversity and Combining: Explain how Maximal Ratio Combining improves the signal-to-noise ratio in a Rayleigh fading channel. If two independent diversity branches each provide an average SNR of 10 dB, describe the qualitative impact on outage probability compared to a single-branch system. (4 marks)
5. Advanced Systems: Describe the role of massive MIMO and beamforming in mitigating the severe path loss encountered in millimeter-wave frequency bands for 5G networks. (4 marks)
Submission instructions: Submit your complete solutions as a single PDF document showing all intermediate calculation steps clearly.

title: Lecture 1: Orbital Mechanics and Classification
description: This lecture examines Keplerian orbital laws and classifies satellite systems from LEO to GEO.
content: Learning objectives: understand orbital mechanics principles, calculate round-trip propagation delays, and compare LEO and GEO coverage characteristics. Satellites remain in orbit by balancing gravitational pull and centrifugal force, governed by Kepler's laws which describe elliptical paths and areal velocity conservation. Altitude determines both the coverage footprint and the transmission delay. For a Geostationary Earth Orbit situated at an altitude of 35,786 kilometers directly above the equator, the satellite matches Earth's rotational period, appearing stationary to ground observers. Lower Earth Orbit constellations operate much closer, requiring numerous fast-moving satellites to maintain continuous global connectivity. Consider the signal propagation delay for a GEO link. Given a slant range of approximately 38,500 kilometers from an earth station to the satellite, the one-way propagation time is calculated by dividing distance by the speed of light, yielding roughly 128 milliseconds. Accounting for both uplink and downlink legs, plus transponder processing, the total one-way terminal-to-terminal delay is about 250 milliseconds, resulting in a 500-millisecond round-trip time. In class exercise: compute the free-space path loss in decibels for a LEO satellite operating at an altitude of 550 kilometers using the Ku-band downlink frequency of 12 gigahertz.

title: Lecture 2: Spacecraft Subsystems and RF Link Budgets
description: This lecture details essential satellite hardware components and mathematical formulations for RF link evaluation.
content: Learning objectives: identify core spacecraft subsystems, calculate equivalent isotropically radiated power, and evaluate system figures of merit. A functioning satellite relies on integrated subsystems including power generation via solar arrays, attitude determination and control systems to maintain antenna pointing, and thermal management. The communications payload utilizes transponders to filter, frequency-translate, and amplify incoming signals using high-power amplifiers. To assess transmission viability, engineers compute the link budget balancing gains and losses. Effective Isotropic Radiated Power measures transmitter performance, combining transmitter power and antenna gain in decibels relative to isotropic. On the receiving side, the earth station figure of merit denoted as G/T combines antenna gain with system noise temperature. Let us compute the received carrier-to-noise density ratio. Suppose an earth station has a receiver input power of minus 110 decibel-watts and a system noise temperature corresponding to a noise power spectral density of minus 204 decibel-watts per hertz. The carrier-to-noise density ratio is found by subtracting the noise density from the received power, yielding 94 decibel-hertz. In class exercise: determine the free-space path loss component for an uplink frequency of 14 gigahertz over a distance of 38,500 kilometers using the standard transmission loss formula.

title: Lecture 3: Propagation Impairments and Frequency Spectrum
description: This lecture explores radio frequency allocations and atmospheric attenuation phenomena affecting satellite links.
content: Learning objectives: analyze frequency band allocations from L-band to Ka-band, and quantify tropospheric rain attenuation effects. Satellite communications rely on designated microwave and radio frequency bands. Lower bands like L-band offer broad coverage and minimal atmospheric degradation, making them ideal for mobile and GPS services. Conversely, higher frequency allocations such as the Ku-band and Ka-band provide significantly greater bandwidth capacity, accommodating high-throughput data demands for modern satellite internet services. However, operating at these elevated frequencies introduces severe propagation vulnerabilities, most notably rain attenuation. Water droplets scatter and absorb radio frequency energy, causing rapid signal degradation during heavy precipitation events. For instance, a Ka-band link operating at 30 gigahertz may experience nominal clear-sky atmospheric losses of less than 1 decibel. During a heavy downpour with a rainfall rate of 50 millimeters per hour, specific attenuation can escalate to 12 decibels per kilometer. For a signal traversing a 4-kilometer storm front, the total additional rain fade reaches 48 decibels, requiring robust fade mitigation techniques like uplink power control or adaptive coding. In class exercise: calculate the remaining signal margin if a clear-sky link budget provides a 10 decibel fade margin and rain attenuation suddenly increases by 14 decibels.

title: Lecture 4: Multiple Access Techniques and Applications
description: This lecture investigates channel sharing methodologies and diverse commercial satellite application domains.
content: Learning objectives: differentiate between FDMA, TDMA, CDMA, and DAMA access schemes, and examine modern satellite applications. Because multiple earth stations share a single satellite transponder channel without causing interference, sophisticated multiple access techniques are required. Frequency Division Multiple Access assigns distinct frequency sub-channels to different users. Time Division Multiple Access allocates specific time slots within a continuous frame, requiring precise synchronization. Code Division Multiple Access employs unique spreading codes, allowing all users to transmit simultaneously across the entire available frequency band. Demand-Assigned Multiple Access dynamically allocates channel capacity based on real-time traffic requirements, optimizing transponder utilization for VSAT networks. These transmission architectures enable widespread commercial applications. Satellite television broadcasting distributes high-definition video globally using high-power GEO transponders. Global Navigation Satellite Systems transmit precise timing and ranging codes from MEO constellations to determine geographic coordinates on Earth. Furthermore, modern remote sensing satellites utilize synthetic aperture radar and multispectral optical payloads for environmental monitoring, agriculture, and disaster management. In class exercise: explain why TDMA requires strict guard times between consecutive time slots in a satellite transmission frame.

title: Assignment 1: Satellite Link and Orbital Parameter Analysis

title: Lecture 1: Fundamentals of Optical Waveguiding and Fiber Types
courses: Millimeter Waves and Optical Wireless Communications
description: This lecture introduces the core optical physics behind light propagation, core-cladding refractive indices, and the structural differences between fiber modes.
content:
Learning objectives: Understand total internal reflection and calculate numerical aperture. Differentiate between single-mode and multimode fiber propagation.

Light propagation inside an optical fiber relies strictly on total internal reflection at the boundary between the high-index core and the lower-index cladding. The light-gathering capacity of the fiber is quantified by its numerical aperture, defined mathematically as NA = square root of (n1 squared minus n2 squared), where n1 is the core refractive index and n2 is the cladding refractive index. For instance, consider a step-index optical fiber where the core refractive index n1 is 1.48 and the cladding refractive index n2 is 1.46. Substituting these parameters into the formula gives NA = square root of (1.48 squared minus 1.46 squared) = square root of (2.1904 minus 2.1316) = square root of 0.0588, which yields an approximate numerical aperture of 0.242. This dimensionless metric dictates the maximum acceptance angle for coupling incident light efficiently into the fiber core. Depending on core dimensions and index profiles, fibers operate either as multimode, permitting multiple discrete propagation paths accompanied by modal dispersion, or as single-mode, restricting light to a fundamental transverse path ideal for extremely long-haul telecommunications.

In class exercise: Calculate the numerical aperture of a fiber with core index 1.50 and cladding index 1.47, and discuss how core radius reduction eliminates higher-order modes.

title: Lecture 2: Signal Degradation Mechanisms, Sources, and Detectors
courses: Millimeter Waves and Optical Wireless Communications
description: This session examines transmission impairments including attenuation and dispersion, alongside the active semiconductor devices used to generate and receive optical signals.
content:
Learning objectives: Analyze signal degradation due to fiber attenuation and dispersion limits. Evaluate the operational principles of optical sources and photodetectors.

Signal propagation over extended distances suffers from degradation caused by optical attenuation and pulse broadening known as dispersion. Attenuation measures power loss logarithmically, reaching an optimal transmission minimum of approximately 0.2 dB per kilometer at the 1550 nm wavelength window. For example, if an unamplified fiber optic link spans a total length of 40 kilometers with a uniform attenuation coefficient of 0.2 dB per kilometer, the pure fiber attenuation equals 40 kilometers multiplied by 0.2 dB per kilometer, resulting in 8.0 dB of total power loss. Additional losses from splices and connectors must be added to this baseline figure during system design. To transmit data, semiconductor light sources such as light-emitting diodes and laser diodes convert electrical signals into optical photons, with laser diodes offering superior spectral purity and modulation bandwidth. At the receiving end, PIN photodiodes and avalanche photodiodes convert optical power back into electrical currents, where avalanche photodiode internal gain provides enhanced sensitivity for weak signals.

In class exercise: Determine the total received power in a 60 km link with 0.2 dB/km attenuation and 3.5 dB total connector losses, assuming an input launch power of 0 dBm.

title: Lecture 3: Advanced Transmission Technologies and Optical Networks
courses: Millimeter Waves and Optical Wireless Communications
description: Students will explore how optical amplification and multiplexing expand transmission capacity, alongside architectures for high-speed access networks.
content:
Learning objectives: Describe the operation of erbium-doped fiber amplifiers and wavelength division multiplexing. Compare passive optical networks and legacy transport systems.

As traffic demands escalate, modern networks bypass electronic regeneration bottlenecks by deploying optical amplifiers like the erbium-doped fiber amplifier to boost optical signals directly across a wide spectral band. Simultaneously, wavelength division multiplexing and dense wavelength division multiplexing allow multiple distinct optical carrier signals, each operating at a unique wavelength, to travel simultaneously down a single physical fiber strand, multiplying aggregate system capacity exponentially. In access and metropolitan environments, passive optical networks facilitate fiber-to-the-home infrastructures by utilizing passive splitters to distribute signals efficiently from a central office to multiple residential subscribers without requiring active intermediate power. These optical architectures integrate seamlessly with legacy transport standards like SONET and SDH to guarantee synchronous, highly reliable framing, multiplexing, and robust error management across wide-area enterprise backbones.

In class exercise: Calculate the total capacity of a dense wavelength division multiplexing system carrying 80 individual channels, where each channel operates at an independent data rate of 10 gigabits per second.

title: Lecture 4: Millimeter-Wave Communications and Optical Wireless Systems
courses: Millimeter Waves and Optical Wireless Communications
description: This lecture investigates wireless radio-frequency extensions and free-space optical methods that complement traditional wired fiber infrastructures.
content:
Learning objectives: Analyze millimeter-wave propagation challenges and beamforming techniques for 5G. Evaluate the benefits and constraints of free-space optics and visible light communication.

Expanding connectivity beyond physical fiber leads to the radio-frequency millimeter-wave spectrum spanning from 30 to 300 GHz, which offers massive available bandwidths crucial for high-capacity 5G cellular deployments. However, millimeter waves experience severe path loss, molecular absorption, and high building penetration attenuation, necessitating advanced active antenna array beamforming to concentrate radiated energy dynamically into focused directional paths. Alternatively, optical wireless techniques use light propagating through unguided media to bridge connectivity gaps. Free-space optics establishes high-speed point-to-point terrestrial laser links across outdoor gaps, while visible light communication utilizes modulated illumination from light-emitting diodes to enable indoor data transmission, commonly known as Li-Fi. Both optical wireless paradigms deliver secure, license-free bandwidth but remain vulnerable to physical blockages, atmospheric turbulence, and weather-induced attenuation such as heavy fog.

In class exercise: Compare free-space optics and Li-Fi regarding typical indoor versus outdoor operational ranges, transmitter safety constraints, and susceptibility to ambient light interference.

title: Lecture 1: Distributed Models and Transmission Line Parameters
description: This lecture introduces the distributed element circuit model for transmission lines and derives the fundamental wave propagation properties.
content:
Learning Objectives: Understand the transition from lumped circuits to distributed parameter models. Compute characteristic impedance and propagation constants for lossless lines.

Explanation: At high frequencies, electrical dimensions become comparable to signal wavelengths, requiring voltage and current to vary continuously along the physical route. We model this using per-unit-length series resistance R, series inductance L, shunt conductance G, and shunt capacitance C. For an ideal lossless line where R equals zero and G equals zero, the characteristic impedance simplifies to Z0 equals the square root of L divided by C. Consider a coaxial cable with distributed inductance L equal to 250 nanohenries per meter and distributed capacitance C equal to 100 picofarads per meter. Evaluating the characteristic impedance yields Z0 equals the square root of (250 times 10 to the minus 9) divided by (100 times 10 to the minus 12), which calculates to the square root of 2500, resulting in exactly 50 ohms. This real value indicates that a matched load absorbs all incident power without reflection.

In class: Calculate the characteristic impedance of a lossless transmission line having an inductance of 400 nanohenries per meter and a capacitance of 100 picofarads per meter.

title: Lecture 2: Reflections, Impedance Transformations, and the Smith Chart
description: This lecture examines wave reflections caused by load mismatches and introduces graphical analysis using the Smith chart.
content:
Learning Objectives: Calculate voltage standing wave ratios and reflection coefficients. Utilize the normalized Smith chart for impedance transformations.

Explanation: When a transmission line terminates in a load impedance different from its characteristic impedance, a portion of the wave reflects back toward the source. The voltage reflection coefficient gamma is defined as load impedance minus characteristic impedance divided by load impedance plus characteristic impedance. The voltage standing wave ratio, or VSWR, measures the maximum-to-minimum voltage amplitudes along the line and is expressed as one plus the magnitude of gamma divided by one minus the magnitude of gamma. For example, consider a 50 ohm transmission line connected to a 75 ohm resistive load. The reflection coefficient is (75 minus 50) divided by (75 plus 50), which equals 25 divided by 125, or 0.2. The corresponding VSWR is (1 plus 0.2) divided by (1 minus 0.2), which equals 1.2 divided by 0.8, yielding a value of 1.5. This indicates a minor standing wave pattern due to the slight mismatch. The Smith chart maps the complex impedance plane onto a circular reflection coefficient domain, simplifying manual calculations.

In class: Determine the reflection coefficient and VSWR for a 50 ohm line terminated by a 25 ohm resistive load.

title: Lecture 3: Impedance Matching Networks and Rectangular Waveguides
description: This lecture covers practical matching techniques including quarter-wave transformers and introduces electromagnetic wave propagation inside rectangular waveguides.
content:
Learning Objectives: Design quarter-wave transformers for resistive load matching. Determine cutoff frequencies for rectangular waveguides.

Explanation: Maximum power transfer requires eliminating reflections through impedance matching. A quarter-wave transformer inserts a line section of length lambda divided by 4 with a specific characteristic impedance equal to the geometric mean of the line and load impedances. For instance, to match a 150 ohm resistive load to a 50 ohm main transmission line, the required transformer characteristic impedance is the square root of the product of 50 and 150, which equals the square root of 7500, calculating to approximately 86.6 ohms. Beyond two-conductor lines, high-frequency systems use single-conductor rectangular waveguides. These guide electromagnetic energy via transverse electric and transverse magnetic modes. For the dominant TE10 mode in a rectangular waveguide, the cutoff frequency depends solely on the broader inner dimension a and the speed of light c, defined as c divided by 2a. If dimension a is 3 centimeters, the cutoff frequency is (3 times 10 to the 8) divided by (2 times 0.03), yielding 5 gigahertz.

In class: Calculate the dominant TE10 cutoff frequency for a rectangular waveguide with a width dimension of 4 centimeters.

title: Lecture 4: Antenna Fundamentals and Wireless Link Budgets
description: This lecture details core antenna performance parameters, arrays, and power transmission calculations using the Friis transmission equation.
content:
Learning Objectives: Evaluate antenna parameters such as directivity and gain. Compute received power using the Friis transmission equation.

Explanation: Antennas act as transducers between guided waves on transmission lines and radiating electromagnetic fields in free space. Key metrics include directivity, radiation efficiency, total gain, beamwidth, and polarization. A standard half-wave dipole exhibits an input impedance close to 73 ohms and a directivity of roughly 2.15 decibels. To achieve directional control and beam steering, engineers configure multiple antenna elements into phased arrays, adjusting relative phase shifts between elements to steer the main beam electronically. For end-to-end communication links, the Friis transmission equation calculates received power Pr based on transmitted power Pt, transmitter gain Gt, receiver gain Gr, operating wavelength lambda, and separation distance d. Consider a link operating at a frequency where the wavelength is 0.1 meters over a distance of 1000 meters. If Pt is 1 watt, Gt is 100, and Gr is 100, the received power is 1 times 100 times 100 times (0.1 divided by (4 times pi times 1000)) squared, which evaluates to 10000 times (0.000007957) squared, giving approximately 6.33 times 10 to the minus 7 watts.

In class: Compute the received power when a transmitter delivers 2 watts at a wavelength of 0.05 meters over a distance of 500 meters, with both antenna gains equal to 50.

title: Assignment 1: Comprehensive Transmission Lines and Antennas Analysis
description: This assignment evaluates student competency in transmission line theory, Smith chart applications, waveguide modes, and wireless link budgets.
content:
Task 1: A 50 ohm lossless transmission line is terminated with a load impedance of 30 plus j40 ohms. Calculate the voltage reflection coefficient gamma, its magnitude, and the resulting VSWR. (4 marks)

Task 2: Using the quarter-wave transformer technique, design a matching section to connect a 200 ohm resistive load to a 50 ohm transmission line. Compute the required characteristic impedance and physical length at an operating frequency of 2 gigahertz. (4 marks)

Task 3: A standard air-filled rectangular waveguide has a broad inner dimension a equal to 2.29 centimeters. Determine its cutoff frequency for the dominant TE10 mode and calculate the guide wavelength at an operating frequency of 8 gigahertz. (4 marks)

Task 4: A uniform linear antenna array consists of 8 isotropic elements spaced by half a wavelength. Calculate the required progressive phase shift between adjacent elements to achieve a main beam steering angle of 30 degrees off broadside. (4 marks)

Task 5: Two identical antennas with a gain of 15 decibels each are separated by 2 kilometers in free space at a frequency of 5 gigahertz. If the transmitter outputs 5 watts, calculate the total received power in dBm. (4 marks)

title: Lecture 1: Advanced Real-Time Operating Systems and Low-Power Design
description: This lecture explores deterministic scheduling, memory protection, and energy optimization strategies in resource-constrained environments.
content: Learning objectives include mastering schedulability analysis techniques and implementing robust dynamic power management schemes. In real-time kernels, managing shared resources requires avoiding unbounded priority inversion, a classic failure mode seen in the Mars Pathfinder mission where a medium-priority task preempted a low-priority task holding a mutex required by a high-priority task. Priority inheritance solves this by temporarily elevating the lock holder's priority to match the blocked high-priority task. Consider a scenario where Task L (priority 1) locks a semaphore. Task H (priority 3) preempts L, tries to acquire the semaphore, and blocks. If Task M (priority 2) becomes ready, it will preempt L under standard rules, starving H indefinitely. With priority inheritance, L temporarily executes at priority 3, runs to completion, releases the lock, and drops back to priority 1, allowing H to proceed immediately. Concurrently, low-power design demands aggressive energy profiling. By scaling the CPU clock frequency from 100 megahertz drawing 50 milliamps down to 25 megahertz drawing 10 milliamps during idle periods, systems extend battery life exponentially based on dynamic power equations where power equals capacitance multiplied by voltage squared and frequency. In class exercise: Calculate the effective duty cycle required to keep average current below 15 milliamps given an active current of 60 milliamps and a sleep current of 2 milliamps.

title: Lecture 2: Embedded Linux and Custom Board Support
description: This lecture covers the embedded Linux boot sequence, device tree compilation, and custom kernel driver development.
content: Learning objectives are understanding the transition from bootloader to user space and writing modular character drivers. The boot process initiates with ROM code fetching the secondary program loader, which initializes RAM and loads U-Boot. U-Boot then parses environmental variables, loads the Linux kernel image and device tree blob into memory, and executes the kernel. The device tree abstracts hardware descriptions from C source code, passing board topology, memory maps, and interrupt assignments dynamically. For example, a device tree node for a custom I2C sensor defines compatible strings, register addresses, and interrupt pins so the kernel can match it against registered drivers without recompiling. Kernel drivers interact with user space through file operations structures, exposing control interfaces via the virtual file system. Consider a basic character driver write function that copies a data payload from user space into kernel buffers using copy_from_user to prevent kernel panics from invalid memory pointers. In class exercise: Write a pseudo-code device tree node fragment for a GPIO-connected LED with an active-high polarity configuration.

title: Lecture 3: Hardware-Software Co-Design, FPGAs, and Communication Stacks
description: This lecture examines heterogeneous system-on-chip architectures, hardware acceleration, and robust automotive networking protocols.
content: Learning objectives involve partitioning algorithms between processing systems and programmable logic, alongside configuring industrial communication buses. Utilizing platforms like the Xilinx Zynq combines a dual-core ARM processing system with programmable FPGA logic, enabling hardware-software co-design. Computational bottlenecks, such as matrix multiplication or encryption hashing, are offloaded to custom hardware accelerators implemented via hardware description languages like Verilog, communicating with the processor through AXI bus interfaces using direct memory access. On the networking side, deterministic protocols are mandatory. The Controller Area Network bus utilizes a multi-master, message-based protocol with differential signaling over two wires, CAN high and CAN low, ensuring high noise immunity in harsh automotive environments. Message arbitration is non-destructive and bit-wise, meaning a message identifier with more leading zeros wins bus access. For instance, if Node A transmits identifier binary 0101 and Node B transmits binary 0110 simultaneously, Node B detects a recessive bit while transmitting a dominant bit during the third arbitration bit, immediately backing off and letting Node A transmit uninterrupted. In class exercise: Calculate the bit transmission time for a CAN bus operating at a nominal bitrate of 500 kilobits per second.

title: Lecture 4: Functional Safety, Secure Firmware, and Edge AI
description: This lecture addresses safety-critical compliance, cryptographic boot verification, and deploying machine learning models on microcontrollers.
content: Learning objectives focus on applying coding standards, implementing secure boot chains, and pruning neural networks for embedded targets. Safety standards such as ISO 26262 for automotive and IEC 61508 for industrial applications demand rigorous verification, including strict adherence to MISRA C guidelines which ban unsafe pointer arithmetic and dynamic memory allocation to eliminate undefined behavior. Secure boot ensures firmware integrity by verifying cryptographic signatures using root of trust keys stored in one-time programmable hardware fuses before executing any application code. During an over-the-air update, the bootloader decrypts the incoming firmware image using AES-256 and validates the RSA-3072 signature against the embedded public key; if verification fails, the system falls back to a safe golden image. Furthermore, deploying Edge AI via TinyML brings intelligence directly to microcontrollers. Because an STM32 microcontroller might only have 256 kilobytes of flash memory, floating-point neural network weights are quantized from 32-bit floating-point numbers down to 8-bit integers, reducing model size by a factor of four with negligible accuracy loss. In class exercise: Determine the memory footprint reduction when quantizing a neural network layer containing 10,000 weights from 32-bit floats to 8-bit integers.

2. Write a custom Linux character driver in C that registers a misc device, implements a read method returning a dynamic sensor value, and includes proper error handling for user space copies. (Marks: 4)

title: Lecture 1: Sampled-Data Systems and the Z-Transform
description: This lecture introduces signal sampling, reconstruction via a zero-order hold, and the foundations of the z-transform.
content: Learning objectives: Understand the continuous-to-discrete conversion pipeline, derive pulse transfer functions, and master s-to-z plane mapping. When we implement a control algorithm on a microcontroller, continuous sensor signals must be sampled at discrete intervals T. A sampler converts a continuous-time signal into a pulse amplitude modulated signal, and a zero-order hold maintains the signal level constant between samples. The relationship between the Laplace domain and the z-domain is established through the mapping z = e^(sT). This mapping transforms the left half of the s-plane into the interior of the unit circle in the z-plane. For instance, consider a continuous system pole at s = -2 with a sampling period T = 0.5 seconds. The corresponding discrete pole in the z-plane is calculated as z = e^(-2 * 0.5) = e^(-1), which evaluates approximately to 0.368. Since this value lies strictly inside the unit circle, the discrete-time system remains stable. Selecting an appropriate sampling period is crucial; too fast strains computational resources, while too slow degrades phase margin and can destabilize the loop. In class exercise: Given a continuous pole at s = -4 and a sampling time T = 0.2 seconds, compute the exact location of the z-plane pole and determine if the discrete system is stable.

title: Lecture 2: Discretization Methods and Stability Analysis
description: This lecture covers algebraic discretization techniques and stability criteria for discrete-time control systems.
content: Learning objectives: Apply Tustin and backward Euler discretization methods, and evaluate stability using the Jury test. Transforming a continuous controller into a digital equivalent requires numerical approximations of derivatives and integrals. The backward Euler method replaces the derivative with the backward difference quotient, yielding the substitution s = (1 - z^(-1)) / T. The Tustin method, also known as bilinear transformation, maps the s-plane to the z-plane using the approximation s = (2 / T) * (1 - z^(-1)) / (1 + z^(-1)), which preserves stability properties much better by mapping the entire imaginary axis to the unit circle. Let us discretize a simple integrator with transfer function 1/s using Tustin approximation with T = 0.1. Substituting the expression gives the discrete pulse transfer function H(z) = 0.1 * (1 + z^(-1)) / (2 * (1 - z^(-1))). Simplifying this yields the difference equation output y[k] = y[k-1] + 0.05 * (u[k] + u[k-1]). Stability in the z-plane requires all characteristic equation roots to reside inside the unit circle. For higher-order polynomials, we apply the Jury stability test, which operates analogously to the Routh-Hurwitz criterion in the continuous domain. In class exercise: Discretize a proportional gain controller using the backward Euler method with T = 0.05 and state the resulting difference equation.

title: Lecture 3: Digital PID Control and Integral Windup
description: This lecture details the implementation of digital PID algorithms in position and velocity forms, addressing actuator saturation.
content: Learning objectives: Implement digital PID controllers, formulate velocity-form algorithms, and design anti-windup schemes. Direct digital control systems read sensors, calculate control laws, and drive actuators directly. A positional PID algorithm computes the absolute actuator signal directly at every step. However, positional algorithms can cause large bumps during parameter changes and require explicit handling of the accumulated integral term. To mitigate this, the velocity form calculates the incremental change in the control signal. Consider a digital PI controller in velocity form given by the equation delta_u[k] = Kp * (e[k] - e[k-1]) + Ki * T * e[k], where the current control output is updated as u[k] = u[k-1] + delta_u[k]. When physical actuators reach their maximum limits, the actuator saturates while the controller integrator keeps accumulating error, a phenomenon known as integral windup. This causes massive overshoot when the error eventually changes sign. Anti-windup mechanisms prevent this by freezing the integrator state or employing back-calculation when saturation is detected. In class exercise: Calculate the next control output u[k] given Kp = 2.0, Ki = 0.5, T = 0.1, u[k-1] = 5.0, e[k] = 1.2, and e[k-1] = 1.0.

title: Lecture 4: Advanced Digital Design and Industrial Networks
description: This lecture explores deadbeat control synthesis and the architecture of industrial computer control networks.
content: Learning objectives: Design deadbeat controllers for finite settling time, and understand SCADA, DCS, and industrial communication protocols. Deadbeat control is a discrete-time design technique that forces the closed-loop system error to reach zero in the minimum possible steps following a step change. Unlike continuous controllers striving for asymptotic stability, deadbeat design places all closed-loop poles at the origin of the z-plane. For a first-order plant, this yields an aggressive controller that achieves exact tracking in a single sample period, though it often demands excessive control effort and high inter-sample ripple if the plant has unmodeled high-frequency dynamics. Scaling up from single loops to plant-wide automation involves industrial computer control systems. Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition systems handle centralized monitoring and data logging over wide areas, while Distributed Control Systems manage critical, time-sensitive loops across local processing nodes. These hardware nodes communicate reliably via deterministic industrial fieldbuses and Ethernet networks. In class exercise: Explain why a deadbeat controller might cause physical actuator wear on a real DC motor and propose a mitigation strategy.

1. Consider a continuous plant with transfer function G(s) = 5 / (s + 5). Select a suitable sampling period T based on the system time constant and compute the discrete pulse transfer function G(z) assuming a zero-order hold. [4 marks]
2. Transform the lead compensator C(s) = (s + 2) / (s + 10) into the discrete domain using the Tustin bilinear transformation method with T = 0.1 seconds. State the resulting difference equation clearly. [4 marks]
